shows.title: Vestiges
shows.description:
Alexandra Lopez Iglesias works in paper and clay, two materials she treats less as substances to be shaped than as stand-ins for skin — things that absorb, scar, and record whatever touches them. Vestiges, her solo show at Keystone Art Space, is built from sculptures that use cutting, piercing, tearing, stitching, and scraping to leave visible traces of contact on their surfaces, insisting throughout that these forms aren't metaphors for bodies so much as bodies themselves.

Lopez Iglesias, who was born in Ciudad Juárez and now works in Los Angeles, has built her practice around a fascination with materiality that reportedly goes back to childhood — an early, almost compulsive attention to the textures of the built world around her. That sensitivity to surface and touch carries through into paper especially, a medium she has also taught as a papermaking process in academic settings, giving her sculptures an unusual technical rigor beneath their raw, worked-over look.

The show takes place in Keystone Art Space's daylit gallery inside the artist-studio complex in Lincoln Heights — a fitting context for work that's this tactile and process-driven. It's a short run, just over a week, so this is very much a catch-it-while-you-can show for anyone interested in sculpture that treats the body's history of being touched, held, or neglected as its actual subject matter.

venue.name: Keystone Art Space
venue.about: Keystone Art Space is a large working-artist complex in the Lincoln Heights/Cypress Park area of Los Angeles, housing more than fifty individual studios for painters, illustrators, sculptors, photographers, jewelers and designers. Within the warehouse, Keystone Gallery mounts rotating group and solo exhibitions and the space regularly opens to the public for a biannual Open Studios event, giving visitors direct access to tenant studios alongside curated shows. Past programming has included group exhibitions built around music, writing, photography and international artist exchanges, often organized by the resident community or visiting curators. The facility is led by Director Melanie Mandl, with Mark Harvey serving as Keystone Gallery Co-Director. Keystone functions less as a commercial gallery than as a hybrid studio building and public exhibition venue supporting a broad, multidisciplinary Los Angeles art community.

shows.title: Revington Arthur: A Retrospective
shows.description:
Beverly Art Boutique's standing exhibition gathers work spanning the long career of Revington Arthur (1908–1986), an American painter, educator, and print-world organizer who trained at the Art Students League under teachers including Arshile Gorky and George Luks. The gallery draws on a large estate holding of more than 700 original works, letting visitors trace Arthur's evolution from nature studies and figurative American-scene painting toward the hard-edged, primary-colored geometric abstraction he developed in the 1950s and after, much of it inflected by the era's fascination with space travel and technology.

What's on the walls ranges from early lyrical landscapes and lifestyle scenes to the later non-objective compositions built from interlocking geometric shapes — canvases that read as a personal register of mid-century American formal experimentation, made by a painter who spent decades teaching as much as exhibiting. Arthur also founded the Chautauqua Art Center and co-founded the New England and National Print Show, and his paintings entered the collections of institutions such as the Brooklyn Museum, the Walker Art Center, and the Albright-Knox (now Buffalo AKG).

This is a small, retail-adjacent gallery rather than a curated museum show, but it functions as an accessible, walk-in survey of an under-recognized figure whose geometric abstractions are otherwise scattered across regional museum vaults and auction houses. Worth a stop for anyone curious about the lesser-known corners of postwar American abstraction, especially the pieces where Arthur's Cold War-era geometric language is at its most confident.

shows.title: Global Fugitivity: UCLA New Wight International Biennial Exhibition 2026
shows.description:
Every two years, UCLA's graduate art students curate the New Wight Biennial by traveling to studio programs around the world and selecting work from a rising generation of MFA candidates. This edition, organized by student-curators Sabaah Folayan, tunmi da silva, and Luke Francis Austin, takes "fugitivity" as its theme — art-world shorthand for practices of escape, refusal, and self-determination that run through Black studies and diaspora theory.

Expect a wide-ranging, multimedia group show: the biennial has historically mixed painting, video, sculpture, and installation from art schools across North America and abroad, giving Los Angeles audiences an early look at artists who haven't yet had gallery representation. Because it's juried through studio visits rather than an open submission, the show tends to have a sharper, more considered feel than a typical student exhibition.

The New Wight Gallery is a teaching space as much as an exhibition venue, tucked into the ground floor of the Broad Art Center just north of the Murphy Sculpture Garden, and this biennial is one of the few times each cycle that its program looks outward past UCLA's own graduate cohort.

shows.title: Dead Relatives
shows.description:
Superchief Gallery's Halloween-season group show rounds up more than 80 artists working in tattoo flash, lowrider culture, punk photography, printmaking, oil painting, airbrush and graffiti for a three-week run timed to close on Halloween itself. Expect the gallery's usual maximalist hang — walls packed salon-style, multiple murals, and a run of pop-up events throughout October rather than a single quiet opening.

The work leans hard into outlaw and underground iconography: skulls, saints, lowrider pinstriping, anarchist slogans and DIY punk ephemera show up across paintings, prints and mixed-media pieces from artists like Bradley Riot, Monte, Andrew Murga and Oscar Rodriguez. It's less a curated thesis show than a communal gathering of LA's tattoo, street-art and DIY scenes, in keeping with Superchief's long-running mission of building a scrappy, anti-elitist alternative to the gallery mainstream.

Superchief has spent over a decade cultivating exactly this kind of crowd — accessible price points, a rotating cast of emerging and outsider artists, and a calendar built around themed group shows rather than solo museum-style presentations. Dead Relatives fits that mold: a loud, dense, unapologetically populist show best experienced in person during one of its October events.

shows.title: William Carson
shows.description:
William Carson paints with a geologist's patience, building his abstract compositions out of dense, mineral-like layers of pigment that recall banded rock, weathered stone and the slow accretion of sediment. This solo show at Nüart's Bergamot Station location gathers new paintings that continue his long-running conversation between geological process and human perception — surfaces that look excavated as much as painted.

Carson has shown with Nüart across both its Santa Monica and Santa Fe locations for years, including a recent two-person pairing with Emilio Lobato earlier this year. This solo outing gives his work room to breathe, letting the shifts in his palette — from warm ochres to cooler veins of white and grey — read as a kind of visual stratigraphy. It's a quiet, materially rich show for anyone drawn to painting that rewards close, slow looking.

venue.name: Nüart Gallery
venue.about: Nüart Gallery was established in Santa Fe at the start of the 21st century and has grown into a 3,000-square-foot, ten-room space on Canyon Road showing contemporary abstract and figurative art. Over more than two decades it has mounted upwards of 250 solo and group exhibitions, introducing many artists to the U.S. market and shipping worldwide. In 2023 the gallery expanded with a second 3,000-square-foot location at Bergamot Station in Santa Monica, extending its reach into the Los Angeles market. The program represents around 40 artists working locally and internationally, with works held in major museum collections such as MoMA, LACMA, the Getty, and the Tate Modern. The gallery also carries limited inventory from blue-chip artists.

shows.title: HAGS (Have a Great Summer)
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page displays this group show (including a second hang, "HAGS II") as current with no exhibition dates published; local press reported it "opened in July" 2026 and remains on view with no closing date given.
shows.description:
HAGS — gallery-speak for "Have a Great Summer" — is Bruce Lurie Gallery's rotating summer group exhibition, bringing together the roster of emerging to mid-career artists the gallery has built its reputation on: painters, photographers, sculptors and mixed-media artists working across pop art, street art and abstract minimalism. It's a survey-style hang rather than a single-thesis show, meant to give a broad look at who the gallery represents.

This is the gallery's first extended summer show since relocating to its current Santa Monica Boulevard space after the January 2025 Palisades fire destroyed its previous location of five years. The larger, higher-ceilinged space gives the gallery more room to show sculpture and larger-scale paintings side by side, and owner Bruce Lurie — a veteran dealer whose career traces back to 1980s New York, including a stint assisting Leo Castelli — has used the show to reintroduce the gallery to its still-loyal Palisades collector base.

Because it's a group show without a single curatorial thread, visitors should expect variety: bold pop-inflected imagery, street-art-adjacent mixed media, and photography sitting alongside more painterly abstraction. It functions less as a statement show and more as a snapshot of where the gallery's program stands as it works to reestablish itself.

shows.title: Fragile Eternity
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page displays this show as current (image uploaded August 2026); no opening or closing dates are published on the venue's own site.
shows.description:
Larisa Safaryan works in an unlikely material: eggshell. Born in Yerevan, Armenia and now based in Los Angeles, she hand-carves and stacks eggshell forms into sculptural and relief works that turn one of the most fragile substances imaginable into a meditation on strength, renewal and impermanence. "Fragile Eternity" at Bruce Lurie Gallery gathers this body of work, pairing the delicacy of the medium with a surprisingly durable, load-bearing physical presence.

Safaryan is self-taught, having come to art after two master's degrees in psychology and public management, and her lack of formal art training shows up as genuine invention rather than deference to convention — she treats the egg's curved surface as a canvas for ideas about rebirth and the passage of time. The results read alternately as devotional objects and as still lifes, each piece balancing precariousness against permanence.

For a gallery that has spent the last year rebuilding after losing its Pacific Palisades space to fire, a show built around fragility and resilience carries an obvious resonance. It's a quieter, more intimate counterpoint to the gallery's bigger group exhibitions, worth a visit for the sheer technical strangeness of the material alone.

shows.title: Live · Nude · Girls
shows.dates_note: Gallery's own homepage presents this as its current exhibition ("...is one of our most popular shows!") but publishes no opening or closing dates.
shows.description:
"Live Nude Girls" is Tracy Park Gallery's recurring flagship group show, a curated survey of nude photography, painting and sculpture that the Malibu Colony Plaza gallery describes as one of its most popular exhibitions. Rather than a single artistic statement, it's a wide-ranging look at how contemporary artists on the West Coast approach the nude figure — from straightforward figurative photography to more painterly and sculptural interpretations of the body.

The show draws on a roster of over a dozen artists working in different mediums, including photographers Vic Huber, Jamie Nelson and Matt Seidel, painters Reisha Perlmutter and Steve Shaw, and sculptor P.K. Comstock, among others. That range gives the exhibition an anthology feel: some works lean toward classical figure study, others toward more stylized or conceptual treatments of nudity and the body.

Tracy Park Gallery has operated in Malibu since 2004, building a program around supporting emerging and mid-career artists alongside a broader roster of West Coast talent, and this show is emblematic of that mixed, crowd-pleasing approach — accessible, visually direct work aimed at Malibu's gallery-going foot traffic rather than a tightly curated thesis show.

shows.title: Charles Arnoldi
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as an "Upcoming Exhibition" with only "Opening Reception October 2" given; no closing date published yet.
shows.description:
Michael Kohn Gallery opens its fall season with a show devoted to Charles Arnoldi, the Los Angeles painter and sculptor who first made his name in the early 1970s fusing raw tree branches into wall-relief constructions before turning that same physical, material-forward sensibility toward vibrantly colored abstract paintings.

Arnoldi came up alongside the Light and Space and Finish Fetish generations in LA but took a rougher, more improvisational path — his work has always been about direct construction rather than illusion, whether he's laying branches into a panel or building up layered, jigsaw-like fields of color on canvas. Now in his eighth decade of practice, with pieces in the permanent collections of MoMA, the Whitney, and the Art Institute of Chicago, he remains one of the defining figures of postwar Los Angeles abstraction.

Details on the exhibition's full scope weren't yet published at the time of writing, but the gallery's announcement image — a close-up of dense, gestural color — suggests a survey of his recent, energetically worked paintings. Worth checking back on for confirmed dates and checklist as the opening approaches.

venue.name: Michael Kohn Gallery
venue.about: Michael Kohn Gallery was founded in 1985 by Michael Kohn, opening first on Robertson Boulevard in West Hollywood before relocating in 2014 to its current home on North Highland Avenue in Los Angeles. The gallery presents historically grounded exhibitions alongside a contemporary program, linking postwar West Coast movements such as Beat assemblage, Light and Space, and California Minimalism to newer generations of painters and sculptors. It represents senior West Coast figures including Lita Albuquerque and Sharon Ellis, oversees the estates of Bruce Conner, Wallace Berman, Joe Goode, and Martha Alf, and maintains a growing roster of emerging and mid-career artists working internationally, spanning painting, assemblage, and mixed-media practice with an emphasis on figuration, identity, and material experimentation.

shows.title: The Brockman Gallery: Los Angeles, 1967–1990
shows.description:
Founded in South LA by brothers Alonzo and Dale Brockman Davis in the wake of the Watts Rebellion, the Brockman Gallery became one of the most important incubators for Black artists in Los Angeles for over two decades — a space that gave early support and exhibitions to David Hammons, Suzanne Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, and many others before their careers took off. This is billed as the first large-scale museum exhibition dedicated to that history, and it treats the gallery itself as a work of art: a community-built institution as significant as anything shown inside it.

With more than sixty artworks across media plus archival material — photographs, ephemera, correspondence — the show reconstructs both the visual output the Davis brothers championed and the social infrastructure they built around it. It's an essential corrective for anyone whose picture of 1970s and '80s LA art history skips over the galleries and spaces that operated outside the traditional (and traditionally white) commercial circuit.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
venue.about: LACMA is the largest art museum in the western United States, holding some 155,000 objects spanning 6,000 years of global art history. It traces its roots to the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, and Art (1910) and became an independent institution in 1961, opening on Wilshire Boulevard in 1965. The campus has grown through additions including the Anderson/Art of the Americas Building, the Pavilion for Japanese Art, BCAM, and the Resnick Pavilion, culminating in the 2026 opening of the Peter Zumthor-designed David Geffen Galleries. Located on Wilshire Boulevard in the Miracle Mile, LACMA presents rotating exhibitions across its global collection alongside public programs, education initiatives, and community partnerships, including a gallery at Charles White Elementary School.

shows.title: You'll Find Yourself
shows.description:
Raymond Argumedo works in small, glowing panel paintings that fuse cosmic imagery with figures rendered like devotional icons — halos of stars, mystic flora, and celestial light standing in for interior states. His pieces feel closer to relics than illustrations, mixing pop-surrealist polish with a genuinely spiritual undertow.

"You'll Find Yourself" gathers new acrylic-on-panel works that continue Argumedo's ongoing series of cosmic portraits, where figures dissolve into or emerge from swirling galaxies and botanical patterning. The paintings are compact and jewel-like, meant to be studied up close, and the show continues Thinkspace's longstanding support of the artist within its New Contemporary program.

Expect a tightly hung solo presentation in the gallery's West Adams space, with an opening reception on September 12 giving visitors a chance to meet the artist directly.

venue.name: Thinkspace Projects
venue.about: Thinkspace Projects is a Los Angeles gallery in the West Adams District, founded in 2005 by Andrew Hosner and L. Croskey. Since its start the gallery has built an international reputation as a leading voice for the New Contemporary Art Movement, a lowbrow-descended, figurative and pop-culture-inflected strain of art that emerged on the West Coast in the 1990s. Thinkspace represents artists ranging from emerging to established, and has expanded beyond its own space to curate exhibitions with museums and partner galleries in cities such as Berlin, Hong Kong, London, New York, Detroit, Chicago and Honolulu. It also produces murals worldwide and works with organizations like POW! WOW! and RAD Napa. The gallery describes itself as artist-focused, family-run, and committed to bridging street-level and institutional art contexts.

shows.title: Dark Energy
shows.description:
"Dark Energy" is a solo turn for the artist KCN, whose title points toward the invisible forces that shape and pull at things — a fitting theme for work that operates in the New Contemporary vein Thinkspace has championed since 2005, where surreal imagery and pop-cultural iconography stand in for psychological and cosmic undercurrents.

Details on the specific body of work are still emerging as the show opens, but the gallery has slotted it into its September lineup alongside solo presentations from Raymond Argumedo and Alex Achaval, suggesting a run of dream-logic, figure-based painting across the space.

Visitors can catch the artist in person at the September 12 opening reception, part of a full night of new exhibitions across the gallery's West Adams space.

shows.title: A Place To Live
shows.description:
Alex Achaval paints quiet, moody oil interiors and landscapes where light does most of the emotional work — a lamp-lit room, a hazy field, a figure caught in the moment just before or after something happens. His palette leans toward dusk tones, and his compositions favor stillness over spectacle, closer to painterly memory than narrative illustration.

"A Place To Live" gathers new framed oil-on-canvas works that continue this sensibility, with titles like "Unspoken," "Weather Eye," and "Collective Notion" hinting at the show's interest in the emotional weather of domestic and interior space — the idea of "place" as psychological as much as physical.

The show opens alongside several other September solo presentations at Thinkspace, with a shared opening reception on September 12 giving visitors a chance to see Achaval's newest paintings in person.

shows.title: Spotlight on Local Creatives (with Ella-V-Ella | Juliette Toma | Daisy Murray)
shows.description:
Session Seventeen brings together three artists — Ella-V-Ella, Juliette Toma, and Daisy Murray — for a group presentation of new work.

As with prior Fresh installments, the show functions as a snapshot of the current local scene rather than a single unified theme, letting each artist's individual approach stand on its own within a shared gallery space.

It opens September 12 with a joint reception alongside the gallery's other new September exhibitions, making for a full night of openings at the West Adams space.

shows.title: Visual and Verbal Cognition
shows.description:
Theodore Svenningsen has spent decades working across two parallel bodies of work, and this solo show at Wonzimer puts them side by side. One strand is textual: paintings and works on paper that use plain, everyday language — about money, belonging, mortality, and the isolation of not fitting in — as both content and formal material, letting words sit as flat, declarative objects on the surface. The other is the "Structures" work, spanning series like the Primitive Structures and Anxious Objects, murky black-and-white compositions of half-recognizable forms glimpsed behind grids and architectural scaffolding, closer to apparition than illustration.

Svenningsen's background is unusual for a painter: he trained in philosophy at UCLA to the doctoral level before finishing an MFA in painting at Otis, and that history shows in the show's operating premise — that verbal and visual cognition are two distinct, only partially overlapping ways of knowing, and that putting both types of work in one room lets each throw the other's limits into relief. It's a quiet, cerebral exhibition, more interested in doubt and ambiguity than resolution, from an artist who has had pieces enter MoMA's collection while remaining a relatively under-the-radar figure in Los Angeles.

venue.name: Wonzimer
venue.about: Wönzimer is an independent gallery in Lincoln Heights, Los Angeles, founded by Swiss artist Alaïa Parhizi and American entrepreneur Aidan Nelson. Its German name, meaning "living room," reflects the founders' aim to create an intimate, home-like exhibition space rather than a conventional white-box gallery. The gallery represents thirteen artists working across painting, sculpture, and mixed media, and presents both solo shows and thematic group exhibitions that bring together established and emerging voices, including international projects. Beyond exhibitions, Wönzimer runs W.A.R.P., an artist residency program with on-site studios, and hosts artist talks, poetry readings, music, film screenings, and other cross-disciplinary programming. The space includes a hidden bookshelf leading to a lounge, continuing the gallery's living-room concept. Wönzimer has operated from earlier locations in Koreatown and downtown Los Angeles before settling in its current Lincoln Heights space.

shows.title: Lights Form Action!
shows.description:
Ashoke Chhabra brings a body of sculptural lamp and light work to ace/121's project space in this solo show, built around illuminated forms that read as much as small-scale sculpture as they do functional objects. The gallery's own preview material centers on a detailed octopus-form lamp base, suggesting an exhibition rooted in playful, biomorphic silhouettes rendered in glowing, tactile materials.

Chhabra's practice sits at the intersection of craft object and gallery sculpture, and this show continues ace/121's pattern of championing Glendale-based and regional artists working in unconventional materials. Expect a tightly installed single room hung and lit to let each piece's glow do double duty as both artwork and ambient installation lighting.

Given the gallery's intimate scale, this is a good show for viewers interested in lighting design, ceramics, and assemblage as much as traditional painting or sculpture — a reminder that the ace/121 artist colony continues to support offbeat, materials-driven practice in the shadow of the YMCA parking structure.

shows.title: The Blab! Show
shows.dates_note: Venue's future-exhibitions page says only "COMING SEPTEMBER 12," no closing date published; this is Copro's long-running annual Blab! Show group exhibition curated by Monte Beauchamp.
shows.description:
Every September for over two decades, Copro Gallery has handed its walls over to Monte Beauchamp, the founder and longtime editor of the underground graphics-and-comics annual Blab!, for a sprawling group show pulling together the illustrators, painters, and printmakers who've populated the magazine's pages. Past editions have drawn seventy-plus contributing artists at a time, mixing lowbrow and pop-surrealist veterans with newer names working in painting, sculpture, and illustration.

Given the gallery's track record, expect a dense, maximalist hang: darkly funny, technically virtuosic work that sits at the crossroads of fine art and outsider comics culture, the kind of show that rewards slow looking piece by piece. The gallery hasn't yet published this year's full checklist or an official title beyond "coming September 12," but based on two decades of precedent this is effectively the newest edition of the Blab! Show, one of Bergamot Station's most anticipated recurring events.

Copro's two exhibition spaces in the back corner of Bergamot Station have long been ground zero for LA's pop-surrealist and dark-illustration scene, and this annual show remains one of the best single snapshots of that world working today.

shows.title: Wayne Thiebaud
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this show only as "Fall 2026," with no specific opening or closing dates published.
shows.description:
Leslie Sacks Gallery devotes its fall program, alongside "Focus Female," to a concentrated selection of prints by Wayne Thiebaud, the Sacramento painter best known for his creamy, confectionary still lifes of cakes, pies, and diner counters. This presentation focuses on his graphic work: lithographs from the 1994 portfolio "The Physiology of Taste" — images of desserts, bistro sketches, and cafe scenes rendered with Thiebaud's signature thick, sugary color and long cast shadows — alongside an etching from his 1979 "Recent Etchings II" series.

Thiebaud's prints translate the same appetite for everyday American subject matter that made his paintings famous into the more intimate, linear language of lithography and etching. The rooster, sorbet, and dessert-tray subjects on view here carry the same deadpan affection for ordinary abundance that has made his work instantly recognizable for over half a century.

It's a modest, connoisseurial show rather than a blockbuster, well suited to Leslie Sacks' longstanding specialty in modern and postwar works on paper, and a good opportunity to see Thiebaud's printmaking practice up close rather than through reproductions of his more famous paintings.

shows.title: Last time I met you the world was a different place
shows.description:
Joakim Ojanen returns to Richard Heller Gallery with a new body of glazed stoneware sculptures, paintings, and works on paper populated by his signature cast of soft, lumpy, big-eyed figures. The Swedish artist, who trained in ceramics almost by accident after abandoning an illustration degree in Stockholm, has spent the last decade building a visual vocabulary that reads like a comic strip crossed with a folk-art shrine — hunched boys, sad dogs, and blobby creatures rendered with a craftsman's touch for glaze and surface.

This is Ojanen's latest solo outing with the gallery that has shown his work in Los Angeles since his 2016 debut, and the title alone hints at the wistful, slightly melancholic humor that runs through his practice: figures that seem to be quietly working through loneliness, awkwardness, and the strangeness of getting older, even as the forms themselves stay playful and inviting. Fans of his earlier shows here, like "A Show for the Lonely Distant Baby Souls" and "Year of the Dog," will recognize the emotional register even as the specific characters and glazes are new.

Worth seeing for anyone drawn to the intersection of ceramics and cartooning — Ojanen's work sits comfortably alongside artists like Ryan Travis Christian and Eric Croes, also on Heller's roster, who share an interest in turning offbeat, intimate feeling into tactile, handmade objects.

venue.name: Richard Heller Gallery
venue.about: Richard Heller Gallery is a contemporary art space in Santa Monica, California, run by director and owner Richard Heller with associate director Barry Belkin. Established in 1997, the gallery presents a program centered on figurative and narrative painting, drawing, ceramics, and photography by an international roster of emerging and mid-career artists. Known for supporting artists early in their careers—several of whom went on to significant critical attention—the gallery has built a reputation for eclectic, often humor-inflected exhibitions spanning painting, sculpture, and works on paper. Located at Bergamot Station, the gallery regularly participates in major art fairs and has been the subject of numerous press features on its artists in publications such as the Los Angeles Times, Juxtapoz, and Artillery.

shows.title: Museum-in-Residence at Hama
shows.dates_note: Venue page says the exhibition is "Beginning June 15th, 2026" and describes it as "an exhibition project that unfolds over the next three months," with no exact closing date published.
shows.description:
For its Museum-in-Residence project, Venice Heritage Museum has taken its archive out of its own building and installed it inside Hama Sushi, the Windward Avenue restaurant that has anchored that stretch of Venice since 1979. The presentation builds on portraits and ephemera already displayed at the restaurant, adding new material — a sweeping 1913 panorama of the Venice lagoon shot from roughly the same vantage as the traffic circle where Hama now sits, a contemporary aerial photograph by Venice-based artist Hso Hkam that mirrors that historic view, and reproduction ephemera like a 1939 Venice Mardi Gras matchbook.

The show is paired with excerpts from VHM's oral history project, including interviews with Hama's own owner Esther Chaing, longtime surfboard shaper Guy Okazaki, and other longtime residents — turning a casual dinner spot into an informal annex of the museum's collection.

It's a low-key but genuinely site-specific idea: using a business that has itself become part of Venice's history as a vehicle for looking at the neighborhood's disappearing landmarks and community memory. Worth a look for anyone eating at Hama over the summer, though visiting hours are the restaurant's own dinner hours rather than the museum's weekend hours.

shows.title: Textiles as Monument
shows.artist: Suchitra Mattai, Jagdeep Raina, and Swapnaa Tamhane
shows.dates_note: Venue page says "Now Open" with no published closing date; opening celebration event was held Aug 8, 2026.
shows.description:
Three artists of South Asian descent — Suchitra Mattai, Jagdeep Raina, and Swapnaa Tamhane — use textile as a way of building memorials to people history has left out of its monuments. The Fowler commissioned new work from each artist, made in dialogue with the communities the pieces honor, turning cloth, thread, and weave into what the museum's own framing calls counter-monuments: forms that claim public memory without bronze or stone.

The result is an exhibition that plays against expectation — where a monument is usually rigid, permanent, and singular, these works are soft, layered, and collaborative. Expect large-scale hangings, dyed and braided fiber installations, and pieces that draw directly on South Asian craft traditions like weaving, embroidery, and quilting, reworked into contemporary sculptural forms that fill the gallery volume rather than sitting flat on a wall.

It's a strong pairing with the Fowler's broader interest in objects, migration, and whose stories get preserved — worth seeing alongside the museum's other current shows on Ifugao rice culture and the afterlives of African art objects, all of which circle similar questions about memory, possession, and who gets to be remembered.

shows.title: subterranean convergence
shows.description:
Commissioned by Clockshop, LaRissa Rogers's subterranean convergence turns a stretch of LA State Historic Park — once the site of the Southern Pacific River Station — into a fragmented, simulated railroad. Chinoiserie-style tracks cast in tabby (a lime-and-shell concrete) carry reproductions of more than fifty objects contributed by community members and institutions across Los Angeles and New Orleans, each chosen for its personal or historical weight. The piece traces the old "Sunset Limited" line that once connected those two cities, using the train as a metaphor for the migrations — forced, hopeful, and everything in between — that shaped both places during Reconstruction and the Great Migration.

Rogers, a sculptor and University of Virginia professor whose work has shown at Documenta 15 and the Wattis Institute, built the project around a score for live performance, developed with collaborator Michelle Sui, that activates the installation on opening day. Because the work sits outdoors on public parkland rather than behind a gallery door, it's as much a piece of civic infrastructure as it is sculpture — visitors can walk the tracks and handle the archive of cast objects long after the opening weekend's performance has ended.

venue.name: Clockshop at Los Angeles State Historic Park
venue.about: Clockshop is a nonprofit arts organization based in the Elysian Valley/Frogtown neighborhood of Los Angeles, founded in 2004 by filmmaker Julia Meltzer. Rather than running a conventional exhibition space, it commissions artists to create site-specific, experimental projects on public land, especially along the LA River at the Bowtie Parcel and at Los Angeles State Historic Park, in long-term partnership with California State Parks. Its program combines artist commissions, publications, and public programming with environmental and community advocacy, focusing on equitable green space, local history, and the relationship between artists, communities, and public lands throughout the LA River watershed.

shows.title: California Visionaries: The Lives and Legacies of Walt Disney and Hubert Eaton
shows.description:
Walt Disney and Forest Lawn founder Hubert Eaton might seem like an odd pairing for an exhibition, but the two men — both transplants from Missouri who built California institutions steeped in fantasy, showmanship, and death-adjacent spectacle — were genuinely close, with Disney serving as an honorary pallbearer at Eaton's funeral before dying himself a few months later. This show, timed to the 60th anniversary of both men's deaths, traces that friendship through Disneyland attraction concept art, sheet music from the Disney Music Legacy Library, and previously unseen photographs pulled from the Forest Lawn archive.

It's a strange, specific bit of California history — two men who each turned death, memory, and myth-making into a business, and who apparently recognized something of themselves in each other. For families who already associate Forest Lawn with its famous stained glass and Great Mausoleum murals, this is a lighter, more pop-cultural entry point into the museum's collection.

shows.title: 75 Years: Art Finds a Home at Forest Lawn
shows.dates_note: Venue page gives only "Opening September 19, 2026" for this exhibition; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Marking 75 years since the Hall of Crucifixion-Resurrection opened in 1951 (with the Forest Lawn Museum following in 1952), this archival exhibition digs into the institution's own history rather than showing outside artists. Expect never-before-exhibited photographs from the museum's archive, remastered audio from the original Hall of the Crucifixion program, and artworks that haven't been on view in nearly a decade — plus attention to overlooked figures, like first museum director Mary Hunt, who built the place from what started as a memento shop.

For a museum best known for its enormous history paintings and stained glass, this is a chance to see the institutional backstory instead — how a cemetery's gift shop grew into a sculpture collection and, eventually, a public art museum with free admission.

shows.title: Idols In Bloom
shows.description:
Rafael Megall's paintings work a rich, jewel-toned register somewhere between religious icon and botanical still life, with figures and floral motifs rendered in the flattened, gilded planes of devotional art. Idols In Bloom leans into that vocabulary directly, pairing the language of veneration with the fragility and excess of flowers in full bloom — worship and decay held in the same frame.

This show looks to be a good showcase for Megall's particular fusion of the sacred and the decorative, ornate surfaces built up with the patience of an icon painter but aimed at very contemporary anxieties about beauty and impermanence.

venue.name: Mek Contemporary
venue.about: Mek Contemporary is a Los Angeles–based gallery presenting contemporary artists working across disciplines and geographies. The program pays particular attention to work engaging memory, migration, displacement, place, identity, and cultural inheritance, favoring artists with distinctive approaches to form, material, and image. The gallery emphasizes close attention to each artist and body of work, developing focused exhibitions and publications alongside sustained relationships with artists, collectors, institutions, and audiences. Through this approach, Mek aims to extend conversations sparked by the work beyond the exhibition space itself, treating each show as part of an ongoing dialogue rather than an isolated event.

shows.title: REALMS
shows.dates_note: Venue page says the exhibition is "opening Friday, September 4 at 7 PM - 10 PM"; no closing date is published yet.
shows.description:
Devin Flynn has spent decades in the margins between disciplines — as an animation director behind the web series Y'all So Stupid, as the bassist in the band Pixeltan, and as a longtime collaborator of underground comics figure Gary Panter. REALMS is his most defined gallery presentation yet, pulling together years of drawing, collage, and mixed-media work into a survey that traces how his visual language has developed alongside his music and animation careers rather than separately from them.

The show's centerpiece is a new series called OTOFORMS, which folds a literal sound element into the work — a fitting move for an artist whose visual and musical practices have always been intertwined. MutMuz is supplementing the new pieces with a survey of earlier works on paper, posters, prints, and drawings upstairs, plus a program of animation screenings running throughout the exhibition, so visitors get both the new focused body of work and the decades of drawing that led up to it.

Flynn's LA roots run deep: he came up in the city's 1980s graffiti scene under the tag RELM before moving into animation and music, and the show's title nods to that history as much as to the idea of his output existing across separate creative "realms." It's a fitting subject for MutMuz.

shows.title: Collective Noise
shows.dates_note: Venue's own site lists Jun 12–Aug 21, 2026 for this exhibition page, but the homepage still marks it "ON VIEW NOW" with "EXTENDED!" as of early Sept 2026 and gives no new closing date, so end_date is left open pending a later pass.
shows.description:
Krikor Tchay is a self-taught Armenian-American painter working in mixed media — acrylic and spray paint built up in dense, layered passages that read somewhere between graffiti, abstract expressionism and pop collage. Collective Noise gathers a body of his recent canvases that circle around vulnerability, desire and resilience, using clashing color and gestural mark-making to visualize emotional static: the "noise" of competing feelings that most people carry quietly.

The paintings on view lean into contrast — hard graphic edges next to loose drips, saturated color fields interrupted by scratched-in text and figures — a language Tchay has been refining since his 2018 "Tangled" series. It's unpretentious, autobiographical work made by an artist who has built his following largely through Instagram and word of mouth rather than gallery representation, which makes this extended run at Eye For Sound (a small storefront space run in partnership with a neighborhood coffee shop) a good chance to see a substantial group of his paintings together in person rather than as scattered studio posts.

shows.title: Mangia! The Evolution of Italian Food in the United States
shows.dates_note: IAMLA's site lists this as an open, current exhibition (linked under "Upcoming Exhibitions" but confirmed live via press coverage as of summer 2026); the museum's own pages publish no exact opening or closing date, though outside press reports it running "through summer 2027." Saved with dates left open pending a later confirmation pass.
shows.description:
Mangia! traces how Italian immigrants reshaped what America eats, using the tools of a history museum rather than an art gallery: vintage advertising, restaurant ephemera, photographs, and everyday objects pulled from nearly a century of Italian American food culture. The show is organized thematically, opening with the poverty and hardship that drove waves of immigration between 1876 and 1914 before following those immigrants' recipes and enterprise into the mainstream of American life.

What makes the exhibition compelling is its attention to specific, often overlooked through-lines: the Americanization of dishes like fettuccine alfredo and spaghetti and meatballs, the rise of espresso culture, and the surprising Italian American roots behind household names like Planters Peanuts and Tropicana. A wall of restaurant t-shirts, hats, and other memorabilia gathered from close to 100 eateries nationwide gives the show a scrapbook intimacy, while a large national map lets visitors flag historic Italian restaurants of their own.

Housed in the Italian Hall, a 1908 landmark building in the heart of the old Little Italy, IAMLA is a small but earnest museum, and this show plays to its strengths: it's not trying to be comprehensive art history, but a warm, well-researched piece of cultural storytelling about identity, migration, and the dinner table. It's an easy, free, and worthwhile stop for anyone curious about the immigrant history baked into American food culture.

venue.name: Italian American Museum of Los Angeles (IAMLA)

shows.title: UAC: The Never Again Now — Child | Separation | Detention | Resistance
shows.dates_note: Venue's future-exhibitions page lists the show "Coming August 29, 2026" with an opening reception that date; no closing date is published anywhere on the site.
shows.description:
Oscar Magallanes turns the Museum of Social Justice's galleries over to the bureaucratic language of immigration enforcement, borrowing the federal designation "unaccompanied alien child" for a show that traces what that acronym does to real families from southern Mexico and Central America now living in the Westlake neighborhood a few blocks from the museum's Olvera Street home. Expect a mix of original artworks, installation elements, and archival material — the kind of assemblage-driven, documentary approach Magallanes has used elsewhere to connect present-day immigration policy to older histories of displacement and cultural erasure.

The show is less an art exhibition in the white-cube sense than a community history project with visual art as its anchor: it's paired with documentary screenings, workshops, and public discussions meant to extend the conversation past the gallery walls. That civic-minded, testimony-based approach fits squarely with the museum's mission of presenting Los Angeles history from the perspective of the poor, immigrants, and other marginalized groups.

Worth seeing for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are responding to immigration detention and family separation policy, and for the museum's rare willingness to let a single, sustained community project fill its whole exhibition program rather than mounting a survey show.

shows.title: Play Date: Toys by Artists
shows.description:
Curated by Axel Wilhite, this group show takes its cue from a landmark 1975 exhibition that asked artists to design toys rather than art objects, and runs with the idea across seven decades and seventy-odd contributors. Chris Burden's original Spyder-Man, made for that 1975 show, anchors the exhibition alongside newly commissioned toys by a wide swath of Los Angeles's sculptors, painters, and ceramicists — from veterans like Peter Shelton, Tony Berlant, and Gwynn Murrill to younger names working in wood, clay, and cast metal.

The premise is playful but not slight: toys are treated here as a serious testing ground for ideas about scale, function, and imaginative possibility, the same terrain sculpture occupies but with a built-in permission to be funny, tactile, and a little absurd. Expect a dense salon-style hang of small, handled objects rather than precious wall-bound pieces — something closer to a toy chest than a white cube.

Wilhite has also produced a limited-edition "five-suit" poker deck as an exhibition catalog, with each artist's toy represented as a card — a nice structural joke that doubles as a keepsake and a curatorial index of the show. Two artist talks during the run (September 19 and October 3) will bring some of the 69 participating artists into the gallery to discuss the work directly.

shows.title: Doyle Lane: Master of Clay
shows.description:
Doyle Lane spent decades in Los Angeles quietly redefining what a clay vessel could be, and this retrospective — the first devoted to him at a major museum — finally gives his career room to breathe. The show spans from his compact, glossy "weed pots," sold for years at studio-craft fairs and flea markets, to the room-sized tile murals he made on commission for Southern California architects like William Pereira and Welton Becket, several of which have rarely if ever left the buildings they were made for.

What comes through is Lane's obsession with glaze as a painter's material: surfaces mottled and pooled with color in ways that put him in conversation with the era's abstract painters as much as with fellow ceramicists like Peter Voulkos. The exhibition doesn't shy away from the harder context either — Lane worked for decades as a Black artist largely excluded from the gallery system that celebrated his white contemporaries, and much of this material is being publicly seen for the first time thanks to years of research with his family, friends, and collectors.

With more than a hundred objects on view, including the Huntington's own 18-foot Mutual Savings and Loan mural, this is as complete a picture of Lane's practice as has ever been assembled, and a chance to see a genuinely under-recognized California modernist get his due.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Laura Aguilar: Day of the Dead
shows.description:
This is the lesser-seen half of a two-part rotation devoted to Laura Aguilar, the San Gabriel Valley-raised Chicana photographer who spent her career photographing the body — often her own — with unusual candor. Where the museum's spring presentation focused on Aguilar's landscape self-portraits, this fall rotation turns to an earlier body of work: black-and-white photographs made between 1984 and 1992 documenting Día de los Muertos celebrations across Los Angeles.

Rather than staged portraiture, these images read as documentary work from inside a community — artists, couples, and families active in the city's Chicano art scene, photographed at altars and gatherings that Aguilar clearly had ongoing access to. It's an early, less-exhibited chapter of her career, and a useful complement to the more widely reproduced nude self-portraits that later made her name.

Drawn from recent acquisitions from Aguilar's estate, the show is part of the Huntington's expanded commitment to Aguilar's work following her death in 2018, and it rewards visitors who want to see a fuller, more community-oriented side of an artist mostly known for photographing herself alone in the landscape.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Venerated
shows.dates_note: Venue's Galleries homepage lists this as its current exhibition with no closing date given; the artist's own site records an opening reception of March 5, 2026, but the gallery page still presents the show as current as of September 2026.
shows.description:
Mark Steven Greenfield has spent five decades reworking the visual language of Christian icon painting — gold leaf, halos, devotional gaze — to canonize Black historical figures whom official history mostly left out. "Venerated" extends his ongoing Halo series with new gold-leaf-and-acrylic panels on wood, each one a portrait-sized "icon" of a resistance leader, folk saint, or survivor drawn from the 1400s through the 1800s.

The individual paintings are modest in scale, roughly 20 by 16 inches, but the iconographic treatment gives each subject an outsized presence: Francisco Manicongo, prosecuted by the Portuguese Inquisition in 1591 in what the gallery describes as the first legal action in the Americas targeting gender nonconformity, appears alongside other figures whose stories connect directly to today's fights over transgender rights, reproductive rights, and voting rights.

Greenfield, an L.A. native who studied under Charles White at Otis and later ran the Watts Towers Arts Center, has built his reputation on this kind of long game — patiently building bodies of work (Incognegro, Black Madonna, Halo) that use appropriated religious form to force a reckoning with erasure. This is a compact but pointed entry in that project, and the Boone Gallery's small scale suits the intimacy of the paintings.

venue.name: Boone Family Art Gallery, Pasadena City College

shows.title: Ecognosis
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as its current show with only an opening date shown ("April 25th"); no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Ecognosis pairs two artists whose work turns an eye toward the entanglement of body and landscape, human systems and ecological ones. Julia Bennett has built a body of work around scorched and shifting terrain in past shows at this gallery, and here her paintings continue to treat the earth as a live, volatile surface rather than a backdrop. Mary Gortani's contributions lean into more intimate, tactile registers, with surfaces and forms that suggest organic growth, decay, and repair happening in close-up.

Installed in One Trick Pony's small Western Avenue storefront, the show relies on proximity — visitors move through a tight run of paintings and objects that reward slow looking. The title, borrowed from ecological philosophy's notion of "ecognosis" (a felt, embodied awareness of one's entanglement with a larger ecosystem), signals the show's ambition to make viewers physically conscious of interdependence rather than just intellectually aware of it.

It's a fitting project for this scrappy, artist-friendly gallery. Worth a visit for anyone tracking younger LA painters working through questions of nature, materiality, and site.

shows.title: Christopher James James
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as current, alongside Ecognosis, with only an opening date shown ("April 25th"); no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Running concurrently with Ecognosis in One Trick Pony's compact Western Avenue space, this self-titled exhibition gives Christopher James James a solo showcase within the gallery's tight quarters. The installation photographs show a cluster of paintings and objects hung salon-style, characteristic of the gallery's approach to giving younger, under-the-radar artists a full-throated presentation despite limited square footage.

One Trick Pony has carved out a niche as an East Hollywood project space that favors direct, unpretentious presentation over slick production — exhibitions here tend to feel like studio visits more than white-cube events. This show continues that spirit, offering a concentrated look at one artist's current output without curatorial padding.

Details on James's practice are thin on the gallery's own materials, which is in keeping with the gallery's low-key, discovery-oriented ethos — worth checking out in person if you want to get ahead of an artist before wider attention catches up.

shows.title: People in Movies
shows.dates_note: Heavy Manners' own homepage banner reads "PEOPLE IN MOVIES: Audrey Densmore Solo Exhibition On View Now!" with no opening or closing date published.
shows.description:
Audrey Densmore is an LA-based puppeteer, builder, and illustrator trained at CalArts, known for her work fabricating puppets and props for film and television (including stints associated with the Bob Baker Marionette Theater world and various stop-motion and puppetry productions around town). "People in Movies" is her solo show at Heavy Manners.

Given Densmore's background, expect the show to lean into her cinematic and puppetry roots — likely illustration, character studies, or handmade objects that read like stills from movies that don't exist. Heavy Manners' gallery wall is a small, intimate space, well suited to this kind of dense, craft-driven personal work rather than a sprawling installation.

venue.name: Heavy Manners Library
venue.about: Heavy Manners Library is a lending library, gallery, and bookstore focused on artist-made and independently published media. It offers an alternative to costly formal art education by making self-published books, zines, and other overlooked or out-of-print materials accessible to the public. Members can borrow items with a library card, while visitors may browse the collection during open hours. Alongside its lending program, Heavy Manners hosts events and exhibitions in its gallery, theater, and classroom spaces, aiming to give emerging artists opportunities to share work and established artists room to experiment, with an emphasis on community-oriented educational programming.

shows.title: I Know You Are But What Am I?
shows.artist: Rebecca Brown, Edgar Bryan, Paul Davies, Kyle De Lotto, Ryan Dobrowski, Sylvia Fernandez, An Hoang, Raina Lee, Jake Longstreth, Jared McGriff, Dave Muller, Jude Pauli, Cindy Phenix, Aaron Michael Skolnick, Kansas Smeaton, and Joe Sola
shows.dates_note: La Loma's page gives only the opening reception date (July 16) and describes it as its "summer show" with no published closing date.
shows.description:
La Loma's summer group show crams sixteen artists into the small Highland Park gallery, working the seam between comedy and unease. Jake Longstreth contributes his signature deadpan paintings of exurban nowhere-places — strip malls and parking lots rendered with the solemnity of landscape painting. Joe Sola's "Birdhouse" applies his conceptual, deadpan humor to a primary-colored birdhouse painting that pointedly doesn't function as a birdhouse should. Jude Pauli's ceramic totems build their own wobbly internal logic, while Kansas Smeaton's lush, Rococo-tinged paintings recast who gets to be the subject of opulence and desire.

The through-line is a kind of genre-bending mischief: paintings that behave like objects, ceramics that behave like paintings, sculptures that edge into architecture. Ryan Dobrowski's and Cindy Phenix's large canvases anchor the show's more painterly, atmospheric register, while Jared McGriff's cosmologically-scaled figure painting pulls the show toward something more meditative. It's a loose, generous survey rather than a tightly argued thesis show — a good entry point if you want a cross-section of what's happening in LA painting and ceramics right now.

venue.name: La Loma Projects
venue.about: La Loma Projects is a Los Angeles gallery founded in 2019 by Kirk Nelson, which began informally in his home near La Loma Road before expanding in 2021 into a more formal exhibition space on North Figueroa Street. The gallery has built long-term relationships with a roster of established and mid-career artists while continuing to introduce new voices. Its program favors idea-driven exhibitions exploring the relationship between objects and meaning alongside painterly, handmade work attentive to humor, domesticity, materiality, and the natural world. La Loma also maintains an appointment-only annex space in Pasadena and regularly presents artists at international art fairs.

shows.title: Everyone's a Winner
shows.dates_note: D2Art's site lists the opening as "Sat Sep 20th" with no closing date published.
shows.description:
Tony Brown works across painting, sculpture, ceramics, and works on paper, taking apart and reassembling found materials until they read as something new. His paper-collage inlays are built as much from removal as addition — cutting away and layering fragments of an original image so that absence becomes a compositional tool rather than an accident.

"Everyone's a Winner" brings together a body of these deconstructed, reworked pieces at D2Art, the La Brea Avenue gallery and art-consultancy space run by Danica Derpic. Expect a mix of scale and material — stripped, painted, and reshaped surfaces sitting alongside more sculptural and ceramic pieces — that rewards close looking at how Brown builds and un-builds an image.

D2Art operates as both a public gallery and a working art-rental business for film and television production, so the space itself has an unusually hands-on, workshop feel. This show is a good chance to see Brown's process-driven work in a gallery context rather than as a backdrop.

shows.title: SomeLove in 8 x 10
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as the current show under the header "AUGUST EXHIBITIONS" with no exact opening or closing dates published; page confirms it is currently on view.
shows.description:
Jinyoung Park's first solo exhibition at Lee & Lee Gallery pairs forty-five small-format photographs with short handwritten texts, all built around the uniform intimacy of an 8-by-10 frame. Park trained in visual design and photography before working in broadcast production, and that background shows in the way these images are staged: quiet, carefully lit glimpses of ordinary domestic moments rather than grand landscapes or portraits.

The through-line is explicitly devotional — Park frames the everyday as evidence of a larger love, and the accompanying texts (in Korean) read like diary entries or prayers rather than didactic captions. It's a modest, sincere body of work.

Visitors should expect an unassuming, contemplative show best taken slowly — the pleasure here is in the accumulation of small, personal images rather than any single showstopping piece.

shows.title: Anida Yoeu Ali: The Buddhist Bug
shows.description:
Anida Yoeu Ali's long-running performance project centers on a single, unforgettable image: a nearly 328-foot saffron-colored creature with a human face wrapped tightly in cloth at one end and a pair of bare feet at the other. Photographs and video document the Bug's journeys through Cambodian markets, temples, rice paddies, and city streets, where it disrupts the everyday with something that reads as equal parts folklore, spectacle, and quiet protest.

Ali, who was born in Battambang and raised in Chicago as a Cham Muslim of Khmer, Malay, and Thai descent, built the character out of her own layered identity. The robe-like orange skin nods to Buddhist monastic dress, while the fabric framing the Bug's face recalls the hijab, a deliberate collision of religious and cultural signifiers that keeps the work from settling into any single reading. It's a costume, a performance vehicle, and a kind of wandering monument to displacement and belonging all at once.

For its VPAM debut, the exhibition brings together large-scale photographic prints, video projections, and documentation of the Bug's public performances across Southeast Asia, along with the suit itself. It's a rare chance to see a major durational performance-art project translated into a museum installation, and a fitting reopening statement for a museum that has spent the summer preparing new galleries.

venue.name: Vincent Price Art Museum
venue.address_detail: East Los Angeles College, Building S1

shows.title: Energetic Connections: The Ki Paintings of Yoshio Ikezaki
shows.description:
Yoshio Ikezaki works with sumi ink, water, and handmade washi paper, letting the interaction of liquid and fiber do much of the compositional work. He grinds his own ink and makes his own paper, and his paintings read less like fixed images than records of a physical event — ink blooming, pooling, and drying according to forces he guides but doesn't fully control. The results range from stormy, atmospheric landscapes to near-abstract fields of tone that hover between painting and residue.

The show's title points to the Japanese concept of ki, the life-force energy that Ikezaki treats as both subject and method: he describes using water as an active agent to steer the ink, so that intention and accident collide on the paper's surface. Trained in traditional Japanese papermaking and steeped in Buddhist practice from childhood, Ikezaki has spent decades translating ideas of emptiness and impermanence into a distinctly physical, process-driven body of work.

Shumei Hall Gallery, a small nonprofit space in Pasadena devoted to art with a contemplative bent, is a fitting home for this material — expect a quiet, meditative installation of ink paintings that reward slow looking.

shows.title: A People's Legacy: Public Memory, Social Justice and the Great Wall of Los Angeles
shows.dates_note: Venue page says the show opened March 19, 2026 and is listed as ongoing with no closing date given
shows.description:
This exhibition traces the origins and ongoing life of the Great Wall of Los Angeles, the half-mile mural along the Tujunga Wash that Judith F. Baca began in 1976 with hundreds of collaborating youth, artists and historians. Rather than presenting the mural itself, the show works as a kind of archival companion piece, using photographs, documents and design material to walk through Baca's formation as an artist and educator and the community-based process that produced the wall.

A throughline of the installation is Baca's period of study at the Taller Siqueiros in Cuernavaca, where she absorbed the compositional and collective-authorship principles of David Alfaro Siqueiros. The exhibition argues, convincingly, that this training is what gives the Great Wall its distinctive visual cohesion despite being painted by so many different hands over so many decades.

For anyone who has driven past the Great Wall without stopping, this is a good excuse to actually learn what's in it and why it was built the way it was. It's a modest-scale show with an outsized subject, presented in SPARC's own Durón Gallery in Venice, just a few miles from the mural itself.

shows.title: Naomi
shows.dates_note: Venue's own page is headed "NOW SHOWING" for this exhibition but publishes no opening or closing date.
shows.description:
Naomi is a suite of drawings by Sophie Roessler centered on a single recurring figure: a dancer at the storied Hollywood dive bar Jumbo's Clown Room. Roessler traces, collages, and reworks the same image obsessively, turning her subject into something between a muse and a mirage — a study in how repeated looking (and repeated digital exposure) shapes desire and identity.

The drawings mix girlish ephemera — swans, bunnies, tattoo flash, airbrushed haze — with the language of parasocial fixation, treating the accumulation of imagery itself as a kind of diary. It's a show about spectatorship as much as it is about the woman being looked at, pulling in ideas from Jungian anima theory and feminist film criticism without ever feeling like an academic exercise.

This solo show is a good example of why it's worth checking in on Leiminspace regularly.

shows.title: Activist Artist
shows.dates_note: Venue page lists this outdoor exhibition as running "April 2025 - Ongoing rolling basis" with no closing date given
shows.description:
Activist Artist is an open-air group exhibition on the fence and lot art space SPARC calls SPARCin' LOTS, next to its Venice Blvd headquarters. SPARC invited artists to respond to the 2024 presidential election and the political climate that followed, and the result is a rolling, outdoor salon of protest paintings, prints and mixed-media pieces that gets new additions on an ongoing basis.

The tone is direct and unambiguous: work by Ralph D'Oliveira, Olivia Ramos, Karen Fiorito, Teresa Greve Wolf, FLACO, sandra tamkin, Jason Kartez and Cesar Garcia takes on immigration policy, reproductive rights, police violence and the erosion of democratic norms, often with wall-text statements from the artists themselves explaining what's at stake in each piece. Karen Fiorito's screenprinted portrait of Shirley Chisholm and FLACO's Greco-Roman-inspired mosaic on abortion access are among the standouts.

Because it's outdoors and free to see any time, it functions less like a conventional gallery show and more like a public billboard for dissent.

shows.title: Sunset at the Pacific's Edge
shows.description:
A small-scale group show built entirely around one subject: the sun going down over the Pacific. The California Art Club's rule for this exhibition caps every painting at 108 square inches total, so the works read as intimate, jewel-like studies rather than grand vistas — a format well suited to plein air painters chasing fast-changing light.

Two dozen or so member artists contribute oils, pastels, and acrylics depicting sunset light along the Southern and Central California coast, from surfers catching last waves at Oceanside to misty harbor mornings in Santa Barbara and glowing cliffs at Laguna Beach. Recurring motifs of silhouetted figures, backlit clouds, and warm-to-cool color transitions tie the group together even as each artist's hand and palette stays distinct.

Installed in the same modest San Marino gallery as the club's other rotating shows, this is a good chance to see a concentrated survey of contemporary plein air and traditional realist painting practice in Los Angeles, with an opening reception planned for the show's first evening.

venue.name: California Art Club Gallery at The Old Mill
venue.address: 1120 Old Mill Road, San Marino, CA 91108

shows.title: iris yirei hu
shows.description:
Iris Yirei Hu's solo exhibition arrives at Official Welcome as the gallery's final announced show of the year, following on the heels of two concurrent September openings. Hu works across weaving, painting, and sculptural installation, often drawing on ancestral craft techniques and personal mythology to build environments that feel handmade and lived-in rather than simply displayed.

Based on the studio and installation imagery the gallery has released, expect richly textured surfaces — woven and painted elements combined into hybrid objects that blur the line between textile and picture. Hu's work frequently engages themes of lineage, care, and the body, translating intimate or domestic materials into larger-than-life forms that invite close, almost tactile looking.

For a gallery that has spent 2026 spotlighting artists working in fiber, paint, and process-driven abstraction (Ann Thornycroft, Sarah Ippolito, Diane Briones Williams among them), Hu's show promises to be a fitting, tactile capstone — well worth the trip to La Fayette Park Place once it opens in late October.

shows.title: Church and State
shows.description:
Todd Gray has spent the past decade building large-scale photographic assemblages that layer images of European palaces, museums, and churches against sites tied to the transatlantic slave trade on the West African coast, interspersed with pictures of Black cultural icons pulled from his own archive. The circular, sculpturally framed photographs, often stacked in clusters, ask viewers to hold two histories of Western wealth and Black cultural production in the same frame at once.

This exhibition at The Brick pairs three of those assemblages, including two new mural-scale works, with an unusual amount of biographical material: photographs and ephemera from Gray's own life as a teenager who shot The Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin around Los Angeles before becoming Michael Jackson's personal photographer and, eventually, a CalArts-trained fine artist alongside classmates like Mike Kelley and Carrie Mae Weems. Seeing the commercial photography and the gallery practice side by side clarifies how much one fed the other.

Organized by the Brick's director Hamza Walker, the show doubles as the occasion for a forthcoming book of an extended interview between the two, who have worked together since Walker's 2008 exhibition at the Renaissance Society. For anyone who has only encountered Gray's assemblages in isolation, this is a rare chance to see the life that produced them.

shows.title: The Poetics of Place
shows.description:
ATLA's fall two-person show pairs Vamba Bility and Shun Kadohashi under the banner of "place" — how a maker's surroundings, materials, and inherited traditions surface in the work. ATLA has built its program around craft-forward practices that bridge East and West, and this exhibition continues that thread, setting two artists with very different vocabularies in dialogue inside the gallery's small Kenmore Avenue storefront.

Without a full checklist yet available, the specifics of medium and scale are still emerging, but ATLA's track record — recent solo shows built around ceramics, textile, and object-based work — suggests visitors should expect handmade, materially attentive pieces rather than large-scale spectacle. The gallery's exhibitions typically reward a slow look at surface and technique.

This is ATLA at its most typical: an intimate, appointment-friendly gallery in a converted Los Feliz-adjacent storefront, showing artists who take the long view on making things by hand.

venue.name: ATLA
venue.about: ATLA is a contemporary gallery in Los Angeles focused on craft-based work, particularly ceramics, that brings together East and West artistic traditions. Its program explores themes of intersectionality, history, heritage, politics, and identity through skilled making. The gallery's name references the Japanese word 'atara,' evoking the sorrow of losing something beautiful, and reflects ATLA's commitment to celebrating endurance and resisting disposability of work, experience, and attention. The gallery operates from a space on Kenmore Avenue and presents exhibitions featuring a wide roster of ceramic and multidisciplinary artists.

shows.title: Between and Beyond
shows.description:
Kat Hutter's new body of paintings runs on a single formal idea pushed hard: a meandering, unbroken line that loops and knots its way across the canvas, sectioning off flat fields of color into geometric, stained-glass-like compartments. The palette swings between moody darks and hot, candy-bright combinations — pink and green in one canvas, blue and violet in another — so the works read as much through color harmony as through the drawn line itself.

Hutter has described the paintings as a record of navigating a full emotional range, from joy to anxiety, using the same constant gesture throughout. That tension between a fixed method and a shifting emotional register is what gives the show its charge — these aren't illustrations of feelings so much as diagrams of trying to hold contradictory ones at once.

It's a tightly-focused solo outing at Face Guts, Tim Biskup's project space and open studio in Verdugo Village, which has built a reputation for championing exactly this kind of graphic, color-driven painting alongside Biskup's own work.

shows.title: Disembodied by Intelligence
shows.description:
Carmen Amengual's installation reworks a piece she first made in 2024 — a multichannel video originally commissioned by Prospect Art — into a denser meditation on how political power colonizes language. Words like "life," "freedom," and "memory" get staged and restaged in short, deliberately crude scenes that borrow from black-light theater, shadow puppetry, and early cinema, a visual language chosen precisely because it's technologically modest and a little absurd against such heavy subject matter.

Two suspended sculptures extend the video's argument into physical space: mobile forms built from ceramic, wood, and leather strap spelling out cursive phrases — "Dismembered by Capital" and "Disembodied by Intelligence" — that double as research objects, since Amengual built them after studying medieval instruments of restraint and discipline. The body implied throughout is left ambiguous on purpose, read as individual, collective, or civic depending on where you're standing.

Amengual is an Argentine-born artist and researcher (CalArts MFA, Whitney ISP alum) whose work usually starts from buried archival material — here, an unrealized documentary project tied to the 1970s Third World Filmmakers Meetings feeds into her broader interest in how resistance movements get remembered, forgotten, and rewritten. This is dense, research-driven work, well suited to Winslow Garage's small, artist-run project space in Silver Lake, which has spent years championing exactly this kind of politically engaged, materially inventive installation art.

shows.title: TOMATÂ
shows.description:
Tomatâ du Plenty was best known as the wild-eyed frontman of The Screamers, the confrontational synth-punk band that never released a studio album yet became one of the most mythologized acts to come out of the late-1970s Hollywood punk scene. Less known is that he was also a working visual artist, and this show at MutMuz Gallery — housed in Mark Mothersbaugh's Chinatown space — gathers a cross-section of that largely unseen body of work.

The exhibition brings together multimedia paintings on wood, works on paper, photographs, and ephemera pulled from du Plenty's archive, giving a sense of an artist whose visual language was as unruly and theatrical as his stage persona. Expect handmade, collaged, and painted objects rather than a polished studio practice — the kind of work that reads as diary, prop, and provocation all at once, in keeping with the anarchic performance-art roots he shared with Screamers bandmates and the broader Hollywood underground of that era.

For longtime devotees of The Screamers and LA punk history this is a rare chance to see du Plenty's actual hand at work rather than just photographs of his performances; for newcomers it's an entry point into a figure who looms large in punk mythology but left behind surprisingly little visual record until now. The show runs through mid-September in MutMuz's compact Chung King Road storefront.

shows.title: The 35th Annual Exhibition of Korean-American Calligraphy Association: Journey of Ink Fragrance
shows.description:
This annual showcase brings together thirty-nine members of the Korean-American Calligraphy Association for the group's 35th consecutive exhibition at KCCLA, themed "Journey of Ink Fragrance." Calligraphy (seoye) occupies a distinct place in Korean visual culture, treated historically as inseparable from painting and poetry, and this show carries that tradition into the Los Angeles diaspora community, mixing classical brushwork with contemporary compositional choices.

Expect large-scale hanging scrolls and framed works built around ink, paper, and brush — some rendering classical Chinese-character poetry, others incorporating Hangul in more experimental, painterly arrangements. As a juried association show rather than a single-artist statement, the range of hands and styles on view gives a useful cross-section of how first- and second-generation Korean-American calligraphers are keeping the discipline alive outside Korea.

It's a brief, free, walk-in show on the second floor of the Korean Cultural Center, and a good entry point for anyone curious about Korean calligraphy who wouldn't otherwise encounter it in an LA gallery context.

venue.name: Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles (KCCLA)
venue.about: The Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles (KCCLA) is a public cultural institution operated by the Republic of Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, located in the Miracle Mile district at 5505 Wilshire Blvd. It functions as a hub for Korean heritage and contemporary culture in the United States, housing a library, a permanent heritage exhibition hall, a second-floor art gallery, an auditorium (Ari Hall), and a media arts wall. Programming spans traditional and contemporary Korean art exhibitions, film screenings, Korean-language classes, and community-oriented shows organized with Korean-American arts associations, alongside field trips and cultural workshops for schools and the public.

shows.title: Small Hours
shows.artist: Cyprien Gaillard, Farah Al Qasimi, Kang Seung Lee, P. Staff, Torbjørn Rødland
shows.description:
Small Hours brings together five artists whose work has each, in different ways, built substantial international reputations — Cyprien Gaillard, Farah Al Qasimi, Kang Seung Lee, P. Staff, and Torbjørn Rødland — for a closing-week group show at Canary Test. The title points to a liminal register: works that operate in dim, in-between light, whether emotional, temporal, or literal.

Given the range of practices involved — Gaillard's found-footage and site-specific interventions, Al Qasimi's staged photography, Lee's work threading queer history and diasporic memory, Staff's visceral moving image and sculpture, Rødland's uncanny studio photography — the show reads less as a thematic thesis than as a curated conversation between artists who share an interest in atmosphere over statement.

This show is a good entry point for anyone who hasn't caught the space before — it's only up through September 2, so this is a last-chance visit.
