hours: Check site for current gallery hours

shows.title: Lying, but only a little
shows.description:
Mark Acetelli and Kristi Head both paint landscape, but neither is much interested in where anything actually is. Acetelli's skies and horizon lines run hot — fire-colored, overexposed, closer to afterimage than observation — while Head builds her scenes out of half-remembered gardens and roadside glimpses, flattened and rearranged until they stop pointing to any real place. Hung together in Interval's single room, the two bodies of work trade in a similar sleight of hand: pictures that look like they're describing somewhere specific until you try to find it on a map.

That's the premise behind the show's title. These aren't vedute or plein-air records; they're landscapes built from feeling and residue rather than topography, which makes the question of whether an image can be "factually false and emotionally exact" feel like the right one to ask while standing in front of them. Acetelli's paintings lean toward big, saturated atmospheric events — fire in the sky, light that doesn't seem to come from any single sun — while Head's are quieter and more domestic in scale, full of flowerbeds and waysides that feel plucked from a half-forgotten errand.

It's a tightly focused two-person show in a small gallery, which suits the work: there's room to look at a handful of paintings slowly rather than scan a crowd of them. For anyone interested in how Los Angeles painters are currently handling landscape after decades of Light and Space and plein-air traditions, this is a useful, unpretentious data point — less about any particular view of the city than about what's left of landscape painting once you take the place out of it.

shows.title: Uncanny Marvels
shows.artist: Ashley Fisher, kAt Philbin, Kate Lawrence, Michael Flores, Nora Thompson, and Scum Choir
shows.dates_note: FOLD's own site currently features "Uncanny Marvels Artists" with on-sale original works by these six artists on its homepage; no opening/closing dates are published, consistent with FOLD's rolling, sell-off-the-wall gallery model.
shows.description:
Uncanny Marvels gathers six Los Angeles-based artists working in a shared register of dark whimsy — skulls, moths, bats, ghouls, and other creatures of the night rendered with a pop-surrealist, lowbrow sensibility. The show leans into the macabre-but-cute aesthetic that has long defined FOLD's programming, timed to the Halloween season but drawing on each artist's ongoing body of work rather than a single themed commission.

Ashley Fisher's fruit bat and Michael Flores's ghoul figures push cartoon horror into something affectionate, while Kate Lawrence pairs a skull with a moth in a small memento-mori still life. kAt Philbin and Scum Choir bring a looser, more illustrative hand, and Nora Thompson's piece carries the bright, slightly sardonic optimism that recurs across her prints and zines. Together the works read less like a single curated thesis and more like a snapshot of the current DTLA pop-surrealism scene that FOLD has quietly supported since 2012.

FOLD occupies an unusual niche: it is a working retail shop and a gallery at once, selling original work directly off its walls above The Last Bookstore. That means this is a changeable, non-ticketed show best seen in person while the pieces are still up — the gallery restocks the wall as works sell, so the roster of "Uncanny Marvels" artists is a living snapshot rather than a fixed checklist.

shows.title: Untethered Journey
shows.description:
Kiki Smith's first Los Angeles solo show in three decades arrives at Jeffrey Deitch as a joint presentation with Pace Gallery, bringing together three-plus decades of her sculpture alongside works on paper and multimedia wall pieces. The show spans the full range of materials Smith has used to render the human body — bronze, beeswax, papier-mâché, polyester resin, fiberglass — and includes signature early pieces that made her reputation in the early 1990s, when she began casting figures stripped of skin to expose musculature, organs, and bone.

What unifies the sprawling checklist is Smith's lifelong preoccupation with the body as a site where the private and the collective meet: fragile, leaking, vulnerable, and occasionally sacred. Expect devotional-looking figures that borrow from Catholic iconography but refuse its comforts, alongside her recurring menagerie of owls, goats, and other animals that carry symbolic weight across her work. Large-scale paper installations dotted with crystal and cast bronze bring in a cosmic, almost folkloric register that contrasts with the visceral body sculptures.

For anyone who knows Smith only through museum surveys, this is a rare chance to see a dealer-organized show with real scale and ambition — effectively a mini-retrospective staged inside a commercial gallery, assembled through Smith's long friendships with both Jeffrey Deitch and Pace founder Arne Glimcher. It's a significant get for Deitch's Hollywood space and one of the most anticipated gallery openings in Los Angeles this fall.

shows.title: Threshold Matter
shows.artist: Alex Voinea, Chris Wood, Alessandro Casetti
shows.description:
This group show pairs three artists for whom material behavior is as much the subject as any image: paint that moves at speed, glass that only completes itself under changing light, and pigment pushed toward fracture. Alex Voinea's large abstractions read as frozen motion — sweeping gestural strokes and suspended drips laid over softly graduated grounds, giving the work a hybrid of velocity and precision.

Chris Wood works in an entirely different register, building compositions from sheets of dichroic glass arranged in restrained geometric grids. The work is only finished by the room it's in: as ambient light shifts through the day, the glass throws overlapping bands of color that the static structure alone doesn't suggest. Alessandro Casetti closes the show with figurative paintings that fracture the human face into fields of saturated color, treating portraiture as a way of visualizing internal, often unresolved, emotional states.

Taken together, the three practices argue for a kind of control that produces its effects indirectly — through material properties, environmental conditions, and the passage of time — rather than through direct illustration.

shows.title: Constructed Fields
shows.artist: Jason DeMeo, Alexander Eulert, Len Klikunas, Krista Reuter, Will Beger
shows.description:
Constructed Fields gathers five artists who treat the picture plane as something to be built rather than simply painted on — a modernist inheritance filtered through very different materials. Jason DeMeo combines hard-edged geometric division with gestural drips and scrapes, a self-described "Synthesism" that keeps order and accident in constant negotiation. Alexander Eulert's stacked, rectangular forms draw on architecture and geology, suggesting pueblos, monoliths, and cultivated fields compressed into flat abstraction.

Len Klikunas takes construction literally, stretching canvas over three-dimensional armatures so the support itself generates the work's geometry, guided by a minimalist, almost meditative restraint. Krista Reuter works in cut, torn, and folded paper, using the material's structural give to build genuinely dimensional reliefs where shadow becomes part of the composition. Will Beger closes the group with stripped-down, high-contrast imagery drawn from Southwestern plant life and desert forms, occasionally painting directly onto shaped wood panels so the object and the image are built together.

The show rewards attention to physical construction as much as visual composition — several of these works are literally built up from or into their support, not just painted on a flat rectangle.

shows.title: Spiraling
shows.artist: Leonardo Aguirre, Rachel Taggart, Brandon Neher, Petra Rös-Nickel, Virginie Schroeder
shows.description:
Spiraling is a study in repetition and recurrence across five abstract practices, where patterns rarely resolve into stillness. Leonardo Aguirre, trained as an architect, loosens the geometric rigor of Uruguay's constructivist tradition with gestural line and fluid color, keeping an underlying structural logic even as the forms get freer. Brandon Neher works the opposite direction, building tightly ordered grids of repeated circles and squares that pulse through shifting color — rigorous pattern made to feel kinetic.

Rachel Taggart's washes of diluted acrylic on raw canvas are built without a predetermined composition, letting color and form settle into place through accumulation rather than planning. German artist Petra Rös-Nickel layers and then scrapes back oil paint and mixed media over geometric understructure, giving her Concrete Art-influenced compositions real physical depth. Virginie Schroeder's raised, syringe-applied acrylic lines — inspired by a beaded curtain moving in the wind — create compositions that visibly shift with the viewer's position, bringing an optical, almost kinetic quality to the surface.

It's a tightly themed show for a gallery that usually reads as an inventory room, and the five approaches to recurring form make a good case for seeing it as a real group exhibition rather than a sales wall.

shows.title: When Feeling Becomes Form
shows.dates_note: Gallery's announcement page lists the opening as September 24th with no stated closing date.
shows.description:
Michael Hafftka has spent five decades making raw, unplanned paintings that come directly out of physical contact with the canvas — no preliminary drawings, no reference photography, just intuitive mark-making that lets each image find its own form as it's being made. That immediacy is the whole point of his work: figures emerge heavily worked and distorted, built from thick, urgent paint handling that reads more like an emotional record than a composed picture.

This is a significant acquisition for a West Hollywood design-district gallery: Hafftka's paintings sit in the permanent collections of MoMA, the Met, the National Gallery of Art, the British Museum, and SFMOMA, and he exhibited early in his career alongside Basquiat, Haring, and Clemente. The paintings on view lean into his signature vocabulary of pressed, elongated faces and bodies rendered in heavy, scraped-back pigment — images that feel closer to psychological states than portraits.

For a gallery whose program otherwise leans toward design-world collaborations and lifestyle-adjacent art placement, a solo show built around an artist of Hafftka's museum standing is worth the detour, especially for anyone interested in the expressionist, physically direct end of American figurative painting.

shows.title: Passages
shows.dates_note: Gallery/press announced the opening reception for Oct 10, 2026 (Fri 6-8pm); no published closing date found yet
shows.description:
Glenn Dean returns to Maxwell Alexander Gallery with Passages, a suite of new oil paintings that began as studies of Arizona's Canyon de Chelly and grew into a wider meditation on the Southwest. Cowboys, cowgirls, and Indigenous riders move through sunburned mesas and desert washes in canvases built on Dean's signature economy of brushwork — big simplified shapes of land and sky that let atmosphere and light carry the emotional weight of the picture.

Dean has built his reputation as one of the leading contemporary painters of the Western genre, and this body of work pushes further into figure-in-landscape territory than his earlier, more purely scenic paintings. The people here aren't incidental staffage; they're treated as continuous with the terrain, their silhouettes rhyming with canyon walls and rock formations. It's a quiet, elegiac take on a well-worn genre, less about frontier mythology than about duration — how long human beings have moved through these particular places.

For anyone who knows Dean's earlier shows at the gallery, Passages reads as a deepening rather than a departure: tighter color harmonies, bigger canvases, and a sustained focus on the idea of journeying as both subject and structure. It's a good entry point for newcomers to contemporary Western painting and a must for those who've followed Dean's evolution over the past decade.

shows.title: Show #39: Joan Heemskerk, Dirk Paesmans, and Amy Alexander
shows.artist: Joan Heemskerk, Dirk Paesmans, and Amy Alexander
shows.description:
And/Or Gallery's 39th show pairs two generations of digital-art pioneers. Joan Heemskerk and Dirk Paesmans, who worked for decades as the net-art duo JODI, are showing new work under their own names for the first time — a shift worth noting given that JODI's chaotic, code-breaking web pages and game mods have been part of the internet art canon since the mid-1990s and sit in MoMA's permanent collection. Each artist in the show presents two pieces, keeping the installation tight and focused rather than a survey.

The other half of the show belongs to Amy Alexander, a longtime net and software artist who performs and exhibits as VJ Übergeek. Her contribution centers on Deep World, an interactive chatbot project that has moved between live performance and installation over the past two years. Visitors can talk to a custom language model trained on writers and thinkers who lived through difficult historical periods, producing a chatbot whose responses swing between philosophical reassurance and visible self-doubt — a sly comment on the therapy-bot and AI-advisor culture of the present moment.

Taken together, the show is a conversation between internet art's first wave and its current AI-driven mutation, staged in a small Pasadena space that has spent two decades quietly championing this lineage of work.

shows.title: Gateway to Himalayan Art
shows.description:
Gateway to Himalayan Art is a primer exhibition, drawing on loans from New York's Rubin Museum of Himalayan Art to walk visitors through the core visual vocabulary of Himalayan Buddhist and Hindu art: the deities, symbols, and ritual objects that recur across Tibetan, Nepalese, Bhutanese, and related Mongolian and Chinese traditions. Rather than a chronological survey, it's organized thematically — symbols and meanings, materials and technologies, and living practice — which makes it as useful for first-time viewers of thangka painting and bronze sculpture as for people who already know the region's art.

Highlights include a painted depiction of the Bodhisattva Kshitigarbha, a narrative thangka tracing the life of Buddha Shakyamuni, and an intricate Mandala of Chakrasamvara, alongside everyday ritual objects like a handheld prayer wheel. The show also brings in a living-tradition angle through contemporary Himalayan artists, including a piece by the Nepal-born, San Francisco-based painter Tsherin Sherpa, whose work recontextualizes traditional thangka iconography in a contemporary idiom — a useful reminder that this isn't a frozen historical art form.

Paired with the concurrent collection show "We Are Connected," this is USC PAM leaning into its deep Himalayan holdings, and it's a good entry point for anyone curious about Buddhist and Hindu visual culture who wants grounding in the basics before diving into the museum's broader collection.

shows.title: We Are Connected: Highlights from the USC Pacific Asia Museum Himalayan Collection
shows.description:
Drawn almost entirely from USC PAM's own holdings, We Are Connected is a deep dive into the museum's substantial Himalayan collection — roughly 42 objects spanning paintings, sculpture, ritual implements, textiles, and decorative arts, many of them off view for decades. Where the concurrent Gateway to Himalayan Art show (built around Rubin Museum loans) works as an introductory primer, this is the home-grown counterpart: a chance to see what USC PAM itself has been quietly holding in storage.

The exhibition is organized around ideas rather than chronology — the cosmos, communal celebration and ritual, and the relationships between humans and animals — and leans on recurring figures from Himalayan art and myth, including the Snow Lion, Garuda, and Ganesha, to carry those themes. It's as much about Buddhist concepts of transformation and connection as it is about specific objects, using the collection to make a case for art's role in binding communities together across Tibet, Nepal, and parts of India and China.

Showing alongside Gateway to Himalayan Art, this is the better pick for anyone who already has some grounding in Himalayan art history and wants to see rarer, lesser-exhibited pieces from a major regional collection.

shows.title: Summer Stock
shows.dates_note: Listed on the gallery's exhibitions page under "ON VIEW" with no stated opening or closing date; page last updated August 2026.
shows.description:
Summer Stock is Jonathan Novak Contemporary Art's seasonal survey of its secondary-market holdings, pulling together blue-chip paintings, sculpture, and editions rather than organizing around a single theme or artist. The checklist reads like a highlight reel of postwar and contemporary heavyweights: Alexander Calder works on paper, a cast-bronze Ed Ruscha pun piece, Michael Craig-Martin's candy-colored steel chair reliefs, a Jean Dubuffet gouache from his Psycho Sites, and a run of Wayne Thiebaud works spanning etching, watercolor, and oil.

What makes the show worth a visit is the range of media on view side by side — Idris Khan's layered photographic reliefs and Julian Opie's lenticular sprinting figures sit alongside more traditional works by Sam Francis, Kikuo Saito, and Jim Dine, giving a condensed overview of how different generations of artists have handled color, repetition, and gesture. It's less a curated argument than a chance to see museum-caliber works in an intimate Century City space.

For visitors who know these artists mainly from institutional collections, Summer Stock is an opportunity to look closely at smaller-scale, often lesser-seen pieces — a Thiebaud watercolor of eyeglasses, a Ben Schonzeit strawberry rendered almost photographically, a Chris Martin collage-painting — that rarely travel to museum walls.

shows.title: Wayne Thiebaud: Icons
shows.dates_note: Exhibition page states "Currently on view at the gallery" but publishes no opening or closing date.
shows.description:
Wayne Thiebaud: Icons is a focused look at the artist best known for turning diner food and Sacramento hillsides into exercises in pure, confectionary color. The works here skew toward works on paper and smaller studies — pastels, watercolors over etching, graphite drawings — rather than the large oil-on-canvas pie cases and cake counters most associated with his name, which makes this a good show for seeing how Thiebaud actually built his effects of light and shadow at a more intimate scale.

The checklist moves between his two recurring subjects: still life (stacked eyeglasses, striped ties, stick candy rendered in thick, creamy color) and landscape (a steep San Francisco-style hill planted with toy-like trees, a solitary cloud hanging over a mesa, a river delta picked out in loose pastel). Thiebaud's late-career clown drawings also appear, a reminder that his interest in isolated objects against blank grounds extended well past food and cityscapes.

Because the gallery deals extensively in Thiebaud's editions and works on paper, this is also a chance to see the mechanics of his printmaking — drypoint, etching, hand-colored impressions — alongside unique works, which is a different experience than encountering his paintings in a museum survey.

shows.title: Pescadería
shows.description:
Pescadería is a two-person show built around hand-painted, hand-cut wooden sculpture — the kind of folk-art-inflected object-making Giant Robot's GR2 space has long championed. Erick Martinez works almost entirely in die-cut and carved wood, turning fish, monsters, flowers, and pop-culture mash-ups (a Batman riding a bulb-lit rocket, a Peanuts-style dog poking out of a toy car) into small shadow-box reliefs and freestanding figures finished in bright, candy-saturated color.

The title points to the show's loose throughline: fish markets, coastal imagery, and the iconography of Mexican and Southern Californian folk art, filtered through a cartoonish, slightly macabre sense of humor — tiki mugs, kaiju faces, and jack-o'-lantern monsters show up alongside sunny flowers and birds. Priscilla Moreno's contributions round out the two-hander, extending the show's handcrafted, object-based sensibility.

It's a tightly scaled exhibition suited to GR2's storefront gallery, with dozens of small works rather than a handful of large statements — the kind of show where the pleasure is in walking the room slowly and catching the jokes and details in each piece.

shows.title: Salvador Dalí: Sculpture and Works on Paper
shows.dates_note: Venue's events page lists this as "On View Now" at the Beverly Hills gallery with no closing date given; a related "Summer Exhibition 2026" collection page lists an opening of June 4 & 6, 2026.
shows.description:
This selling exhibition gathers a wide cross-section of Salvador Dalí's work on paper alongside a run of his limited-edition bronzes, giving a walk-in audience an unusually broad look at his output beyond the famous paintings. The standout grouping is a suite of illustrations Dalí made for Dante's Divine Comedy, rendered as richly colored prints keyed to specific cantos — Inferno's fraudulent counselors and blasphemers, Purgatorio's penitents, Paradiso's angels — each one compressing a whole canto's imagery into a single dense, hallucinatory scene.

Seeing the Dante suite alongside the bronzes makes the throughline in Dalí's work easier to track: the same elongated, melting, mythologized figures recur whether he's working in etching ink or cast metal. It's a useful corrective to the popular image of Dalí as a one-painting artist (the melting clocks), showing instead a prolific, restless draftsman who treated printmaking and sculpture as extensions of the same surrealist universe.

As a commercial gallery show, everything here is for sale and priced accordingly, from editioned prints in the low four figures up to larger sculptural pieces — worth knowing going in, but it doesn't make the work less worth seeing. For anyone curious about Dalí's graphic work specifically, this is a denser and more focused presentation than most general-interest museum surveys offer.

shows.title: Rooted In What Carries Us
shows.description:
This juried group exhibition gathers thirty-eight contemporary Native and Indigenous artists from Southern California and beyond, working across painting, drawing, fiber, ceramics, basket weaving, beadwork, and photography. The jury — Joe D. Horse Capture, chief curator at the Autry Museum of the American West; Emma Robbins, founder of Chapter House in Los Angeles; and Laurie Steelink of San Pedro's Cornelius Projects — pulled together a cross-section of practices rather than a single thesis, and the result reads less like a themed survey than a wide-angle snapshot of who is making Native art in the region right now.

The premise, loosely, is continuity: how craft, material, and story get carried forward across generations even as the specific forms shift from beadwork to illustration to large-scale installation. Works by artists such as Weshoyot Alvitre sit alongside painting, sculpture, and photographic work from dozens of others, each approaching the question of Indigenous identity on Turtle Island from a different angle — personal, political, ancestral, or all three at once.

It's a big, democratic kind of show, the sort AGCC has built its reputation on: less about a single curatorial argument than about giving a large number of working artists real wall space and a real audience. Worth the trip up Gaffey Street for anyone interested in contemporary Native art practice in Southern California, especially since the center's hilltop campus and small-museum scale make it an easy, unhurried visit.

shows.title: A Theater of Dreams
shows.description:
Reggie Burrows Hodges paints figures emerging from fields of flat, velvety black — his signature move is to build a canvas's ground first in black paint, then let faces, limbs, and gesture surface out of that darkness in color and light. The effect is theatrical in the literal sense: his scenes read like stage pictures, lit from within, where memory and invention share the same unstable footing.

A Theater of Dreams, organized in collaboration with the California African American Museum and the Getty, gathers that practice around the idea of dreaming as both private refuge and collective myth-making. Hodges has spoken about growing up between Maine and Tacoma and the way his own biography gets refracted through invented figures rather than straightforward self-portraiture, and this show looks to extend that approach into new, larger-scale compositions.

As the latest installment in CAAM's five-year residency inside Art + Practice's Leimert Park exhibition space, the show continues a run of ambitious, museum-organized exhibitions in a storefront setting — worth catching both for Hodges's increasingly recognized painting and for the chance to see major-museum programming in an intimate, free, walk-in gallery.

shows.title: Rest Stops
shows.description:
After the Eaton Fire destroyed her family's home and studio in Altadena, Kenturah Davis turned toward the scorched landscape itself as material. Rest Stops, co-presented with Destination Crenshaw, shows the prototypes and drawings behind a three-year project to build a network of sensory gardens on burned residential lots — adaptive, fire-resilient plantings meant to support soil remediation while giving displaced families a place to sit with what's been lost.

Davis is best known for large-scale figurative drawings that incorporate debossed text — literary excerpts, legal transcripts, sheet music — pressed into the paper beneath carbon-pencil rubbings of bodies in motion. Here that same interest in inscription and memory gets applied to landscape design: her drawings for the gardens borrow structural logic from Black quilting traditions, treating planting plans like pieced fabric, stitching individual lots into a larger communal pattern.

The show is less a conventional art exhibition than a working document of a long-term public project, grounded in Davis's own history in this stretch of Los Angeles — she's also the artist behind the 2019 mural at the Downtown Inglewood Metro station. Seeing the drawings and prototypes at Crenshaw Dairy Mart, an Inglewood gallery built around art as community repair work, underscores how closely the project's aesthetic and civic ambitions are entwined.

shows.title: Willie Birch: Stories to Tell
shows.description:
This is the first career-spanning retrospective of Willie Birch, a New Orleans-born artist whose work moves across six decades and several distinct mediums without ever losing its central subject: the dignity of ordinary Black life. The show tracks his evolution from early social-realist works through a period of painted papier-mâché sculpture in the 1980s and into the large-scale charcoal-and-acrylic drawings on paper that define his recent practice.

Birch calls the threads he's chasing "retentions" — the ways African cultural memory persists, often invisibly, inside American music, gesture, and daily ritual. His subjects are neighbors, street musicians, and family groups rather than public figures, rendered with a monumental weight more often reserved for historical or religious painting. Front porches, parade routes, and domestic interiors become, in his hands, sites of collective memory and quiet resistance.

Organized by the American Federation of Arts and the New Orleans Museum of Art and curated by Russell Lord, the exhibition brings together some 85 works spanning painting, drawing, sculpture, and prints — a rare chance to see the full arc of an artist whose reputation has, until now, been built on scattered regional exposure rather than a show of this scale.

shows.title: How to Fly
shows.description:
Sadie Barnette has built a career out of what she calls "liberating the Black archive" — most famously by drawing directly onto her father's 500-page FBI surveillance file in glitter and pink spray paint. How to Fly takes a gentler approach to the same project: a 3,300-square-foot photomural wrapping CAAM's atrium, built from her own family snapshots and studio photographs rather than state documents.

The mural reads as a personal archive going public. Birthday cakes, well-loved paperbacks, chrome car rims, costume jewelry — ordinary objects of Black domestic life get blown up to mural scale and arranged in a gradient that runs the length of the color spectrum, left to right, red through violet. Barnette has talked about wanting to work at two speeds at once: the intimacy of a family photo album and the public scale of a mural meant to be seen by everyone who walks through the building.

Commissioned for CAAM's 50th-anniversary programming, the piece functions as a kind of welcome — the first thing most visitors see, and a thesis statement for a museum devoted to exactly the kind of "basement and attic" archives Barnette is interested in surfacing. Its long run means it's effectively become part of the architecture, but it rewards a second look alongside whatever temporary exhibition happens to be sharing the building.

shows.title: Phyllis Green: Of My Own Making
shows.description:
This is a career survey, not a new body of work — more than twenty-five sculptural and performative objects drawn from fifteen years (and, in spirit, fifty) of Phyllis Green's practice, marking the Los Angeles sculptor's half-century as an exhibiting artist. Green works across clay, fiber, resin, and found materials to build body surrogates: hand-sewn garments, wearable furniture, masks, and hybrid creature-forms that riff on modernist sculpture while quietly undoing its assumptions about gender and the body.

The anchor piece is "Lion/Lamb," a large suspended resin-and-mixed-media work from 2020 that typifies Green's approach — materials that look soft or domestic (fabric, feathers, fur-like textures) built into something sturdier and stranger, half-creature, half-monument. The show's framing device is the idea of the monument itself: not a bronze general on a plinth, but a different kind of durability measured in studio hours, teaching, and the accumulated craft of a working life.

Green has an unusually direct connection to this campus — she taught in LMU's art department from 1989 to 2011 — which makes this homecoming survey feel less like an institutional retrospective than a reunion. Her work sits in LACMA's and the Long Beach Museum of Art's collections, and she's been recognized with a Guggenheim Fellowship and grants from the NEA and the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, among others, so this is a rare chance to see a wide swath of a serious, idiosyncratic career in one room.

shows.title: Lost Mind in the Tall Grass
shows.dates_note: La Loma Projects' homepage currently features "Lost Mind in the Tall Grass" as its show but the exhibition subpage on the gallery's own site could not be reached to confirm an exact closing date; third-party listings (the artist's own account, Artrabbit, Glyph) give an opening of Sept 12, 2026 with closing dates cited as either Oct 17 or Oct 26, 2026.
shows.description:
Skylar Hughes paints landscapes that have been stripped of their horizon lines, reduced to passages of color, light, and gesture that feel more like memories of a place than a place itself. Working in oil on modestly scaled canvases, she builds up atmospheric fields of green, ochre, and violet that hover between representation and abstraction — a fallen leaf, a patch of sky, a tangle of brush rendered as much through what's left out as what's put in.

Lost Mind in the Tall Grass continues the quiet, intuitive practice Hughes has developed over a decade of painting the woods, fields, and gardens around Los Angeles. The show's title piece imagines the disorientation of being swallowed by overgrowth, and the surrounding paintings extend that feeling of being pleasantly lost: canvases built from layered washes and worked surfaces that reward slow looking over quick reads.

This is Hughes' latest exhibition with La Loma Projects, the Highland Park gallery that has given her several solo outings since 2023. Her recent studio work leans into seasonal change — falling leaves, dusk light, the last warmth of autumn — rendered in a palette that's softer and more melancholic than straightforward landscape painting, closer to the "innerscapes" critics have used to describe her approach.

shows.title: Neither Land Nor Water
shows.description:
Amy MacKay makes paintings out of other people's memories of an evening she staged. In 2023 she restaged the Irish play By the Bog of Cats — Marina Carr's bog-set retelling of the Medea myth — as a private performance around a heated Pasadena pool, with a cast, a cinematographer, and an invited audience all documenting the night from different vantage points. Those competing, imperfect records of a single live event are the raw material she translates into oil paint.

The result is a body of work built through layering and erasure: thin veils of oil paint wiped back with spirits, clouds of white gesso sanded down to a ghostly residue, surfaces that accumulate and dissolve in the same gesture. Figures and settings surface and recede — a coat, a changing room, the shape of a dancer mid-turn — never quite resolving into a single fixed image, which is the point. MacKay is less interested in what happened than in how memory distorts, multiplies, and fades every time it's retold.

This is MacKay's second solo show with la BEAST built from the same source material, following her 2024 exhibition To the Bog of Cats I One Day Will Return. Where that show tracked the paintings closely to the text of the play, Neither Land Nor Water pushes further into the subjective experience of the performers and audience members themselves, with works ranging from small, intimate studies to large sculptural panels. It's a show about the unreliable, generative space between an event and its retelling — fitting territory for a painter who treats documentation itself as a kind of drawing.

shows.title: Yes and LA Dust
shows.description:
Thirteen years after Urs Fischer turned MOCA's galleries into a communal clay-sculpting studio, Jeffrey Deitch brings that project's afterlife home in two simultaneous shows. At the Orange Drive space, nineteen of the bronze casts pulled from that 2013 public happening stand together as a strange, democratic forest of figures — some clearly the work of a trained sculptor, others with the lumpy, sincere energy of a stranger's first attempt at clay. Fischer selected and cast them himself, and the result reads less like a survey of "good" sculpture than a group portrait of collective imagination under one artist's editorial eye.

A short walk away at the Santa Monica Boulevard gallery, the mood shifts entirely. LA Dust revives a body of work Fischer began in 2007: paintings on metal panel made from scanned dust swept off his studio floor, blown up and rendered in mirror-like, reflective surfaces that shift color depending on where you stand. Installed on the diagonal to suggest a passage from day into night, the panels turn something as inconsequential as floor grime into an argument about scale — the show's underlying idea being that dust sits in a kind of mesoscopic no-man's-land between what we can see and what we can't.

Taken together, the two venues make the case for Fischer as one of the few artists moving fluently between monumental sculpture and quiet, optical painting, and the show's Los Angeles setting is not incidental — Fischer has lived and worked in the city on and off since 2001, and both projects trace directly back to his history with this city's museums and streets. It's a rare chance to see a blue-chip artist's studio-scale ambition laid out across two full galleries at once.

venue.name: Jeffrey Deitch
venue.about: Jeffrey Deitch is a contemporary art gallery founded by dealer, curator and writer Jeffrey Deitch, who opened its Los Angeles space in September 2018 after directing Deitch Projects in New York (1996–2010) and serving as director of MOCA Los Angeles. The gallery is known for ambitious thematic group shows such as People, Punch and Shattered Glass, alongside solo exhibitions with artists including Ai Weiwei, Judy Chicago, Urs Fischer, Robert Longo, Nari Ward and Rammellzee. Its program spans painting, sculpture, performance and street-art-influenced practices, continuing Deitch's long engagement with artists such as Keith Haring, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Jeff Koons. The gallery also maintains a New York space and participates actively in international art fairs.

shows.title: Dictation from the Other Side
shows.description:
Curated by novelist Laura Whitcomb, this group show gathers a sprawling, multi-generational cast of visionary and outsider-adjacent artists united by an interest in the occult, automatism, and channeled or "dictated" imagery. The checklist spans Surrealist-era figures like André Masson, Kurt Seligmann, Roberto Matta, and Esteban Francés alongside California mystics and mediums such as Cameron, Paulina Peavy, and Wallace Berman, plus outsider and self-taught visionaries like Madge Gill and Anna Zemánková.

The through-line is process as much as subject: automatic drawing, trance states, séance-derived compositions, and works their makers described as received rather than invented. Betye Saar and George Herms represent the assemblage strain of LA's own occult-tinged art history, while Louise Janin's delicate "Cosmogramme" works on paper form an entire mini-suite within the exhibition.

It's an ambitious, loosely woven survey that treats the irrational and the spiritual as a serious throughline in twentieth-century art rather than a curiosity, and it rewards slow looking — many of the works are small, dense, and diaristic rather than showy.

shows.title: Fragmented Thought
shows.description:
Carole Vanderlinden has spent decades making paintings that refuse to settle into one style, and this show — her latest body of oil paintings made over the past three years — is a good introduction to why that refusal is the point. Shapes drift between figuration and abstraction, surfaces build up in visible, almost sedimentary layers, and passages that look like collage are actually painted illusions of collage. The overall effect is of a mind thinking out loud on canvas, doubling back on itself and letting contradictory ideas sit side by side.

The Belgian painter's reference points are eclectic and mostly submerged — early modernists like Malevich and Picabia, her own sketchbooks, stray bits of art history — but none of it surfaces as direct quotation. What comes through instead is a sustained interest in the gap between form and content, in how a mark can carry meaning without illustrating anything in particular. It's an intellectually restless kind of painting that rewards slow looking rather than quick reads.

This is Vanderlinden's second solo outing with Karma's Los Angeles space, and it arrives alongside the artist's first monograph. For anyone interested in painting that treats its own materials and history as raw subject matter, rather than in service of a tidy image, this is a worthwhile stop on Santa Monica Boulevard.

shows.title: Private Show
shows.description:
Long before his Weimaraners made him a household name, William Wegman was one of the sharpest conceptual photographers to come out of 1970s Los Angeles, and this show digs into that formative decade with rare vintage prints and video alongside later work that shows where those early ideas ended up. After relocating to Southern California in 1970, Wegman fell in with Ed Ruscha, John Baldessari, and Allen Ruppersberg, and his photography grew directly out of performance — deadpan visual jokes that double as small philosophical experiments about looking and language.

Pieces like A Basic Guide to Lettering literally flip an instructional format on its head, while later Polaroids featuring his dogs — Eye On, Trio of One — bring the same absurdist precision to a completely different scale and subject. Seeing the two eras side by side makes clear how consistent Wegman's wit has been across fifty years, even as the tools and subjects changed.

It's a smart, funny, image-rich show from an artist people tend to underrate precisely because he's so good at being funny.

shows.title: Silent Shades
shows.description:
This tightly focused exhibition zeroes in on a pivotal but less-seen chapter of Lee Mullican's long career: the year he spent painting in Rome on a 1959 Guggenheim Fellowship, plus the terracotta sculptures he made shortly after returning to the U.S. Mullican co-founded the Dynaton group with Wolfgang Paalen and Gordon Onslow Ford, a postwar circle that tried to fuse European Surrealist automatism with a more expansive, cosmic strain of American abstraction, and that project runs straight through the work here.

The Rome paintings are large-scale works on paper built from dense, staccato fields of marks in black, white, and ivory — surfaces that read at once as star charts, ancient scripts, and topographical maps. Mullican described them as translations of the city's sensory static (traffic, scooters, church bells, birdsong at dusk) into abstract rhythm, and the effect is meditative and busy at the same time. The terracottas that followed, made after his return to the U.S., shrink that same sensibility down into small totemic forms that nod to the pre-Columbian and indigenous art he collected and admired throughout his life.

It's a good show for anyone who knows Mullican only through the big, later, brightly patterned "meditation" canvases he's most associated with — this is an earlier, more austere, and more historically specific moment, made concrete through the coincidence of the Guggenheim year and the palazzo studio he worked from in Rome. The gallery notes it as a companion to a wider survey of the Dynaton movement that ran at Chateau Shatto earlier this summer, for those wanting the fuller context.

shows.title: All Signs Fail
shows.description:
Patrick Jackson has built a career out of taking familiar objects and images and pushing them slightly out of register, and this installation is one of his most ambitious stagings of that idea. The centerpiece is a reprint of an "Eye Syphilis Is Serious" public-health billboard that once hung around Los Angeles, blown up to 44 feet wide and stripped of its text, so that the image's original urgency curdles into something more ambiguous and unsettling. Standing in front of it are two purchased figures — an adult companion doll dressed in a hand-knitted sweater and a "reborn" baby doll — a mother-and-child tableau assembled entirely from objects made for other purposes.

Ringing the gallery walls is a run of found bus-shelter posters for remakes, sequels, and franchise films, arranged by release date and marked with screenprinted seasonal motifs — leaves, snow, flame — as if tracking the passage of time through recycled culture. Behind the billboard, a two-story scaffold structure conceals a small, maze-like memorial building visitors can walk through, turning the whole installation into something between an advertisement, a shrine, and a stage set.

Jackson, a Los Angeles-born sculptor who's shown at the Hammer and the Huntington, has described the show simply as "a lot of images and a memorial," and that plain description undersells how strange and effective the piece is in person. It's a show about how mass-produced images of care, warning, and grief circulate and lose their charge — and about what happens when an artist reassembles that debris into something that feels, unexpectedly, like a monument.

shows.title: Rapido
shows.description:
François Ghebaly resurrects a piece of Los Angeles conceptual art history with this presentation of Alexis Smith's 1975 installation "Rapido" — a model train that circles an otherwise empty gallery on an endless, lonely loop — shown for the first time since its original outing at UC Santa Barbara half a century ago. It's a spare, almost deadpan gesture that plays games with scale, turning the gallery into a vast landscape and the viewer into an oversized trespasser.

The second half of the show is a genuine discovery: a suite of collage-based works on paper from 1974, among the earliest pieces Smith ever made and never before exhibited publicly. Originally shown only in private, one-on-one sessions in her studio, these works reveal the found-image, cut-and-paste vocabulary — pop culture fragments, appropriated text, chance juxtaposition — that would define Smith's celebrated collage practice for the next five decades.

Smith, who died in 2024, was a central figure in LA's conceptual and feminist art scenes of the 1970s, with major retrospectives at the Whitney and MOCA and public commissions including "Snake Path" at UC San Diego. This show is valuable less as spectacle than as archaeology: a look at the raw material and nascent ideas of an artist who spent the rest of her career refining exactly what shows up here in embryonic form.

shows.title: Presence
shows.description:
Havana-based Roberto Diago makes his West Coast debut with a suite of mixed-media portraits and still lifes built from reclaimed wood, nails, cord, and canvas. The portraits are deliberately withholding: faces reduced to a pair of eyes, a beaded necklace, a wedge of shadow, set into grids of scavenged material that fracture the picture plane the way early modernist collage once did. The still lifes strip a vase and a few flowers down to flat, graphic silhouettes against saturated color.

Diago has spent three decades using found materials from his Havana neighborhood to talk about the afterlives of racism in Cuban society, and the rawness of his materials, splintered wood, exposed nails, is the point rather than a stylistic flourish. The grid structures running through many of these works read as a visual metaphor for the divisions imposed on Afro-Cuban communities, with the scavenged materials pointing to both scarcity and resilience.

This show arrives while Diago is also representing Cuba at the Venice Biennale, and it's a good introduction to an artist who's had a substantial institutional exhibition history in the U.S. (the Halsey Institute, the Art Museum of the Americas) but comparatively little gallery exposure in Los Angeles until now.

venue.name: Vielmetter Los Angeles
venue.about: Vielmetter Los Angeles is a contemporary art gallery in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles, located at 1700 S Santa Fe Avenue. It is owned and directed by Susanne Vielmetter and operates three exhibition spaces at that address. The gallery represents a multigenerational group of artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video, and installation, including figures such as Nicole Eisenman, Arlene Shechet, Mickalene Thomas, Wangechi Mutu, Mary Kelly, and the estate of William Pope.L. Represented artists have participated in major international biennials, museum surveys, and art fairs, and have received sustained critical attention in publications including The New York Times, Artforum, The Guardian, and Artnet. The gallery's program spans several decades of contemporary practice, with a consistent focus on socially engaged, figurative, and materially inventive work by artists based in Los Angeles, New York, and internationally.

shows.title: Ongoingness
shows.description:
A gallery-wide group show anchored by Pope.L's "Heaven (Vielmetter Version)," 28 columns of yellowed, stacked disposable plastic cups that reads simultaneously as minimalist sculpture and a pointed reference to Jim Crow-era segregation at public drinking fountains. Vielmetter built the show around that single work, timed to the country's 250th anniversary, and populated it with pieces by nearly the whole roster of gallery artists — Andrea Bowers, Nicole Eisenman, Liz Glynn, Karl Haendel, Mary Kelly, Rodney McMillian, Wangechi Mutu, Robert Pruitt, Deborah Roberts, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, and more.

The connective thread is less stylistic than temperamental: work made by artists processing an unsettled national moment through personal, often laborious means, whether that's Bowers's meticulous graphite rendering of the AIDS memorial quilt in storage or Pope.L's endurance-based sculptural gesture. It's a useful snapshot of where one of LA's most consistently interesting mid-size galleries sees its program heading, and a chance to see a lot of strong individual pieces by artists more often shown solo.

shows.title: Object Poetry
shows.description:
"Object Poetry" gathers artists who treat sculpture and assemblage as a kind of compressed language, where everyday materials and cast-off objects are recombined until they start to read like verse. The checklist spans generations and temperaments: Bruce Conner's uncanny assemblage sensibility sits alongside Tony Oursler's video-inflected sculptures, large-scale photographic works, and pieces that play with domestic scale and architectural miniature. Across the two galleries, the through-line is a fascination with objecthood itself — the way a chair leg, a lens, or a scrap of fabric can carry more meaning once it's pulled out of use and set into a composition.

Seeing the works installed together across the gallery's two main rooms makes clear how much these different practices share: a belief that objects, arranged with enough attention, behave like sentences.

This is a good show for anyone who likes sculpture that rewards close looking — pieces built from many small decisions rather than one big gesture. It's on view concurrently with a solo survey of Mark Innerst's paintings in the gallery's third room, making a visit worth the time for two very different but complementary shows under one roof.

venue.name: Michael Kohn Gallery
venue.about: Michael Kohn Gallery was founded in 1985 by Michael Kohn, opening first on Robertson Boulevard in West Hollywood before relocating in 2014 to its current home on North Highland Avenue in Los Angeles. The gallery presents historically grounded exhibitions alongside a contemporary program, linking postwar West Coast movements such as Beat assemblage, Light and Space, and California Minimalism to newer generations of painters and sculptors. It represents senior West Coast figures including Lita Albuquerque and Sharon Ellis, oversees the estates of Bruce Conner, Wallace Berman, Joe Goode, and Martha Alf, and maintains a growing roster of emerging and mid-career artists working internationally, spanning painting, assemblage, and mixed-media practice with an emphasis on figuration, identity, and material experimentation.

shows.title: Trophies
shows.description:
David Hicks makes ceramics that look like they've been through something. For his third solo show with Diane Rosenstein, the Central Valley-based sculptor fills the gallery with hand-built earthenware bowls, bottles, jars, and ewers whose surfaces have been pushed through repeated firings until the glazes crack, run, and pool like weather damage. He calls the results "trophies" — not in the triumphant sense but as reliquaries for agricultural and floral cuttings, the discarded plant matter of Central California's farmland that most people never think twice about.

There's a deliberate friction in the work between the classical vessel forms Hicks builds and the chaos he then invites onto their surfaces. Titles like Sun Bleached, Red Leaf, and Marigold and Strawberries point to specific botanical sources, but the vessels themselves read as abstract fields of color and rupture — glazes in what Hicks describes as a state of "optimal softening," caught mid-collapse. The effect sits somewhere between still life and geological record.

Hicks has spent his career working at the edges of the decorative and the conceptual, and Trophies continues that project by dignifying the overlooked: agricultural byproduct, roadside scrub, the stuff that gets mowed down without ceremony. Seeing a full room of these vessels together, glazed in wildly different palettes but united by that same cracked, sun-worn surface, makes the case for paying attention to what usually gets discarded.

venue.name: Diane Rosenstein Gallery
venue.about: Diane Rosenstein Gallery is a contemporary fine art gallery founded in 2012 by Diane Rosenstein, located in the Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles. The gallery represents emerging, midcareer, and established artists working across a wide range of media, including painting, drawing, photography, sculpture, and ceramics. Its program has featured artists such as Eleanor Antin, Julian Stanczak, Amir Zaki, and Terran Last Gun, reflecting an interest in both historical and contemporary practices. The gallery participates regularly in major art fairs, including Independent, Untitled Art, and Art Basel Miami Beach, and its artists' work is frequently reviewed in national art publications.

shows.title: The Cars of Los Angeles
shows.artist: Carlos Agredano, Merlin Carpenter, Fiona Connor, Sylvie Fleury, Max Göran, Jason Hirata, Alan Michael, Josephine Pryde, Ed Ruscha, Lucien Samaha, Nicole-Antonia Spagnola, Angharad Williams
shows.description:
Curated by Dan Mitchell and Richard Sides as a companion to their own two-person show "The Woods" upstairs, this group exhibition treats the automobile as Los Angeles's central cultural artifact and elegy in waiting. The checklist ranges wildly in tone and medium: Carlos Agredano's large canvas built from smog and tire particulate collected off a Lynwood freeway sits near Ed Ruscha photographs and prints of gas stations and studio backlots, while Angharad Williams contributes a sprawling charcoal drawing of a fantasy Maserati and Merlin Carpenter presents a heap of Barbie Ferrari boxes as sculpture. A fabricated "fake John Chamberlain," made from card packaging and spray paint, needles at the market mythology around crushed-car sculpture, and Sylvie Fleury's mixed-media pit-stop installation and vintage beauty-industry video bring her long-running fascination with glamour and speed into the mix.

Video work anchors the show's emotional register: Nicole-Antonia Spagnola's looping silent-film pastiche "Ragged Dick" stages a fatal collision between an early twentieth-century shoeshine boy and a horse-drawn carriage, framing the space to follow as one long meditation on automobility's violence, and Max Göran's "Nothing Runs Like a Deere" extends that unease into contemporary machine culture. Jason Hirata's readymade sculpture built from a catalytic converter and cable spacer, and Fiona Connor's graphite skid mark drawn directly onto the gallery wall, ground the show's more theatrical gestures in blunt, sculptural fact.

It's a smart, dryly funny group show for a city defined by its highways, treating car culture less as subject matter than as a shared American nervous system — one that runs on nostalgia, pollution, and speed in equal measure. The accompanying essay by Sophia Roxane Rohwetter, threading together Gorky's reaction to early cinema and Soviet auto-fiction, gives the show unusual literary heft for what could otherwise read as a novelty theme exhibition.

venue.name: Bel Ami
venue.address: 709 N Hill St #105, Asian Center, Los Angeles, CA 90012
venue.about: Bel Ami is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles, founded in the summer of 2016 by Naoki Sutter-Shudo and Sabrina Tarasoff. The gallery operates from a space inside the Asian Center on N. Hill Street in Chinatown. Its program centers on emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, ceramics, and mixed media, with a roster spanning Los Angeles, Europe, and Japan. Bel Ami has built a reputation for adventurous, often narrative or satirical bodies of work, exhibiting artists such as Guillaume Dénervaud, Olivia Hill, Ben Sakoguchi, and Soshiro Matsubara. The gallery is a regular exhibitor at international art fairs, including Frieze, Liste, FIAC, Paris Internationale, miart, and the Dallas Invitational, and its exhibitions have been reviewed in numerous art publications.

shows.title: The Woods
shows.description:
Dan Mitchell and Richard Sides pair two deceptively plain vocabularies of sign-making: Mitchell's fabricated street and trail signposts, stamped with words like "Boredom," "Gulag," and "Nowhere," and Sides's monochrome enamel paintings, each bearing a single word for a family role — father, mother, brother, stepmother — rendered in a different typeface. Both bodies of work borrow the authority of public signage and domestic labeling, then let that authority curdle into something more ambiguous: directions that point nowhere useful, family names that name nothing beyond themselves.

The show also includes small collaborative sculptures, including a modified microwave mounted on a motorized plinth, and a series of Mitchell's graphite drawings that catalogue the same charged, generic vocabulary — Crying, Molesting, Gossip, Spanking — in a schoolbook hand. Shown alongside its companion exhibition The Cars of Los Angeles, the show sustains Bel Ami's long-running interest in artists who use institutional or vernacular formats (road signs, product packaging, family taxonomies) against themselves.

This is a two-person show for two artists with long, overlapping exhibition histories in London, Berlin, and Los Angeles, and the works reward close, patient looking rather than a quick pass — the wit is dry, and the show's real subject, per its own framing, is the difficulty of finding language and gesture that mean anything at all in an over-mediated moment.

shows.title: Transportation of the Spheres
shows.description:
Dorothy Hood spent decades moving between Mexico City's postwar avant-garde and the wide skies of her native Texas, and that dual inheritance runs through everything in this show. Her large-scale canvases fuse hard-edged abstraction with billowing, cosmic fields of color — dense charcoal or violet voids punctuated by sharp geometric intrusions, as if a piece of Mexican muralism collided with an astronomer's diagram of deep space.

"Transportation of the Spheres" gathers paintings and works on paper that lean into Hood's lifelong fascination with celestial imagery and interior landscape. The pictures often read as thresholds: a dark, saturated ground opens onto a smaller, glowing shape, suggesting portals, planets, or psychic apertures. It's abstraction with a metaphysical charge, made by an artist who talked about her own work in terms of spirit and scale rather than formal problem-solving alone.

Hood, who died in 2000, has been having something of a critical resurgence, with recent gallery and museum attention finally catching up to a body of work that was often overlooked relative to her male Abstract Expressionist peers. This Fernberger presentation is a good chance to see that work up close in Los Angeles, in a gallery space that suits her ambition for scale and atmosphere.

venue.name: Fernberger
venue.about: Fernberger is a Los Angeles gallery founded by Emma Fernberger in January 2024. Located on North Western Avenue, it presents an intergenerational program of artists with a global outlook, placing particular emphasis on women-identifying practitioners. The program is unified by a sense of intensity and immediacy, favoring work that produces an instant visceral reaction while remaining thoughtful and historically grounded. Fernberger has described an interest in art's transformative and unifying potential, seeking pieces that are high-impact yet cerebral. The gallery has participated in major art fairs and been the subject of coverage in international publications, reflecting a growing profile within the Los Angeles gallery scene, particularly around the Melrose Hill area.

shows.title: The Page Before Me
shows.description:
Susan Te Kahurangi King has been drawing obsessively since childhood in rural New Zealand, and this show — the first dedicated to her work on the West Coast — traces that practice from the late 1950s to the present. King, who stopped speaking as a young child and has used drawing as her primary form of expression ever since, builds dense, multi-planar compositions that mix cartoon characters like Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck with private, map-like structures and rhythmic abstract fields. The drawings resist any clean split between figuration and abstraction; recognizable cartoon iconography gets folded into passages that read as pure pattern and structure.

The show's anchor is an untitled scroll drawing from around 1967 that stretches more than sixteen feet — the largest of only four such scrolls King made — built in pastel and graphite on found paper across what appears to be many separate working sessions, each one sealed off from the next by drawn borders and dotted lines. It's a good entry point for a body of work that can otherwise feel dauntingly idiosyncratic: a single sustained piece that shows how King's private visual language accumulates over time rather than arriving whole.

King's belated recognition — MoMA, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the American Folk Art Museum all hold her work, and she's had solo shows from Miami to Paris — makes this West Coast debut a genuine event rather than a routine gallery booking, and James Fuentes' Melrose Hill space is a fitting, unpretentious place to encounter it.

shows.title: Cordillera Mexicana: Alfredo Ramos Martínez and the Mexican Landscape
shows.description:
Alfredo Ramos Martínez is often called the father of Mexican Modernism — he mentored David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo and pushed a generation of painters out of the studio and into the landscape. This exhibition, drawn from the artist's estate, gathers tempera-on-paper and oil landscapes made after his 1929 move to Los Angeles, when homesickness for Mexico's mountains and markets became a lifelong subject.

The show's anchor works trace a single mental thread: the Cordillera, the mountain spine that runs from the Sierra Madre down through the Americas. Martínez's Cordillera Mexicana pays tribute to the Sierra Madre Oriental peaks above his native Monterrey, while other paintings place indigenous women bearing flowers and produce beneath the volcanoes ringing the Valley of Mexico. Even his delicate studies of floripondio blossoms — a South American flower he found growing as an ornamental in both Mexico and Southern California — read as a metaphor for his own transplanted life.

It's a quieter, more historical show than most of what's on view in LA's contemporary-leaning galleries right now, but a good one for anyone curious about the roots of Mexican modernism as seen from Los Angeles, a city where Martínez spent his final two decades and where his legacy is held in depth at LACMA and beyond.

venue.name: Louis Stern Fine Arts
venue.about: Louis Stern Fine Arts is a gallery in West Hollywood's Design District focused on Mid-Century West Coast Geometric Abstraction, representing the artists who defined California Hard Edge painting, including Lorser Feitelson, Helen Lundeberg and Karl Benjamin, alongside other Mid-Century abstractionists such as John McLaughlin, Frederick Hammersley and Roger Kuntz. The gallery also manages several artist estates, among them Mark Feldstein, Ynez Johnston, Matsumi Kanemitsu, Alfredo Ramos Martínez, Mimi Chen Ting, Doug Ohlson and Frederick Wight. Its contemporary roster includes painters, sculptors and photographers who extend this historic program. Beyond exhibitions, the gallery is active in the secondary market, with particular strength in Impressionist, Post-Impressionist, Modern and Latin American art, and oversees the catalogue raisonné project for Alfredo Ramos Martínez.

shows.title: Take the Bitter with the Sweet
shows.description:
Pony Ma is a Brooklyn-based, Taiwanese-born painter whose acrylic-on-panel works pull from pop iconography and dream logic — cartoonish figures, disembodied smiles, and surreal props arranged like clues in a puzzle that never fully resolves. His paintings favor bright, flat color and graphic clarity even as the imagery underneath stays genuinely strange.

"Take the Bitter with the Sweet" is his second solo show with Thinkspace and gathers eleven new acrylic-on-panel paintings. By his own account the work grew out of a genuinely hard year — a serious injury, a cross-country move, financial stress — filtered not into visible anguish on the canvas but into paintings meant as a retreat from all of it.

The result is a body of work that reads as escapist on its surface but carries real weight underneath: bright, almost storybook imagery standing in for private difficulty, each painting functioning less as a narrative than as a small, self-contained refuge.

venue.name: Thinkspace Projects
venue.about: Thinkspace Projects is a Los Angeles gallery in the West Adams District, founded in 2005 by Andrew Hosner and L. Croskey. Since its start the gallery has built an international reputation as a leading voice for the New Contemporary Art Movement, a lowbrow-descended, figurative and pop-culture-inflected strain of art that emerged on the West Coast in the 1990s. Thinkspace represents artists ranging from emerging to established, and has expanded beyond its own space to curate exhibitions with museums and partner galleries in cities such as Berlin, Hong Kong, London, New York, Detroit, Chicago and Honolulu. It also produces murals worldwide and works with organizations like POW! WOW! and RAD Napa. The gallery describes itself as artist-focused, family-run, and committed to bridging street-level and institutional art contexts.

shows.title: Kiddos
shows.description:
Matthew Grabelsky is best known for dropping wide-eyed animal-headed figures — his signature mash-up of human bodies and cartoon or animal faces — into the fluorescent-lit purgatory of the New York subway. "Kiddos" narrows that lens to childhood: playground scuffles, temper tantrums, sibling rivalries, and the small dramas of growing up, all rendered with the same uncanny, hyper-real polish he brings to his transit paintings.

The effect is somewhere between Norman Rockwell and a fever dream — technically dazzling figurative painting that uses its animal-headed cast to sidestep easy sentimentality about childhood. A kid mid-tantrum or a "cool kid" in a playground standoff reads as funnier and stranger with a fox or rabbit head than it would with an ordinary human face, and Grabelsky clearly knows it.

shows.title: SMOL 3.0
shows.dates_note: page's exhibition-archive header lists Aug 8 - Sept 5, 2026, though the show's own body text mentions an earlier Aug 29 close for a prior edition; going with the header dates as current
shows.description:
SMOL is Thinkspace's annual survey of small-scale work — everything on view is 12x16 inches or under — pitched as an approachable entry point for new collectors and a chance for longtime gallery artists to show something looser and less precious than a full solo body of work.

The 2026 edition, SMOL 3.0, is a genuinely sprawling group show: roughly fifty artists from the gallery's roster are included, spanning painters and illustrators working across the New Contemporary spectrum, from pop-surrealist figuration to graffiti-adjacent abstraction. Names range from gallery mainstays like Kelly Vivanco, Fumi Nakamura's stylistic peers, and KOLA DPW to muralists and printmakers who don't often get wall space in a group context this democratic.

It's less a curated thesis than a salon-style hang, and that's the point — visitors can find a manageable, collectible piece from an artist whose larger work they might otherwise only see in a museum-scale mural or a five-figure canvas.

shows.title: Spotlight on Local Creatives (with Roger Betka | Jordan Tacker | Juri Umagami)
shows.artist: Roger Betka, Jordan Tacker, Juri Umagami
shows.description:
Session Sixteen of Thinkspace's Fresh Series, curated by Cannibal Flower, spotlights three Los Angeles-area artists — Roger Betka, Jordan Tacker, and Juri Umagami — in a compact group showcase running alongside the gallery's bigger solo exhibitions.

The series exists specifically to give local, often earlier-career artists gallery wall space without waiting for a full solo slot, and each session functions more as an introduction than a thesis show — a rotating snapshot of names worth watching in LA's current scene.

It runs through September 5 in the gallery's West Adams space, concurrent with Pony Ma's and Matthew Grabelsky's solo shows.

shows.title: Marilyn Monroe: A Silent Life
shows.description:
Marilyn Monroe has been photographed more than almost any other human being, and this group show at Peter Fetterman assembles the work of the photographers who actually stood in the room with her — Eve Arnold, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Cornell Capa, Elliott Erwitt, Philippe Halsman, Douglas Kirkland, Bert Stern, Sam Shaw, George Barris, Andre de Dienes, Milton H. Greene and others. Rather than the tabloid iconography most people carry around in their heads, the prints here lean toward the quieter, more observational end of the spectrum: Monroe resting between takes on the set of "The Misfits," going over lines in the Nevada desert, or caught mid-laugh at the Actors Studio.

Because so many of these photographers were friends or colleagians of Monroe rather than paparazzi, the exhibition reads less like a celebrity retrospective and more like a study of trust between subject and camera. Bert Stern's "Last Sitting" images, made just weeks before her death, sit alongside Cartier-Bresson's spare reportage from the set of "The Misfits" and Andre de Dienes's early, unguarded pictures of her near Malibu in 1946 — a useful reminder that her image was constructed over more than fifteen years by dozens of different eyes.

Peter Fetterman's gallery has long specialized in vintage and estate prints of classic 20th-century humanist photography, and that connoisseurship shows here in the range of processes on view — gelatin silver prints, platinum/palladium prints, and archival pigment estate prints spanning the 1940s through the 1960s. For anyone interested in mid-century photojournalism as much as in Monroe herself, it's a rich survey of how the top photographers of the era approached a single, endlessly complicated subject.

venue.name: Peter Fetterman Gallery
venue.about: Peter Fetterman Gallery is a Santa Monica photography gallery founded by Peter Fetterman, a London-born collector and former filmmaker who opened his first gallery in 1988 and became one of the original tenants of Bergamot Station when it opened in 1994. The gallery holds one of the largest inventories of classic twentieth-century photography in the United States, with particular depth in humanist photography. Its holdings include work by figures such as Henri Cartier-Bresson, Sebastião Salgado, Steve McCurry, Ansel Adams, Paul Caponigro, Willy Ronis, Michael Kenna, André Kertész, Manuel Alvarez Bravo, Lillian Bassman, Pentti Sammallahti, Sarah Moon and Jeffrey Conley. The gallery presents this work in an intimate, salon-style setting intended to promote appreciation of the photographic medium.

shows.title: The Hunter
shows.description:
Daido Moriyama's first major Los Angeles exhibition gathers decades of the grainy, high-contrast street photography that made him one of the defining figures of postwar Japanese image-making. Associated with the radical Provoke movement, Moriyama built a visual language out of what most photographers try to eliminate — blur, grain, and loss of focus, known in Japanese as are-bure-boke — treating the camera less as a recording device than as an extension of his own restless movement through the city.

The images here are fragments rather than scenes: a stray dog's eyes, a passing gesture, a flash of signage, a body glimpsed and gone. Moriyama has always insisted he wasn't going out to photograph life so much as to experience it, camera in hand, and that sense of pursuit — of the hunter chasing something that won't hold still — gives the show its title.

For a photographer this influential to still feel dangerous and unresolved on the wall says something about how good the prints are. It's a compact but intense survey, well worth the trip out to Bergamot Station.
