shows.title: A Certain Slant of Light
shows.artist: Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, Sung Jik Yang
shows.description:
*A Certain Slant of Light* brings together ten artists of different generations and backgrounds to explore how painting, sculpture, and assemblage can interrogate interiority and personal vision. Carl Cheng, Holly Coulis, Tim Garwood, Sky Glabush, Pamela Jorden, David Korty, Aaron Morse, Hubert Schmalix, Sophie Treppendahl, and Sung Jik Yang each navigate their own visual languages—from Coulis's contemplative still lifes and landscapes to Glabush's evocative gestures, from Morse's engagement with environment and narrative to Schmalix's late works reflecting on color and light.

The exhibition emphasizes how these artists, separated by geography and artistic practice, share a commitment to the picture plane as a site of experiential investigation. Their works resist simple categorization: paintings layer abstraction and representation; sculptures occupy the space between material presence and visual illusion. Together, they pose quiet, persistent questions about how we see ourselves and the world around us.

Drawn from different moments in each artist's practice—some historic works, many recent—this group show celebrates the sustained conversations happening within the gallery's roster, where careful observation and emotional resonance remain central to contemporary practice.

venue.name: Philip Martin Gallery
venue.about: Philip Martin Gallery is a contemporary art gallery based in Los Angeles that presents innovative, experimental and ambitious artworks in all media, both at its own space and at art fairs in the United States and abroad. In January 2023 the gallery moved into a new 4,000-square-foot location at 3342 Verdugo Road in Los Angeles. The gallery represents a roster of artists working across painting, photography, video, sculpture and textile, including figures such as Ericka Beckman, Kwame Brathwaite, Brian Bress and Carl Cheng, alongside a group of emerging and mid-career painters and sculptors. The gallery has a history that traces back to its earlier incarnation as Cherry and Martin.

shows.title: MARILYN 100
shows.description:
Russell Young's diamond-dusted silkscreen paintings of Marilyn Monroe anchor this centennial tribute, staged in Los Angeles as part of a global program organized with the Marilyn Monroe Estate and Authentic Brands Group. Young, who owns a printmaking press once used by Andy Warhol, works squarely within the pop-art lineage that turned Monroe into an image before she was allowed to remain a person — his high-contrast, glitter-flecked canvases lean hard into that tension between glamour and exposure.

The show pairs new paintings made with access to the Monroe Estate's archive with a broader survey of Young's career-long fascination with fame, celebrity iconography, and the American Dream's underside. Expect large-scale portraits rendered in his signature saturated palettes and diamond-dust surfaces, a technique that makes the images shimmer and shift as you move past them.

It's a commercial, glossy kind of show — closer to spectacle than critique — but that's the point: Young is interested in how fame flattens a person into a symbol, and Monroe remains the ultimate case study. Worth a look for anyone curious how pop art's Warhol-era obsessions get recycled for a new generation of collectors.

venue.name: Art Angels
venue.about: Art Angels is a female-owned contemporary art gallery with its flagship space in the Beverly Hills Design District of Los Angeles, at 318 S Robertson Blvd. It is owned and operated by Jacquelin Napal and Kat Emery. The gallery represents a broad roster of contemporary artists working across photography, painting, sculpture and street-influenced practices, with a stated emphasis on supporting women and emerging talent alongside established international names. Beyond its main gallery, Art Angels maintains display partnerships in hotel and retail settings in Los Angeles, Miami and New York, and operates a design consultancy assisting developers and design firms. The gallery has also explored NFT drops with several of its artists.

shows.title: 20th Anniversary Group Show
shows.description:
Corey Helford has spent two decades building one of the country's most reliable homes for New Contemporary art — the pop-culture-inflected, technically virtuosic, narrative-driven painting and sculpture that mainstream galleries were slow to take seriously. This anniversary show, the first of a two-part celebration, gathers new work by artists who defined the gallery's program across those twenty years, from hyper-detailed figurative painters to the sculptors and muralists who've made CHG's three-gallery Downtown space a destination beyond the traditional art-world circuit.

What's notable about Corey Helford's roster is how much genuine range sits under the "lowbrow" or "pop surrealist" label: airbrush-smooth portraiture next to gothic fantasy, cartoon-adjacent character work next to fairly serious formal painting. An anniversary show like this functions as a group portrait of that range, with each artist contributing new pieces rather than simply pulling from inventory.

A second edition opens in September, so this first round is really the opening act of a longer celebration — a good excuse to see how a gallery built entirely outside the blue-chip system has quietly become an institution of its own.

venue.name: Corey Helford Gallery
venue.about: Corey Helford Gallery (CHG) was founded in 2006 by Jan Corey Helford and her husband, television producer Bruce Helford. The gallery focuses on New Contemporary art, encompassing New Figurative Art, Pop Surrealism, Neo Pop, Graffiti and Street Art, and Post-Graffiti, representing a diverse roster of international artists ranging from emerging to established names. After nine years in Culver City, CHG relocated in December 2015 to a 12,000-square-foot building in Downtown Los Angeles, where it now operates three separate gallery spaces hosting individual and group exhibitions roughly every six weeks. The gallery has also exhibited at major art fairs and partnered with international institutions such as Bristol's City Museum & Art Gallery for a transatlantic exhibition in 2010.

shows.title: Ornélie and Molly Devlin
shows.description:
A two-artist pairing in Corey Helford's Gallery 3, bringing together the French-born painter Ornélie and Los Angeles artist Molly Devlin. Devlin's contribution includes lush, deep-cradled acrylic works like "Fern Echoes," dense botanical compositions rendered with a jewel-toned, almost decorative intensity that recalls both folk illustration and contemporary pop-surrealism.

Pairing two painters rather than staging solo debuts is typical of CHG's Gallery 3 program, which often uses the smaller space to test complementary sensibilities against each other. Here, the throughline is a shared interest in nature rendered through a saturated, illustrative lens rather than by observation, giving the show a warm, almost storybook register distinct from the gallery's harder-edged pop and street-art leaning artists.

shows.title: Deep Dive in the Archive
shows.description:
Corey Helford's Gallery 2 turns inward with this exhibition pulled from the gallery's own back rooms, resurfacing works by artists in its stable that have not been on public view in years. Rather than a single-artist survey, it operates like a cabinet of curiosities from two decades of the gallery's program, letting visitors trace throughlines between the pop-surrealist and lowbrow-adjacent painters CHG has championed since its founding.

Shows built from archives are as much about a gallery's institutional memory as they are about any one artist, and that's the appeal here: a chance to see how CHG's identity has shifted (or held steady) since it opened in the Arts District two decades ago, presented alongside its 20th Anniversary exhibition in the main gallery this same month.

shows.title: Building an Audience
shows.description:
Brad Eberhard makes paintings and ceramic sculptures that feel like pages torn from a private notebook. His works are small in scale but dense with incident — shapes and colors that hover somewhere between abstraction and figuration, built up intuitively until fragments of the recognizable start to surface. For this show, he's gone a step further than usual by hand-building the frames themselves, so that a painting and the object holding it arrive as a single, inseparable decision rather than an artwork plus its display.

The imagery draws from an eclectic private archive: record-collecting, sporting geometry, archaeology, folklore, his son's patterned shirts. Eberhard has spoken about his fascination with Matisse's The Red Studio and its collapse of pictorial space, and about aspiring to the coded symbolism of Jasper Johns and the mystical smudge of Cy Twombly — lofty reference points he treats with a healthy dose of self-aware humor. The ceramic pieces, sagger-fired and glazed, extend the same sensibility into three dimensions, turning everyday objects like sconces into small, strange totems.

What ties the show together is the question posed by its title: can art exist without someone there to receive it? Eberhard's answer seems to be that the making itself is already a form of reaching out, an "oblique diary" that only completes itself in the act of being looked at. It's an intimate, unpretentious show from an artist who clearly enjoys the mechanics of painting as much as its meaning.

venue.name: Timothy Hawkinson Gallery
venue.about: Timothy Hawkinson Gallery is a Los Angeles space on Beverly Boulevard that presents contemporary painting and drawing-based practices, largely through art-fair presentations such as NADA New York, NADA Miami, and Felix Art Fair. Its program pairs emerging and mid-career Los Angeles artists—among them Alise Spinella, Marc Pally, Mason Saltarrelli, and Samantha Yun Wall—with historically significant figures such as the Wiyot artist Rick Bartow and Mexico City-based Adrián S. Bará. The gallery emphasizes intuitive, process-driven abstraction, drawing, and works that explore the body, time, and cultural identity. It is a member of NADA and the Gallery Association Los Angeles (GALA).

shows.title: The Development Center: A Clownache Store
shows.description:
For ten days, NOON Projects hands its Chinatown storefront over to Alex Chaves and lets him blur every line between gallery, studio, and shop. The Development Center is a working outpost of Clownache, Chaves's ongoing direct-to-consumer curatorial project that mixes painting with fashion and merchandise, and for the run of the show Chaves is in residence, painting a mural on-site drawn from the geometric, low-slung architecture of early modern Los Angeles.

Alongside the mural, the space fills with new watercolors and a run of hand-produced T-shirts and editions, priced and displayed like retail goods rather than precious objects behind glass. That flattening of gallery hierarchy is very much the point: Chaves treats a hand-painted tee and a framed watercolor as equally legitimate carriers of an idea, and the installation's constant state of in-progress-ness — wet paint, a working easel, product on tables — makes the whole space feel like a stage set for the artist's process rather than a finished exhibition.

It's a small, quick-turnaround show on Chung King Road, the historic strip of storefront galleries in Chinatown that has long served as an incubator for exactly this kind of scrappy, hybrid programming, and it rewards a visit precisely because it won't look the same from one day to the next.

venue.name: NOON Projects
venue.about: NOON Projects is a contemporary art gallery in Chinatown, Los Angeles, founded by Ryan Noon in 2022. The program presents emerging and historical artists working across painting, sculpture, performance, craft, and sound, with a focus on spirituality, eroticism, the natural world, queerness, and social practice. The gallery is known for close, collaborative relationships with its artists and an interdisciplinary curatorial approach that pairs exhibitions with a regular schedule of community programming, including concerts, lectures, dinners, workshops, salons, and performances. Noon brings a background in fashion and creative direction, having worked with Alexander McQueen and Henrik Vibskov and built a design studio and think tank at Nike, which informs the gallery's artist-centered, experimental sensibility and emphasis on long-term collaboration and dialogue between artists and audiences.

shows.title: Graven Images to the Major Deities
shows.description:
John Collins is best known around Los Angeles for Moonlight Graham, a daily devotional practice he's kept up since 2019: every night during baseball season, he picks a play from that day's games and renders it in brushwork and ink wash before posting it online. The series now numbers over a thousand works, and this show — Collins's second dedicated to the project at Track 16 — catches it mid-evolution, as he's swapped his original Arches paper for Asian rice and mulberry bark stock that makes the marks looser and more immediate, and ventured into drypoint printmaking for the first time with a set of prints depicting the final games of the 2025 World Series.

The project's charm is in its stubborn earnestness: Collins named the series after Archibald "Moonlight" Graham, the real-life ballplayer immortalized in Shoeless Joe and Field of Dreams who moonlighted as a doctor, and he treats his own nightly ritual — sketching after a day spent working as a handyman — as a similarly quixotic double life. Baseball, for Collins, isn't a subject so much as a structure for daily discipline, a deadline he sets for himself as if filing to tomorrow's sports section.

Outside the baseball works, Collins is known for brooding, autobiographical paintings on scavenged materials — linoleum scraps, chunks of stucco, torn fabric — that read as private ruminations rather than public statements. Seeing both bodies of work together at Track 16, in the gallery's Bendix Building space downtown, makes the case for an artist whose sincerity and repetition are the whole point.

venue.name: Track 16
venue.about: Track 16 is a Los Angeles gallery with two exhibition spaces, one in East Hollywood and one downtown in the historic Bendix Building. Sean Meredith serves as director. The program centers on a small roster of California-based and international artists working across painting, ceramics, sculpture, and installation, often engaging social and political themes—from feminist critiques of domestic craft (Elyse Pignolet) to politically charged painting (Sandow Birk, Robbie Conal) and reworked found ceramics (Debra Broz). The gallery also represents the estates of Pedro Álvarez and Simone Gad, and has shown Latin American collectives such as Mondongo. Track 16 participates in art fairs, publishes artist books under its Pinspot imprint, and has placed artists' work in institutions including LACMA, SFMOMA, and the Getty.

shows.title: One Last Group Show (untitled friends exhibition)
shows.artist: Kuma Enomoto, Marilyn Garcia, Filomena Leimone, Santiago Orellana, Lucia Penick, and Eloise Wong
shows.description:
This send-off show gathers six recent graduates of an LA arts high school who've spent years crossing paths at each other's shows, gigs, and film shoots — scoring one another's movies, photographing one another's bands, modeling one another's clothes. Painting, photography, animation, and mixed media all show up here, tied together less by a curatorial thesis than by the fact that everyone in the room has been each other's audience and collaborator for years.

This show captures that spirit at a bittersweet moment: several of the artists are leaving Los Angeles just as the show closes. Expect work that's rougher and more personal than a typical gallery show, dealing openly with community, heartbreak, and the anxiety of growing up in a hostile world, with a closing-night musical send-off from two of the artists' bands.

venue.name: Junior High
venue.about: Junior High is a multi-purpose art gallery, event space, and artist sanctuary in Glendale, California, founded by Faye Orlove. It describes itself as a community-driven venue dedicated to arts expression and arts education for people of all ages and backgrounds. Programming spans gallery shows, music events, workshops, panels, and editorial projects, with a particular focus on supporting marginalized and emerging artists, including beginners, women, queer and nonbinary artists, and artists of color. The space, which holds over 80 people, emphasizes radical empathy, accessibility, and safety as guiding values, positioning itself as an alternative to traditional, exclusionary art-world spaces.

shows.title: Take Your Sweet Time
shows.description:
Scott Hove is best known around Los Angeles for "Cakeland," his long-running walk-in installation of frosting-slathered, faux-confectionary environments that turn sugary kitsch into something a little sinister. For this solo show at La Luz de Jesus, he trades cake stands for clockwork, building a body of new sculptural and wall-based work out of clock faces, gears, and timepiece fragments. The pieces use the familiar iconography of timekeeping to needle at bigger questions about whether time is really the fixed, linear thing we treat it as, or something more slippery.

It's a fitting subject for an artist who has spent his career splicing together things that don't belong side by side — candy-shop cuteness with body horror, mechanical precision with entropy. Expect dense, layered constructions where actual clock parts get embedded in sculpted, cake-like or organic forms, so that the works read simultaneously as functional-looking objects and as reliquaries for a concept (time) that Hove clearly doesn't fully trust.

The show runs alongside two other solo presentations opening the same night at La Luz de Jesus. Hove's clock-crammed constructions should be a good anchor for an evening that also includes new work from Wini Brewer and Susie Ketchum.

venue.name: La Luz de Jesus Gallery
venue.about: La Luz de Jesus Gallery is a Los Angeles gallery founded in 1986 by entrepreneur and art collector Billy Shire. Housed inside the Soap Plant/Wacko complex on Hollywood Boulevard, the gallery is credited with helping foster what became known as the Lowbrow or Pop Surrealist movement in California art. Its program favors figurative, narrative painting and unconventional sculpture, with content spanning folk, outsider, religious, and sexually charged themes. The gallery states its mission is to bring underground art and counter-culture to a wider audience, and it also operates an Art Advisor Service connecting collectors, curators, and designers with contemporary artists worldwide.

shows.title: The Long Way Home
shows.description:
Billed as a "mini solo exhibition," Susie Ketchum's The Long Way Home fills La Luz de Jesus's smaller gallery wall with dense, symbol-laden imagery — a mask trailing dangling skulls, a red flower rendered with fetishistic precision, a tree-woman hybrid figure — that fits comfortably within the gallery's decades-long identity as ground zero for Pop Surrealism and lowbrow art.

The pieces work in a register somewhere between illustration and folk-horror talisman: skulls, embers, and shedding skin recur as motifs, suggesting a loose narrative of transformation, protection, and reckoning with mortality that runs through the small body of work. Ketchum's rendering is tight and graphic, closer to tattoo flash or album art than academic painting, which suits the show's compact, charm-like scale.

Opening the same first-Friday night as Wini Brewer's solo show next door in the gallery, The Long Way Home is a good entry point for anyone curious about the darker, more occult-inflected end of the lowbrow tradition La Luz de Jesus helped define.

shows.title: Aesthetic Strategies
shows.description:
Wini Brewer's solo show Aesthetic Strategies takes over La Luz de Jesus's main gallery for a run of new work that, per the artist's promotional material, leans into bold, graphic composition and a considered, almost design-driven approach to image-making — hence the exhibition's title.

La Luz de Jesus has spent forty years as the launching pad for pop-surrealist and lowbrow artists working outside the traditional gallery pipeline, and Brewer's inclusion in the September calendar continues that mission, putting a contemporary illustrator's sensibility on the walls of what is still one of the genre's most storied showcases.

Without a full install shot or checklist yet published, the show is best approached as a first-Friday discovery: it opens alongside Susie Ketchum's mini solo next door, giving visitors two very different, tightly-hung bodies of work to compare in one visit.

shows.title: New Skies
shows.description:
Severin Hallauer's first Los Angeles solo show builds an entire vocabulary around inheritance — the things, memories, and even traumas we're handed before we have any say in the matter. The Mexico City-based Swiss artist works across sculpture, installation, video, and text, and the pieces here range from intimate to genuinely startling: a modified airline carry-on reworked with cut-paper patterns drawn from Swiss papercutting tradition; a single-frame video confronting a childhood memory involving a gun; and a wall of 355 stained-glass microscope slides, each one tracing a branch of Hallauer's family tree back to 1560, suspended so that moving air makes the slides gently chime against one another.

That installation, Bloodlines, is the emotional center of the show — genealogy turned into both a visual field and a soft, ambient soundscape, memory made audible. A companion piece, Left Overs (Sono stata uui), sets a table with hand-painted ceramics referencing his great-grandmother's floral motifs and embroidered napkins bearing his grandmother's phrase "I was here," treating domestic labor itself as an archive worth preserving.

The show's anchor series, LONG HAUL (i'm only crying on...), takes its title from the specific psychic space of air travel — jetlagged, anonymous, suspended between departure and arrival — and uses it as a metaphor for a life spent between countries and identities. It's a dense, personal body of work from an artist still early in his exhibition history, shown in an intimate gallery space that suits its confessional scale.

venue.name: induction gallery
venue.about: induction gallery is a Los Angeles gallery founded and directed by artist and curator John Zinonos. Located at 672 S. La Fayette Park Place in the city's Westlake area, the space works by appointment and presents a roster of emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, collage, and new media. The program reflects Zinonos's own multidisciplinary curatorial interests, bringing together Los Angeles-based and out-of-state artists whose practices engage material experimentation, personal narrative, and technology-driven or ecological themes.

shows.title: Moth To A Flame
shows.description:
Moth To A Flame is a collaborative installation by the artistic team Kelly Cox and Eric Mullis, who have been making work together for decades since meeting on a high school ceramics field trip in Wisconsin. Now based in Boise, Idaho, the two build environments that sit somewhere between architecture, product display, and psychic space — treating the built world's mythologies, from retail staging to civic monuments, as material to be dismantled and reassembled.

The installation reportedly works through a vocabulary of symbols without fixed answers, favoring sensation over explanation.

Given the collaborative duo's description of the work as responding to "persistent violence and misinformation," expect an installation that's more atmospheric and symbol-laden than didactic — worth the trip for anyone interested in how two people build a single visual language across a decades-long creative partnership.

venue.name: Monte Vista Projects
venue.about: Monte Vista Projects is a Los Angeles artist-run collective founded in 2007. Operating from a fifth-floor space on Maple Avenue downtown, it presents exhibitions, lectures, events, and performances that question standards set by academia and mainstream contemporary art institutions. The collective prioritizes under-represented artists and regularly partners with local, national, and international artist-run spaces, including collaborations and exchanges with groups in Rotterdam, Berlin, and across Southern California. Monte Vista Projects is run collectively by a rotating roster of member-artists who organize its programming, and it maintains an open internship and volunteer program supporting exhibitions, gallery hosting, and installation.

shows.title: Popsicledelic Trip / Pause
shows.description:
KP Projects pairs two Brazilian painters for late summer, each working a very different register of hyper-saturated realism. Rafael Silveira's Popsicledelic Trip leans into candy-colored, almost hallucinatory still lifes and figures — surfaces so glossy and lit they read like renderings of a sugar rush, with titles ("Visual Mantra," "Wonders of Human Nature") that hint at a wry, semi-spiritual undercurrent beneath the pop sheen.

Flávia Itiberê's Pause works in a quieter but equally intense key, built around close studies of single figures and objects — a mask-like face, a wrapped or held object — rendered with the same airbrushed precision but pulled back into stillness rather than trip-like excess. Placed side by side, the two bodies of work argue for hyperreal technique as a vehicle for two opposite moods: one accelerant, one suspended.

This two-hander is a solid entry point into that scene — vivid, technically showy work that photographs well but rewards a slow look in person for the airbrush-level detail.

shows.title: California Poppies
shows.description:
Roger Herman has been a fixture of Los Angeles painting since the late 1970s, and this show finds the German-born, UCLA-affiliated artist doing what he does best: turning flowers, mountains, and skulls into loose, saturated fields of brushwork that refuse to sit still. The poppy paintings are the emotional center — layered, almost gaudy stacks of leaf and petal built from dashes and smears rather than careful description — while a companion landscape painting renders a mountain in broad strokes of blue, turquoise, and white.

What makes the show more than a painting survey is the ceramics. Herman throws large, irregular vessels on the wheel and then treats the glazing the way he treats a canvas, letting color pool and shift unpredictably across the surface. A dining table and coffee table extend that same logic into furniture, their tops built from painterly ceramic panels, and a set of tiny mezcal cups modeled on the traditional jicara round out the display at a much more intimate scale.

Pairing an untidy, expressionist painter like Herman with this gallery is a smart bit of counter-programming — proof that the gallery's West Hollywood outpost isn't just showing polished design pieces but also giving space to an artist whose work resists polish on principle.

shows.title: Moses@100: A Centennial Exhibition
shows.description:
Marking what would have been Ed Moses's hundredth year, William Turner Gallery has assembled a focused survey of paintings that trace the restless, decades-long experimentation of one of Los Angeles's founding postwar artists. Moses came up through the legendary Ferus Gallery circle alongside Robert Irwin, Ed Ruscha, and Billy Al Bengston, but unlike many of his peers he never settled into a single signature style — the show's selection, drawn from series with names like Roses, Wedges, Crackles, and Waterfalls, makes that restlessness the whole point.

What comes through in these canvases is less a fixed "look" than a working method: Moses treated painting as a physical, almost ritual practice, one he described as trying to be "in tune" rather than in control. He kept at it in his Venice studio until his death in 2018 at ninety-one, and the works on view here — bold, gestural, materially varied — reflect an artist who kept mutating his own vocabulary well into old age.

For a gallery that has represented Moses's circle and legacy for decades, this centennial show functions as both tribute and reminder of how much of today's Los Angeles painting scene still traces back to his example. It's a good one to catch before it closes September 5.

shows.title: Lorena Alvarez Gómez Solo Exhibition
shows.description:
Lorena Alvarez Gómez, a Bogotá-based illustrator best known for the children's-book series that culminates in her new collection "The Nightlights Collection," returns to Gallery Nucleus with a body of new paintings built around her recurring vocabulary of glowing plants, small creatures, and nocturnal gardens. The show leans into botanical and fungal motifs — mushrooms, water lilies, tangled vines — rendered in the saturated, jewel-toned palette that has made her work a favorite in the children's-illustration and gallery-pop-surrealism crossover scene.

Pieces like "Maleza" (weeds/undergrowth), "Mycena" (a mushroom genus), and "From Decay We Grow" reflect an ongoing interest in cycles of growth and decomposition, treated not morbidly but as sources of quiet wonder — very much in keeping with the world-building of her book illustrations, where tiny stars and mysterious garden spirits populate a child's bedroom at night. Alongside the paintings, the gallery is releasing a set of limited silkscreen prints of individual motifs (Agua, Nenúfar, Marigold, Congo) that let collectors take home single images from the larger visual universe.

Nucleus has hosted Alvarez Gómez multiple times over the past decade, and this show doubles as a launch event for her new book — she is flying in from Colombia for the opening to give a talk on her writing and creative process before signing books and prints. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about the contemporary illustration-gallery scene that Nucleus has built its reputation on: colorful, narrative-driven, and clearly rooted in a children's-book sensibility even as it's sold as fine art.

shows.title: Portraits of the Wildly Polite
shows.description:
A group show built around a simple, funny premise: what happens when wild or feral creatures are dressed up, framed, and posed with the decorum of an old-master portrait sitter. The roster reads like a who's-who of contemporary pop-surrealist illustration — Jorge R. Gutierrez (of "The Book of Life" and "Maya and the Three"), Hermann Mejia, Justin Parpan, Brianne Drouhard, and more than a dozen other artists each contribute a piece or two riffing on animals behaving with exaggerated civility: a rooster in formalwear, a fox out for a proper "dog walk," an ermine minding an artist-alley table.

The tone throughout is deadpan-comic rather than cute — these are "portraits" in the classical sense, complete with ornate frames and painterly lighting, applied to subjects that have no business sitting for one. Justin Parpan contributes sculptural pieces alongside his paintings, giving the show some three-dimensional variety, while Gutierrez's boldly graphic, Day-of-the-Dead-inflected animal characters (Rooster Lopez, Don Jaguar, Burro Zebra) anchor the show's more stylized end.

It's a quintessential Nucleus show: playful, character-driven, aimed at the crossover audience between fine art collecting and illustration/animation fandom, and worth a visit for anyone who enjoys seeing a gallery wall used for jokes as much as craft.

shows.title: Autumn Enchantment
shows.description:
Autumn Enchantment is a large international group show that bG Gallery is hosting at its Bergamot Station space in collaboration with LarkGallery and Vivid Art Studio Gallery, two organizations that run juried themed exhibitions and invite artists from around the world to submit work. The result is a salon-style hang of dozens of paintings, works on paper and mixed-media pieces loosely bound by the idea of autumn as a season of transition — the shift from abundance to stillness, from color saturation to quieter tonalities.

Because the show was assembled through open submission, the range of styles is wide: sun-drenched landscapes and still lifes sit near abstract color-field paintings, textured mixed-technique works on rice paper, and more expressionistic figurative pieces. Artists in the exhibition work in oil, acrylic, and mixed media, and several pieces directly reference autumnal imagery — orchards, forests, pomegranates and turning leaves — while others use the season more as a mood or palette than a literal subject.

For visitors to Bergamot Station, this is a chance to see a broad cross-section of contemporary representational and abstract painting under one roof, gathered less around a single artistic vision than around a shared curatorial prompt. It's an approachable, salon-hang way to sample a lot of working artists at once before the show closes on September 5.

shows.title: Between a Memory and Me
shows.description:
Rahim Fortune's black-and-white photographs read like a long, unhurried conversation with the American South. Working across Texas and Oklahoma, where he grew up in the Chickasaw Nation, Fortune trains his camera on Black communities, church parades, family kitchens, and the land itself, treating landscape and portraiture as inseparable parts of the same story. His Hardtack series, the backbone of the show, is full of quiet, dignified moments — a grandmother's hands, brothers dressed up for a parade, a queen's coronation — that build into a portrait of inheritance and endurance rather than any single dramatic event.

The exhibition also debuts new color photographs and a short film Fortune made in response to the Texas African American Photography Archive, giving the show a second register alongside the black-and-white work: archival material reanimated through a contemporary lens. Organized by the Center for Photography at Woodstock and co-presented with the California African American Museum as part of the ongoing CAAM at A+P partnership, the show runs concurrently with a companion exhibition of archive selections, so visitors effectively get two conversations about Black Texan life in one visit.

This is Fortune's first solo exhibition in Los Angeles, a notable milestone for a photographer who has quickly built a reputation for tender, unsentimental documentary work. Seeing the prints at scale, in a space designed for close looking, is a very different experience than seeing them reproduced in a book — worth the trip to Leimert Park on that basis alone.

shows.title: Listening to the Great Wall of Los Angeles
shows.artist: Judith F. Baca (with SPARC and LA Phil Insight)
shows.description:
This small exhibition inside Walt Disney Concert Hall's Library of Congress/Ira Gershwin Gallery is a companion piece to a very unusual concert: in March 2026, Gustavo Dudamel led the LA Phil in a program of newly commissioned music inspired by Judy Baca's Great Wall of Los Angeles, the half-mile-long mural painted into the concrete of the Tujunga Wash starting in 1976. Baca's mural is one of the great works of California public art — a community-built visual history of the state told from the perspective of the people usually left out of the official version, from Indigenous California through the Chicano Movement of the 1960s.

The gallery presentation, curated with the Social and Public Art Resource Center (SPARC), the nonprofit Baca co-founded, walks through the mural's origins and its decades-long, multigenerational painting process, using photographs, archival material and documentation of the concert's video component by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and Emmanuel Lubezki. It's a compact but well-chosen selection of images that gives newcomers a real sense of the mural's scale and the community labor behind it, while giving anyone who attended the Dudamel concert a way to go back and connect specific painted scenes to the music they inspired.

It's a modest, free display, tucked into a concert hall rather than a gallery proper, but it's a rare chance to see substantial documentation of one of LA's essential artworks up close — and it's only up for another week, so this is very much a now-or-never entry.

venue.name: Library of Congress / Ira Gershwin Gallery at Walt Disney Concert Hall
