shows.title: Rainbows, Sponges, Flies, and Spoons
shows.description:
SUPERFLEX, the Danish collective founded in 1993 by Jakob Fenger, Bjørnstjerne Christiansen, and Rasmus Rosengren Nielsen, brings three decades of work into R.M. Schindler's 1922 Kings Road house — itself an experiment in communal living, which gives the show an unusually direct dialogue with its site. Rather than one installation, the exhibition splits into several discrete bodies of work, each given its own room: an early lightbox photograph of spoons arranged in a circle, mirrored rainbow photographs that create an artificial, uncanny symmetry, a ceramic sponge sculpture proposed as a new architectural form, and a hyper-precise sculptural tableau of two flies staring at each other over a glass of water.

The connecting thread is SUPERFLEX's long-running interest in systems — ecological, architectural, social — approached through humor and quiet estrangement rather than didacticism. That interest has taken the collective everywhere from energy infrastructure and public parks (their Superkilen project in Copenhagen) to museum walls at Tate Modern and MoMA, and biennials from Venice to Sharjah.

Seeing this work inside the Schindler House is the real draw: a building designed to hold both collective and private life becomes the backdrop for objects that keep splitting the difference between the natural and the artificial, the individual and the shared. It's a tightly focused show rather than a survey, which suits the intimate scale of the house itself.

venue.name: MAK Center for Art and Architecture — Schindler House

shows.title: Summer Show
shows.description:
Francis Gallery's first open call turned into a sprawling group show: 79 paintings by 66 Los Angeles-based artists, submitted and juried rather than curated from the gallery's regular roster. The panel — a mix of curators, collectors, designers, and cultural strategists — was assembled deliberately outside the usual dealer-critic axis, which shows in the range of work on the walls: abstraction, figuration, still life, landscape, and everything in between, hung together with more emphasis on variety than a unifying theme.

The gallery's own description of the works gives a sense of the spread — a hovering diamond form in a spiritual composition, a crumpled space blanket rendered with exacting precision in a gilded frame, a circular canvas built from thousands of tiny marks, an interior scene with the loose warmth of an old master painting. Two juried prizes, the Francis Prize for abstraction and the Clara Prize for figuration, each carrying $15,000, were awarded on opening night, named for the gallery founder's parents.

This is Francis's first show with its Los Angeles space as the gallery's sole location, following the closure of its original outpost in Bath, UK last year — making it as much a statement about the gallery's future direction as a survey of the city's painters. Worth seeing for the sheer density of working artists represented in one room, many of whom don't otherwise show together.

shows.title: We Breathe the Same Air
shows.description:
Curated by The Pioneers, this group show treats Los Angeles's long fascination with the occult and esoteric — Theosophy, the Krotona Institute, Kenneth Anger's devotion to Aleister Crowley, the Marciano Art Foundation's former-Masonic-temple building — less as subject matter than as atmosphere, something that circulates through the city's art and culture the way marine air does. Rather than illustrating belief systems directly, the works trace how symbols and forms migrate between people, generations, and neighborhoods.

The lineup mixes different generations and mediums: Kenneth Anger's ritual-drenched film work sits alongside Catherine Corman's psychologically charged urban photography, Emma Gray's process-based paintings that let portrait and landscape dissolve into each other, and Jon Pylypchuk's bronze sculptures that turn grief into ghostly, enduring form. Rebekah Rubalcava's paintings work the territory between religious symbolism and feminine sexuality, while Saul Appelbaum's contribution expands past single paintings into a collaborative counter-archive built with several other artists and a text by scholar Susan Aberth.

It's a show more interested in accumulation and coincidence than argument — a loose constellation of LA-connected artists whose work keeps circling similar spiritual and symbolic territory without anyone trying to resolve it into a single thesis.

shows.title: Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive
shows.description:
This exhibition draws on the Texas African American Photography Archive to reconstruct a visual record of Black life in small towns and rural communities across eastern Texas between 1944 and 1984. The photographs are the work of local studio photographers who spent careers documenting their own neighborhoods rather than working for outside publications, and the result is an intimate, unglamorous archive of portraits, church gatherings, rodeos, parades, school pictures, and family celebrations.

What makes the material compelling is its scale and specificity: this isn't a survey of famous images but a deep well of vernacular photography, much of which has never been widely seen and a great deal of similar material from the era has simply been lost. Seen together, the pictures trace four decades that span the height of Jim Crow segregation through the civil rights era, without editorializing — the politics are present in the everyday texture of the images rather than in overt protest photography.

The show is organized by the Center for Photography at Woodstock and curated by Nicole R. Fleetwood, a scholar whose research often centers marginalized visual archives. It's presented at Art + Practice as part of the ongoing five-year collaboration with the California African American Museum, which brings CAAM-organized exhibitions to A+P's Leimert Park space. For anyone interested in photography as community record-keeping rather than fine-art spectacle, this is a rewarding, quietly moving show.

shows.title: 1911 Sunset Boulevard
shows.artist: Marcel Alcalá, Maxfield Hegedus, Kittipong, Arturo Soto, Abdi Taslimi, Evan Whale
shows.description:
Taix French Restaurant sat on Sunset Boulevard in Echo Park for nearly a century before it closed and was gutted for redevelopment, and this show is essentially six photographers and one mixed-media artist working through what that kind of loss looks like. Maxfield Hegedus shot the interior room by room before demolition — bar, ballroom, dining room, both bathrooms, the private room — turning a beloved but unglamorous restaurant into a document of a particular strain of mid-century LA design. Abdi Taslimi's acrylic-laminated photographs of the dining room and the Rhône Room work a similar vein in a different register, more saturated and object-like on their aluminum mounts.

The show nods explicitly to Ed Ruscha's "Every Building on the Sunset Strip," and that reference gives the whole project its logic: this is vernacular architecture photography as elegy, cataloguing a stretch of the city's built environment right before it disappears. Evan Whale's altered c-print, carved and chemigrammed until the image partially dissolves into smoke and texture, is the most physically worked-over piece in the show and a good counterpoint to the more straightforward documentary images around it.

This show uses a single closed restaurant as a lens onto memory, urban change, and the particular melancholy of watching a familiar place get erased.

shows.title: You want to hear echoes
shows.description:
Leo Mock's paintings read like fragments of overheard conversation — each one titled with a wistful, slightly melancholic phrase ("The stars have grown old," "Pull the smiles inside," "We can pretend we're that") that sets up a small emotional scene before you've even looked at the paint. The works themselves are moody, layered figurative compositions, built up with a loose, expressive hand that leaves plenty of drips, scrapes, and second thoughts visible on the surface.

Presented at M+B's Casa MB space, an intimate, house-like extension of the gallery's main Almont Drive location, the show benefits from close, room-scaled viewing. Mock's palette tends toward bruised blues and warm ochres, and figures often seem to be dissolving into or emerging from their backgrounds, which suits the show's overall tone of longing and half-remembered feeling.

It's a quiet, literary kind of painting show — good for anyone who likes work that rewards spending real time with the titles as well as the images. The exhibition closes September 5, so this is very much a last-chance viewing before it comes down.

shows.title: Joel-Peter Witkin: Selected Works 1974–2018
shows.description:
Joel-Peter Witkin has spent five decades building elaborately staged photographs that look like they were unearthed from some forgotten wing of art history — tableaux populated by cadavers, amputees, hermaphrodites, and other figures excluded from conventional pictures of beauty, arranged with the same compositional seriousness Velázquez or Goya brought to a royal court. This survey, pulling together prints from 1974 through 2018, traces how consistent that vision has been: the theatrical backdrops, the scratched and toned negatives, the constant citation of old-master painting even as the subject matter refuses every one of its comforts.

What makes the work more than shock value is the craft underneath it. Witkin doesn't just photograph his tableaux — he attacks the negative and print afterward, scratching the emulsion, bleaching sections, sometimes drawing directly on the surface, so that each finished piece sits somewhere between photograph and hand-worked object. The pictures reference Picasso, Courbet, and Christian iconography as often as they reference the darkroom, and the effect is a body of work that treats mortality and the marginalized body as subjects worthy of the grandest possible visual language.

This show is a fitting occasion: a chance to see a genuinely singular, still-controversial photographic practice presented with the scholarly care usually reserved for painting retrospectives.

venue.name: Fahey/Klein Gallery
venue.about: Fahey/Klein Gallery is a Los Angeles photography gallery founded in 1986 by David Fahey and Randee Klein Devlin. Ken Devlin joined as co-owner in 1998; David Fahey has led the gallery since 2016. Located on North La Brea Avenue, the gallery specializes in 20th-century and contemporary fine art photography, with an inventory of more than 8,000 prints spanning portraiture, nudes, landscapes, still life, reportage and documentary work. Its exhibition program has featured photographers from Edward Weston and Man Ray to Herb Ritts and James Nachtwey, and the gallery mounts new two-person shows roughly every five weeks. Staff also curate touring exhibitions for museums and galleries abroad, contribute to photography publications, and maintain an active secondary-market and private-collection advisory practice.

shows.title: Origins of Matter
shows.artist: Hibiscus TV (Amy Kaps and Kaye Freeman)
shows.description:
Amy Kaps and Kaye Freeman have worked together as the collaborative duo Hibiscus TV since 2018, and "Origins of Matter" is the fullest airing yet of their joint practice: paintings, sculpture, hand-built costume and video knitted into one sprawling, maximalist environment. Industrial scrap and cast-off domestic objects get remade into feral, glittering regalia that the two artists then wear in staged performances against room-sized, neon-hot canvases — the show functions less like a static exhibition than an ongoing theatrical residency inside the gallery.

Both artists are past 60, and part of what makes the project pointed is its refusal of any quiet, tasteful late style — instead there's an appetite for excess, color and physical risk that reads as a deliberate argument about what older women artists are allowed to do. Thematically the work keeps circling the same tension: abundance next to scarcity, glamor next to waste, connection next to isolation, using the detritus of consumer culture as its raw material.

Over the run of the show Matter Studio Gallery is hosting three live performance-and-film events (Aug 23, Aug 30, Sept 6) plus a poetry reading, so the gallery itself becomes a stage as much as a viewing room — worth timing a visit to one of those dates if possible, though the paintings and sculptural costumes are on view throughout.

shows.title: Duskborn
shows.description:
Helena Reis's first mini-solo at Copro Gallery gathers six small works on wood panel, each about a foot square, built up with watercolor pencil, watercolor, acrylic, gouache and gold leaf. The Lisbon-based artist paints a private bestiary of hooded figures, birds and half-human creatures rendered in a palette of dusky blues and warm ochres — imagery she's described as balancing something creepy and cute in equal measure.

The small scale and mixed-media layering give the paintings the feel of illuminated manuscript pages or storybook illustrations gone slightly feral. Reis has said the work grew out of turning her own fears and nightmares into something she could look at directly, even find humor in — a kind of exposure therapy carried out one gilded, moody little panel at a time.

It's a quiet, densely worked show, worth a close look on the same visit as Mook Simpson's "America Dreaming" and Dale Sizer's mini-show, both hanging concurrently in the same space.

shows.title: SURFACE/TENSION
shows.description:
Brooks Shane Salzwedel builds his landscapes the way a draftsman builds a bridge: layer by layer, in graphite, tape, colored pencil, and resin poured over mylar and panel. The results are hazy, backlit scenes — conifer stands, water towers, industrial armatures — that seem to hover somewhere between a photograph, a blueprint, and a memory going soft at the edges. SURFACE/TENSION gathers a new body of these layered works, continuing the LA-based artist's long-running interest in the friction between built infrastructure and the wild land it interrupts.

Salzwedel has spent nearly two decades refining this resin-and-graphite technique, showing from Seattle to Honolulu to London, and the works here extend that vocabulary into new territory. The pieces reward close looking: what first reads as fog or distance turns out to be a literal buildup of translucent material sitting on top of the drawn image, so the "atmosphere" in these landscapes is physically present on the surface, not just illustrated.

At Lola Gallery's light-filled Chinatown space, the show benefits from the room's natural light and movable walls, which let the paintings breathe individually rather than crowding into a single sightline. It's a tightly focused solo outing — a good entry point for anyone curious about the current crop of LA artists working at the intersection of landscape painting and industrial material.

shows.title: America Dreaming
shows.description:
Mook Simpson paints over reproductions of 19th-century American frontier paintings — Bierstadt, Remington, Charles Marion Russell, George Caleb Bingham — inserting bronco-riding tentacled creatures, alien visitors, and other invasive oddities into the found Western tableaux. The effect is a sly, cartoonish vandalism of Manifest Destiny iconography: the same wagon trains and buffalo hunts that once mythologized the American frontier are recast as sites of strange visitation, undercutting their heroic tone with pulp-comic humor.

The show runs alongside solo presentations by Helena Reis and Dale Sizer in Copro's other rooms. Reis contributes small, jewel-toned panels — gold leaf, oil and acrylic renderings of birds and winged figures rendered with a devotional, illuminated-manuscript intensity that plays well against Simpson's rowdier revisionism next door.

shows.title: Vanished Venice: Ship Cafe + The Annual Venice Canal Festivals
shows.description:
This two-part exhibition inaugurates the Venice Heritage Museum's project of documenting the pieces of the neighborhood's built environment and public life that have disappeared. The first strand, Vanished Venice: Ship Cafe, traces the history of a landmark restaurant and hotel built in the shape of a galleon that anchored the boardwalk from 1905 to 1946, using photographs and ephemera from the museum's archive to reconstruct a piece of the original Venice-of-America fantasy that Abbot Kinney built and that long ago burned away.

The companion strand, The Annual Venice Canal Festivals, assembles photographs and documents from the community archive covering the canal festivals held between 1969 and 1976 — grassroots celebrations that doubled as public declarations of the canals' worth at a moment when their future as a neighborhood, rather than a parking lot or freeway easement, was very much in doubt.

Together the two shows are a compact history lesson in how Venice residents have repeatedly had to fight for and reimagine their own neighborhood, told entirely through the museum's community-sourced photographs and records rather than official archives. It's a fitting subject for a museum that itself only recently found a permanent home, and it rewards the kind of close looking that a small, single-room museum makes possible.

shows.title: To Witness Is Never Entirely Passive
shows.artist: Sahab Zaribaf, Ximena Del Cerro, Mary Linda Moss, Mei Xian Qiu, Michal Greenfield, Maria Adela Diaz
shows.description:
Tiger Strikes Asteroid's Los Angeles outpost turns its project space over to a loose coalition of artists, journalists and activists for this six-person show built around a single question: what do we owe the things we witness? Curated by TSA-LA member Fatemeh Burnes, the exhibition treats photography, sculpture, installation, painting and performance documentation as different tools for the same job — holding a mirror up to conflict, migration and injustice without pretending to resolve them.

The roster mixes practicing photojournalists with studio artists, which gives the show an unusual friction. Sahab Zaribaf, an Iranian-born photographer whose images have run through Getty and AFP, contributes press-honed images of moments that resist tidy narratives. Mei Xian Qiu's scroll-and-puppet installation Angel Island revisits the poetry Chinese detainees etched into the walls of the Angel Island immigration station, while Guatemalan-born, LA-based Maria Adela Diaz brings her body-centered performance practice to bear on questions of patriarchy and displacement. Sculptor Mary Linda Moss and painter Michal Greenfield work in more interior registers, using organic materials and portraiture to trace how history and trauma settle into the body.

It's a modest, artist-run show rather than a blockbuster. Worth a visit for anyone interested in how contemporary art is grappling with journalism's crisis of authority and the ethics of looking.

shows.title: Dale Sizer: Mini Show
shows.description:
Dale Sizer's four-painting mini-show at Copro turns Old Hollywood into pulp-glamour icon painting: Barbara Payton, Gene Tierney, Marilyn Monroe and a trio of "Valley of the Dolls" stars (Sharon Tate, Barbara Parkins, Patty Duke) get the mixed-media, acrylic-on-canvas treatment, their faces rendered with the graphic punch of vintage movie-poster art.

Sizer's background is exactly what you'd guess from the work — decades as an illustrator and animation background painter for studios including Disney, Warner Bros. and 20th Century Fox, plus record-cover and ad work for major labels and brands. That commercial-art fluency shows in how cleanly these portraits read: bold, poster-ready compositions built for maximum star-power at a glance, tinged with the melancholy that tends to follow stories about doomed Hollywood starlets.

It's a small, focused hang running alongside Mook Simpson's "America Dreaming" and Helena Reis's "Duskborn" in Copro's August rotation.

shows.title: From Delicate to Dynamic
shows.dates_note: Venue site gives no exact opening date; closing confirmed by its calendar entry "Closing of 'From Delicate to Dynamic'" on 9/12/2026. Start date estimated from show being third in a run of exhibitions this year — treat as approximate.
shows.description:
Curator Dale Youngman has put together a group survey of abstraction that deliberately avoids picking a side in the old quiet-versus-loud debate. The checklist runs from spare, meditative compositions to thickly worked, high-contrast pieces built on color and gesture, and the point seems to be showing visitors how much territory the word "abstract" actually covers.

Seventeen artists are in the mix, including Bill Sherwood, Clara Berta, Cody Bayne, DAK (David A. Knudsen), Gil Tepper, Lina Kogan, and Varoujan Hovakimyan, giving the show enough range that no single hand or palette dominates. The gallery has paired the exhibition with two artist panels — one on tool-driven process, another on whether abstract work can carry narrative — which suggests the curatorial interest here is as much in method as in finished surface.

Blue & The Muse is a small Little Tokyo-adjacent space, and shows like this one are exactly its niche: accessible entry points into abstraction for a general audience, without the market-driven throat-clearing of a blue-chip gallery.

shows.title: Words Matter
shows.description:
Words Matter gathers seventeen artists from Tierra del Sol's studio program around a single, deceptively simple question: what happens when text itself becomes the material of art? The show turns its walls over to visitors as well — inviting people to write, draw, and tag directly on the gallery walls, turning the exhibition into a growing collective mural over its run.

Among the standouts are Leon Fuller, a longtime Tierra artist since the late 1990s whose text-and-drawing works pull from mass media and celebrity culture, and Joe Zaldivar, whose fictional advertisements mimic real brands while subverting their language. Mary Lou Dimsdale contributes electric, mosaic-toned pieces built from scavenged news text. A sound piece, Exquisite Dream, stitches together studio artists' recorded dream accounts into one collaborative audio work playing in the gallery's Annex, echoing the show's larger interest in voice, collectivity, and what gets said versus what gets silenced.

It's a rare kind of group show — genuinely interactive, unpretentious about its methods, and a useful reminder that outsider and disability-inclusive art spaces in LA are producing some of the city's most inventive text-based work right now.

venue.name: Tierra Del Sol Gallery
venue.about: Tierra del Sol Gallery is the exhibition space of the Tierra del Sol Foundation, a Los Angeles-area nonprofit founded in 1971 that supports artists with disabilities through studio space, career development, and materials. A dedicated gallery opened in West Hollywood in 2019 to expand the foundation's programming and connect its artists with a wider audience. The gallery organizes year-round exhibitions and events, frequently inviting guest curators such as Alison Saar, Darren Romanelli, and jill moniz. Its program centers on drawing, painting, ceramics, and textile work by self-taught and outsider artists, with pieces acquired by institutions including MoMA, the American Folk Art Museum, and El Museo del Barrio. Proceeds from sales support the artists and the broader foundation.

shows.title: Faces Explained Away by the Light of Day
shows.artist: Exene Cervenka, David Buckingham, Edward Carbajal, Gary Wong, and Cesar Massturd
shows.description:
This Chinatown group show gathers five artists whose work grew out of Los Angeles' underground music, skate, and street scenes rather than art-school pedigree, and the results feel appropriately unpolished and personal. The marquee name is Exene Cervenka, co-founder and singer of the punk band X, whose collages and mixed-media pieces recombine found photographs and scavenged ephemera into small, plainspoken statements — visual cousins to her lyric writing. Alongside her, David Buckingham welds and paints on salvaged desert steel, turning rusted industrial scrap into wall works with a wry, Americana-inflected sense of humor.

Gary Wong, a Chouinard-trained painter who co-founded Gallery 66 in the 1960s and later ran with the Jook Savages collective, contributes layered paintings that fuse his Chinese American background with blues music and California car and surf culture — a long career's worth of cross-pollination distilled into a handful of canvases. Edward Carbajal, a longtime editorial cartoonist for La Opinión and co-founder of the Boathouse Gallery at Plaza de la Raza, shows selections from his surreal, satirical "Mutant Picasso" series, while Cesar Massturd, an Otis grad and founder of the TURD skate/art collective, brings a rawer, punk-adjacent graphic sensibility shaped by East LA street life.

Taken together, the show reads less like a themed group exhibition and more like a loose portrait of a specific corner of LA's creative underground — the overlapping worlds of punk, lowrider and skate culture, and Chicano art institutions that rarely get grouped together this explicitly. It's a solid pick for anyone curious about the scrappier, music-adjacent side of the city's art history rather than its gallery-circuit mainstream.

shows.title: Madonna: The Rise of the Material Girl (1980–1985)
shows.description:
Before "Madonna" meant stadium tours and reinvention as a career strategy, it meant a downtown New York dancer-turned-singer who insisted on writing her own songs and building her own image from the ground up. This photography show pulls together seven photographers — Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Marc Canter, Mark Weiss, Mick Rock, and Richard Corman — who were in the room during those first five years, from club gigs and cassette-tape hustling to the arena-scale Like a Virgin tour of 1985.

What comes through across the prints is less a chronicle of stardom than a document of instinct: Madonna turning down a packaged pop career in Paris to keep creative control, bringing demos straight to New York DJs instead of waiting for a label, and treating her collaborators — photographers, stylists, dancers — as co-authors of a visual identity rather than hired help. Feingold's and Rock's early portraits catch her still becoming that persona in real time, all lace and attitude and un-self-conscious ambition, while Canter's tour photographs from the Universal Amphitheatre show the finished performer arriving.

Musichead Gallery, a Sunset Boulevard fixture built around rock-and-roll photography, timed the show to Madonna's new album and her first partnership with Grindr — proof, as the gallery's curator puts it, that the risk-taking on display in these early pictures never really stopped. For anyone who thinks of Madonna as pure spectacle, this is a useful corrective: a look at the specific, unglamorous decisions that built the spectacle in the first place.

venue.name: Musichead Gallery
venue.about: Musichead Gallery is a Los Angeles gallery devoted to fine-art music photography, founded in 1998 by Detroit-born music entrepreneur Sam Milgrom, who previously ran the record store Sam's Jams and the live venue The Magic Bag before relocating to the West Coast. Located on Sunset Boulevard in Hollywood, the gallery represents more than eighty music photographers and offers vintage and contemporary prints spanning decades of rock, pop, jazz, and soul history, alongside in-house custom framing and art-consultancy services. Its rotating exhibitions have focused on individual artists and eras, from Miles Davis and Joni Mitchell to Oasis and Madonna, often drawing on photographers' archives and estates.

shows.title: A Gaze Through Time: Contemporary Reflections on Memory and History
shows.artist: Tahmineh Javanbakht, Shadi Yousefian, Rashin Kheiriyeh, Mohammad Barrangi, Nicky Nodjoumi
shows.description:
This group show inaugurates ADVOCARTSY's new Downtown LA space and gathers five artists of Iranian origin whose work circles around memory as something unstable and alive rather than fixed. Tahmineh Javanbakht's mirror-mosaic wall reliefs draw on the geometric mirror-work found in Iranian shrines and palaces, turning fractured reflection into a metaphor for fragmented recollection. Rashin Kheiriyeh contributes large, richly worked paintings — built up with oil, ink, gold and copper leaf, even espresso — that reimagine episodes from the Shahnameh, Iran's great medieval epic, as a way of asking what old stories still have to say to the present.

Mohammad Barrangi's reverse-transfer prints on raw canvas rework Qajar-era portrait conventions into looser, more contemporary figures, while Shadi Yousefian's collaged panels of actual handwritten letters turn personal correspondence — the residue of migration and family separation — into abstracted, textured surfaces. The inclusion of two paintings by Nicky Nodjoumi, a senior figure known for decades of biting political allegory, gives the show its sharpest edge, tying private memory to the performance of political power.

Taken together the works move between the intimate and the historical, using craft-intensive, materially dense processes — gold leaf, mirror, layered paper — to slow down looking itself. It's a strong first outing for the gallery's new location and a good entry point for anyone wanting a broad, well-chosen sample of contemporary Iranian diaspora art in one room.

shows.title: f8 Group Photography Show
shows.artist: Cyndi Bemel, Steve Hymon, Richard Johnston, Dennis Lee, Krishna Malhotra, Jim Staub, and Bill Wishner
shows.description:
Once a week for nearly two decades, a small circle of photographers has been meeting in Pasadena to talk seriously about pictures — not just their own, but the history of the medium generally, from old masters to whoever the group happens to invite that week. This show is the public face of that private habit: seven members of the f8 Pasadena Salon, founded by Bill Wishner in 2007, presenting a cross-section of what nearly twenty years of close looking has produced.

Because the show comes out of a discussion group rather than a single curatorial premise, it reads less like a thesis and more like a conversation captured mid-sentence — different photographic sensibilities and subjects sitting side by side, unified mainly by a shared seriousness about craft. It's the kind of show that rewards slow looking, less about any single knockout image than the cumulative sense of a community that has spent years teaching each other how to see.

LA Artcore has operated as a scrappy, community-minded nonprofit in Little Tokyo since 1979, and a photo salon show like this one is squarely in its wheelhouse: modest, unglamorous, and genuinely rooted in the city's amateur and semi-professional art ecosystem rather than its market.

venue.name: LA Artcore Union Center for the Arts

shows.title: To Share a Stomach
shows.description:
Organized by Aram Moshayedi with a circle of Iranian curators, writers, and artists as consultants, this group exhibition grew out of an unusual constraint: the works on view were conceived through proposals, instructions, and letters sent by artists living and working inside Iran, then physically realized by other artists and collaborators acting as their proxies. The project took shape in the shadow of specific, recent crisis — daily bombardment and an extended nationwide internet blackout — conditions that made direct authorship and even ordinary communication impossible for the artists who originated the ideas.

The result is less a conventional survey than a study in transmission and trust: what happens to an artwork when the hand that finishes it is not the mind that conceived it. The Brick's installation photographs suggest a spare, deliberately unresolved installation, appropriate to a show built on incomplete information and long-distance instruction rather than finished objects arriving intact.

It's a timely, quietly political exhibition, and it rewards visitors willing to read wall text and press materials as carefully as the art itself.

shows.title: Through the Sun
shows.description:
Shaghayegh Cyrous builds immersive video and sound installations out of Persian mythology, treating ancient stories as living material rather than historical decoration. Through the Sun draws its structure from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh — the medieval Persian epic — pulling on the story of Siavash, who walks through fire to prove his innocence, and Rostam's trials in the Haft Khan, to build a meditation on passage, endurance, and transformation. Fire and light become recurring thresholds throughout the work: forces that test, reveal, and ultimately renew whoever moves through them.

The show's centerpiece is Bagh (The Garden), a collaged video and sound work combining original and archival footage, staged within the gallery as a theatrical, dreamlike environment rather than a straightforward screening. Cyrous, who trained in Tehran and later earned an MFA in Social Practice at California College of the Arts, has built a career translating inherited myth and oral tradition into contemporary, often site-specific installations — her work has appeared everywhere from Tehran's MOCA to the British Museum to billboards around Los Angeles.

What makes Through the Sun land is its refusal to treat Zoroastrian cosmology and Persian epic poetry as museum-piece antiquity. Cyrous treats the search for light as both a cosmic drama and a deeply personal one, shaped as much by contemporary political and geopolitical pressure as by ancient text. The show runs concurrently with a companion presentation, Breathe the Sun, at Telematic Media Arts in San Francisco.

shows.title: The Shadow Side of Everything – Pt 3
shows.description:
This exhibition is the third chapter of an ongoing painting exchange linking artists across London, Yorkshire, New York, Memphis, and now Los Angeles. Curated by Robert Melzmuf, Christopher Blyth, Karl Bielik, and Rob Hall, it gathers 46 painters whose work ranges from loose, gestural abstraction to tightly structured composition.

The through-line isn't a shared style but a shared commitment to painting as a live, cross-border conversation — each iteration of "The Shadow Side of Everything" has added new cities and new participants, and this LA leg treats the gallery's walls less like a finished statement than a snapshot of an evolving network of studios.

shows.title: Unlimited
shows.description:
Ji Oh's first solo show at Shatto Gallery gathers years of a genuinely restless, multidisciplinary practice under one loosely ironic title. Rather than settling into a single medium, Oh treats photography, textile, and found objects as raw material to be cut apart and rebuilt: photographs get cleaved and rewoven into new spatial patterns, fabric is dyed and sculpted until it behaves like paint, and salvaged objects get reassigned new functions and meanings.

The show's centerpiece, Light and Spirit, is a large fabric installation that patchworks translucent textile remnants into a quilt meant to catch light the way stained glass does — a fairly literal demonstration of Oh's core move, finding the latent "otherness" hiding inside an ordinary material. It's a smart, tactile show for anyone interested in where painting, textile art, and assemblage overlap, and Shatto's compact Wilshire Boulevard space suits the intimacy of the work.

Coming from a Southern California-based artist with an extensive multidisciplinary history, Unlimited reads as something like a career self-portrait — less about declaring a signature style than showing how many different things a single artistic sensibility can be made to do.

shows.title: Group Exhibition of Abstract Work
shows.description:
Not There closes out the summer with a straightforwardly titled group show built entirely around abstraction — a chance to see how a roster of artists working outside representational imagery handle color, gesture, and surface differently from one another. Given the gallery's mission of opening its Chinatown walls to under-represented artists, expect the checklist to skew toward names you won't already know from the bigger Chinatown or Culver City spaces.

Judging from the installation photography the gallery has posted, the show favors large-scale canvases hung salon-style against the gallery's raw walls, with plenty of texture — layered paint, torn and reworked surfaces, and some pieces that push into collage and mixed media. It's the kind of show that rewards wandering rather than a single guided read.

Not There has built a strong run of solo and two-artist shows in its small Gin Ling Way space over the past few years; this group format is a departure that lets the gallery show its range across several practices at once before the space cycles into its next solo commitment.

shows.title: all the ways to hold tender this land
shows.artist: Anais Franco, Francesca Lalanne, Maddy Inez, Brie Ruais
shows.description:
This group show, curated by Armory Exhibition Manager Danielle A. Hill, gathers four artists whose work grows out of direct physical relationships to land and material — ceramics, steel, wood, film, and even living organisms — to think through memory, ancestry, and ecological repair. It's a quietly urgent exhibition given its framing: the wall text draws on bell hooks' writing about Appalachia to ask what collective listening to land might look like in the aftermath of disaster.

That framing lands with particular weight in Pasadena, where the Eaton Fire of early 2025 devastated Altadena and the surrounding foothills just a year before this show opened. Brie Ruais, whose large-format clay works often record the physical act of pushing and shaping earth with her own body, contributes a video piece here; the other three artists work across sculpture and craft-adjacent processes that treat making as a form of care rather than pure aesthetics.

The show sits in the Armory's Mezzanine Gallery and is accompanied by public programs, including a hands-on Batchelder tile workshop with exhibiting artist Anais Franco and a curator-led walkthrough on the exhibition's closing weekend — both useful entry points if you want more than a quick look at the work.

venue.name: Armory Center for the Arts
venue.about: Founded in 1989, Armory Center for the Arts is a nonprofit visual arts organization based in a historic 1932 California National Guard Armory building in Old Pasadena. It operates as a hybrid museum and art school, presenting contemporary art exhibitions alongside artist-led education programs for children, teens, and adults. Its roots trace back to the Pasadena Art Institute's Junior Museum program (1922), later evolving through the Pasadena Art Museum's Children's Art Workshop and the Pasadena Art Workshops before becoming the Armory in 1989. The organization emphasizes socially engaged, often BIPOC-centered contemporary art and free community-based art education, serving over 18,000 people annually across Pasadena and Los Angeles County, with particular focus on under-resourced neighborhoods and system-impacted communities.

shows.title: The American Road Trip
shows.description:
This juried group exhibition from the California Art Club gathers dozens of plein air and studio painters working in the club's signature traditional, representational style, all riffing on the great American road trip. Timed to the 250th anniversary of the United States and the 175th anniversary of California statehood, the show is less about cars than about the landscapes and roadside moments a cross-country drive turns up: lone cypresses on coastal highways, diner-adjacent gas stations, farm stands, mission-era trails, and river crossings rendered in oil, watercolor, pastel, and colored pencil.

The work ranges widely in subject and mood, from Cliff Barnes's weathered cypress on Pebble Beach's 17-Mile Drive to John Kosta's twilight view of the Los Angeles River and its Beaux-Arts bridges, to Sandy Delehanty's glowing watercolor of Sedona's red rocks. Many of the artists write short first-person notes about the specific place and moment behind each painting, giving the show the feel of a collective travelogue as much as a themed art exhibition.

It's a good entry point for anyone curious about the California Art Club's ongoing commitment to representational and plein air painting traditions that trace back over a century in Southern California, exhibited in the modest historic setting of the Old Mill gallery in San Marino.

venue.name: California Art Club Gallery at The Old Mill
venue.address: 1120 Old Mill Road, San Marino, CA 91108

shows.title: Our Beautiful Nature
shows.description:
Galerie Lakaye pairs two very different painters in this two-person show built around landscape and the natural world. Patrick DeCastro's canvases lean into vivid, saturated color and loosely figured scenes — birds, water, foliage — that sit somewhere between observation and reverie, while Simon Edery's contributions bring a more graphic, patterned sensibility to similar subject matter, breaking the natural world into rhythmic shapes and repeated forms.

Seen together, the two bodies of work read as complementary takes on the same premise: nature not as a backdrop but as a set of colors, patterns, and moods to be reinterpreted on canvas. It's a lighter, warmer summer show — a chance to see how that curatorial eye extends to a broader, more international group of contemporary painters.

shows.title: Case Study: Adapt
shows.description:
"Case Study: Adapt" is the inaugural exhibition at Santa Monica's brand-new municipal gallery, and its subject is urgent and local: how architecture responds to disaster. The show gathers architectural models built by USC Architecture students working alongside ten professional firms, each proposing resilient, climate-adapted housing for families displaced by the 2025 Pacific Palisades and Altadena wildfires.

Rather than abstract design exercises, these are scaled, tangible studies of what rebuilding could look like — homes engineered to withstand fire while still feeling like homes, not bunkers. The project traces back to the Charles & Ray Eames Foundation's original Case Study House program, an explicit reference point for using architecture as a public, optimistic response to crisis.

As the city's first-ever municipal gallery, this space marks a notable civic experiment: using a corner of Bergamot Station's dense private-gallery ecosystem to showcase public-facing, socially engaged design work and pieces from Santa Monica's own Art Bank collection. It's a worthwhile stop for anyone interested in how Los Angeles is thinking, concretely, about rebuilding after fire.

shows.title: Ain't it Fun Always Being on the Run?
shows.description:
This group show, subtitled "Cole Dallas' Last Picture Show," gathers a loose crew of painters, sculptors, filmmakers and performers around designer Cole Dallas's own artisanal clothing label CD1974. Curated by Dallas together with Jordan Hubert, Mona Cesario, and Siena Soltis, it treats the gallery as a kind of backstage-meets-showroom, mixing garment-as-sculpture with more conventional studio work.

The roster — Charmont des Noir, T. Antonakis Kane, Luis Miguel Anaya, Wally Waliszewski, Hannah Baskin, Bella Stacia, and the collective Hot American Girls — spans painting, sculpture, and film, and the checklist is rounded out with live performance elements on select nights, keeping the exhibition from sitting still for its short two-and-a-half week run.

It's a good example of the scrappy, artist-driven programming that Art/Space 114 has built a reputation for in the Old Bank District: less a tidy thesis show than a snapshot of overlapping downtown LA social and creative circles, staged with real fashion-world flair.

shows.title: Eyes on the World / Americana Cookie Jar Icons
shows.description:
This paired presentation splits TAG's project rooms between two very different bodies of work. Noah Hass-Cohen's "Eyes on the World" is a ceramic sculpture practice, while Amit Cohen's "Americana Cookie Jar Icons" repurposes the kitschy, nostalgic form of the mid-century cookie jar as a vehicle for commentary on American pop iconography — taking a domestic collectible object and pushing it toward something more pointed and art-historically self-aware.

Pairing a sculptor working in clay with an artist reworking a specific vernacular ceramic form makes for a natural conversation about material, craft history and kitsch, even though the two practices arrived at the material from different directions. It's a good entry point for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are re-engaging with ceramics and "low" collectible forms rather than treating them as decorative background.

This is one part of TAG's broader September calendar of concurrent solo and group shows across the gallery's several rooms, running alongside the group show "LIGHT."

venue.name: The Artists Gallery (TAG)
venue.about: The Artists Gallery (TAG) is an artist-founded, not-for-profit arts cooperative now based in the Miracle Mile district of Los Angeles. Established in Santa Monica in 1993, TAG is run and staffed by its member artists rather than commercial dealers. Its program centers on Southern Californian, national, and international artists working across media, with monthly solo and group exhibitions plus recurring juried shows such as Made in the USA, the L.A. Open, and the Shelley Lazarus Excellence in Watercolor Exhibition. The gallery also hosts artist talks, studio nights, and community events, reflecting its mission to support free exploration of media, technique, and content among its member artists.

shows.title: Follow the Feather
shows.description:
GOBI's current show gives Ruoyi Shi a solo platform. "Follow the Feather" leans into the gallery's interest in objects that sit between art and function, and Shi's work continues that conversation between material, craft, and image.

Based on the installation photos, the show favors a light, airy hang with sculptural and wall-based pieces that play with fragility and motion, fitting the exhibition's avian title.

Catching "Follow the Feather" before it closes in late September is worthwhile for anyone interested in emerging sculpture and object-based practice.

shows.title: Unbound
shows.artist: Ariane Callender, Julia Deckman, Mel Deva, Shelly Floyd, Kyle Goderwis, Ashley Perez, Mark Rebennack, Sarah J.
shows.description:
Unbound gathers a roster of K&K's emerging and mid-career artists for a show built entirely around abstraction — work that has, as the gallery puts it, cut loose from realistic representation to chase feeling through layers, color, and line. It's a fitting subject for this Culver City Arts District storefront, which has made a mission of demystifying collecting for first-time buyers rather than chasing museum-scale statements.

Expect a wall of variety rather than a single unifying style: hard-edged geometric compositions next to loose gestural fields, mixed-media surfaces built up in layers, and color-forward pieces that read as much as mood as image. With eight artists sharing the space, the show works like a sampler platter of where non-objective painting is right now among LA's working studio artists — useful for anyone building a collection who wants to see a range of approaches side by side before committing to one.

K&K keeps its shows on a brisk roughly six-week rotation, so Unbound is very much a snapshot rather than a survey — see it while the paint is still fresh on the gallery walls. The opening reception doubled as an informal meet-the-artists mixer, in keeping with the gallery's low-pressure, "art is for everyone" ethos.

shows.title: LIGHT
shows.description:
"LIGHT" is one of TAG's regular themed group shows, gathering member artists of this longtime Wilshire Boulevard artists' collective around a single loose prompt — in this case light itself, in whatever medium or approach each participant chooses. TAG has run these seasonal theme shows for years (past editions have tackled water, fire, earth and force & energy), and they function as a kind of snapshot of the collective's range: painters, photographers and mixed-media artists all responding independently to the same word.

Because TAG is an artist-run cooperative rather than a commercial gallery with a single curatorial voice, these group shows tend to be eclectic by design — expect a wide swing in style and subject rather than a tightly argued thesis. That variety is part of the draw: it's a good way to get a broad sample of what a working, membership-based Los Angeles gallery looks like right now, alongside TAG's concurrent solo presentations in its adjoining project rooms.

venue.name: The Artists Gallery (TAG)
venue.about: The Artists Gallery (TAG) is an artist-founded, not-for-profit arts cooperative now based in the Miracle Mile district of Los Angeles. Established in Santa Monica in 1993, TAG is run and staffed by its member artists rather than commercial dealers. Its program centers on Southern Californian, national, and international artists working across media, with monthly solo and group exhibitions plus recurring juried shows such as Made in the USA, the L.A. Open, and the Shelley Lazarus Excellence in Watercolor Exhibition. The gallery also hosts artist talks, studio nights, and community events, reflecting its mission to support free exploration of media, technique, and content among its member artists.

shows.title: The Sound of Gordon Parks
shows.description:
Everyone knows Gordon Parks the photographer — the FSA images, the Life magazine essays, "American Gothic" with Ella Watson posed in front of a flag. Fewer people know that Parks composed music for most of his adult life, writing piano concertos and film scores with the same fluency he brought to a camera. CAAM's exhibition, built with the Gordon Parks Foundation and Parks's longtime musical collaborator Mario Sprouse, is the rare show that treats that second career as a subject in its own right rather than a footnote.

Expect an immersive mix of recordings, video, and archival material — sheet music, correspondence, session photographs — that reframes Parks's visual work as part of a single, continuous creative practice rather than a separate hobby. It's a smart curatorial move for an artist whose photographs are so iconic they can overshadow everything else he made.

For a museum whose galleries sit just off the Coliseum in Exposition Park, this is exactly the kind of deep-cut biographical show that rewards the trip: intimate, well-researched, and focused on an artist whose reputation could easily fill a much shallower exhibition.

shows.title: SPACE IS THE PLACE: Selections from the Hammer Contemporary Collection
shows.description:
Borrowing its title from Sun Ra's 1973 album and 1974 film, this Hammer Contemporary Collection survey turns "space" into a wide-open curatorial question. Rather than a single thesis, the show works through a constellation of ideas — Afrofuturism, migration, domestic space, and the simple, radical act of taking up room in the world — using nearly thirty artists drawn entirely from the museum's own holdings. It's a smart way to make an encyclopedic collection feel like a pointed argument.

The range of material is the pleasure here: Arthur Jafa's charged image-work sits near Betye Saar's assemblage and Fred Eversley's polished resin lenses, while younger voices like Lauren Halsey, Juliana Huxtable, and Danielle Dean push the same questions of belonging and placemaking into sculpture, photography, and video. Thomas J Price's monumental bronze of a Black woman glancing at her phone anchors one gallery with a quiet, outsized authority, and Cauleen Smith's moving-image work threads a more lyrical, essayistic register through the show.

Because this is a free-admission museum presentation rather than a commercial gallery show, there's room to wander and let the connections accumulate — between Nayland Blake's early assemblage and Rodney McMillian's material politics, between Michael Queenland's tiled wall pieces and Arcmanoro Niles's saturated interiors. It's a strong, generous survey of how Los Angeles-connected artists have used the museum's collection to think about space as both a physical and political condition, and a good reminder of how deep the Hammer's contemporary holdings actually run.

venue.name: Hammer Museum
venue.about: The Hammer Museum is a UCLA-affiliated contemporary art museum in Westwood, Los Angeles, founded by Armand Hammer and opened in November 1990. Since a 1994 partnership agreement, it has been operated by UCLA, absorbing the collections of the Wight Art Gallery and the Grunwald Center for the Graphic Arts as well as the Franklin D. Murphy Sculpture Garden. Directors have included Henry Hopkins, Ann Philbin (1999–2024), and current director Zoë Ryan (from 2025). The museum is known for its Made in L.A. biennial, the ongoing Hammer Projects series, and an active calendar of lectures, film, and public programs. Admission is free.

shows.title: The Expanding Field: MOCA's Collection from the 1940s to 1970s
shows.description:
MOCA turns to its own holdings for this survey, using the postwar decades as a case study in how contemporary art actually got that way. Rather than a tidy march from Abstract Expressionism to Pop to Minimalism, the show leans into the tangle of movements that competed and overlapped in the 1940s through 70s, pulling together painting, sculpture, and assemblage from the museum's deep permanent collection.

It's the kind of show that rewards close looking rather than a quick lap: expect the density of a collection exhibition, with lesser-shown works from the vault set alongside the postwar heavyweights MOCA is known for. For a museum literally founded to steward this era of art, this is as close to a mission statement as it gets, and a good primer for anyone trying to understand how Los Angeles's own postwar scene fit into the larger story.

As a collection show drawing entirely from MOCA's holdings, it's a good complement to more thematic, single-artist exhibitions elsewhere in the building, and free admission days make it an easy add to a Downtown museum visit before it closes in late September.

venue.name: MOCA Grand Avenue
venue.about: MOCA, founded in 1979, is Los Angeles's leading museum dedicated to contemporary art, built around a collection of nearly 8,000 works with deep holdings in LA-based practice alongside international art. MOCA Grand Avenue, the museum's original and flagship site in downtown LA, was designed by architect Arata Isozaki in the 1980s and opened as his first completed US project, announcing MOCA as a major architectural presence on Bunker Hill. The museum also operates The Geffen Contemporary at MOCA, a renovated warehouse in Little Tokyo, and stewards Michael Heizer's land-art work Double Negative in Nevada. Programming spans monographic and thematic exhibitions, education initiatives, publishing, and new-media engagement.

shows.title: Outsiders, Outcasts, Rebels + Weirdos: Punk Culture 1976–86
shows.description:
It's a little disorienting to find safety pins and Xeroxed flyers in a museum best known for its Jewish ceremonial art collection, and that's precisely the point. The Skirball's punk survey traces the decade between 1976 and 1986 through gig posters, stage-worn clothing, zines, and photography, with particular attention to the Jewish musicians, promoters, and scene-builders who shaped Los Angeles punk from the inside — a history that rarely gets its due next to the CBGB-centric New York narrative.

The show leans into ephemera over relics: hand-lettered flyers for shows at the Masque and the Whisky, cut-and-paste zine pages, and the visual language of a subculture that treated the photocopier as its primary printing press. Cliff Roman of the Germs and other LA scene veterans figure into the accompanying programming.

Paired with the concurrent comic-book survey down the hall, it makes for an unexpectedly countercultural season at a campus better known for Noah's Ark installations and Passover programming — proof that the Skirball's curators are willing to get a little scrappy.

shows.title: Sonsonetes y Menjurges (Tunes and Concoctions)
shows.description:
Avenue 50 Studio opens its fall season with a solo presentation from Rigoberto Soltero, whose Spanish-language title — roughly "tunes and concoctions" — hints at a practice built from mixture: sound, memory, and folk imagery blended into a single visual vocabulary. Given the venue's long-standing commitment to Chicano and Latino visual culture, expect work that draws on vernacular and popular traditions filtered through a personal, handmade sensibility.

Avenue 50 has spent more than two decades as one of Northeast LA's most consistent platforms for Latino and Chicano artists, and a solo show like this one is typical of its programming: modest in scale, rooted in community, and unafraid of bilingual, culturally specific titling that doesn't get diluted for a broader audience.

Located on Figueroa Street in Highland Park, the gallery remains a rare fixture of the neighborhood's original arts enclave, and this exhibition offers a good entry point for anyone curious about the Chicano-art through-line that still runs through NELA's gallery scene.

venue.name: Avenue 50 Studio
venue.about: Avenue 50 Studio is a nonprofit arts presentation organization in the Highland Park neighborhood of Northeast Los Angeles. Founded in 2000 by Kathy Gallegos, who continues to serve as its Founding Executive and Artistic Director, the space describes its mission as bridging cultures through content-driven visual art grounded in Latina/o culture and the Northeast LA community. The program mixes exhibitions of emerging and established artists with literary programming, including a long-running poetry series, workshops, and community projects such as mural restoration. Governed by a volunteer board of directors alongside its staff, the studio positions itself as a destination gallery for socially engaged, culturally rooted contemporary art.

shows.title: Ecce Artifex
shows.description:
Michael Flechtner has spent decades pushing neon past its signage roots into full sculptural territory, and this survey at the Museum of Neon Art gathers work spanning that career. Flechtner came up learning the trade in a six-week bending class in Kansas before moving to Los Angeles to work commercial neon by day and his own sculptures by night, and that hybrid background shows in the work: pieces that use the vocabulary of signage — bent glass tubing, buzzing color, graphic punch — but bend it toward visual puns and conceptual play rather than advertising.

The show's title, "Ecce Artifex" ("Behold the Craftsman"), answers his 1991 MONA solo debut "Ecce Signum" ("Behold the Sign"), and the pairing frames this as a kind of career-spanning victory lap for an artist who has quietly shaped how the medium is treated as art rather than commerce. Flechtner is also the fabricator behind neon elements in works by artists like Bruce Nauman, Doug Aitken, and Betye Saar, so this is also a rare chance to see his own authorial voice front and center rather than in service of someone else's piece.

Flechtner's show anchors the museum's current run of exhibitions and is worth catching before it closes in late September.

shows.title: Deep Cuts: Block Printing Across Cultures
shows.description:
Block printing might be the oldest way humans figured out how to make the same image over and over, and this sprawling survey — more than 150 objects from Asia, Europe, and the Americas — treats it as both an art form and a communication technology. Patterned Indian textiles sit alongside illustrated Kelmscott Press books, German Expressionist woodcuts, and the razor-sharp contemporary prints of Christiane Baumgartner, tracing a single technique across wildly different cultures and centuries.

A section built with the Los Angeles textile studio Block Shop brings the story into the present, showing how a centuries-old process still has working artists and designers finding new uses for it. It's a show built for close looking — the pleasure here is in noticing how a carved block, whether cutting fabric patterns or fine art editions, keeps generating new visual possibilities out of a very old constraint. Note that this is in its final month, closing September 13.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
venue.about: LACMA is the largest art museum in the western United States, holding some 155,000 objects spanning 6,000 years of global art history. It traces its roots to the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, and Art (1910) and became an independent institution in 1961, opening on Wilshire Boulevard in 1965. The campus has grown through additions including the Anderson/Art of the Americas Building, the Pavilion for Japanese Art, BCAM, and the Resnick Pavilion, culminating in the 2026 opening of the Peter Zumthor-designed David Geffen Galleries. Located on Wilshire Boulevard in the Miracle Mile, LACMA presents rotating exhibitions across its global collection alongside public programs, education initiatives, and community partnerships, including a gallery at Charles White Elementary School.

shows.title: A Palace in Time
shows.description:
Two Los Angeles painters and life partners share a gallery for an exhibition built around the idea of the Sabbath as, in Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase, "a palace in time." Robert Russell contributes softly rendered still lifes of Jewish ritual objects — Kiddush cups, yahrzeit candles — painted with a hazy, almost dissolving touch that turns ordinary domestic objects into vessels of memory and quiet loss.

Lisa Edelstein works from her own family photo archive, reconstructing scenes of 1970s suburban New Jersey Jewish life: crowded multigenerational gatherings, patterned wallpaper and furniture, small unposed moments of touch and affection. Her palette and subject matter read as warmer and more anecdotal than Russell's, and the pairing of the two bodies of work sets an intimate, personal register against a more symbolic, object-based one.

Together the two painters build a meditation on ritual, domestic time, and inherited memory — what gets held onto materially versus what only survives as recollection. It's a modestly scaled, human-sized show, and it closes the same week as the museum's punk exhibition, so it's worth pairing on one visit.

shows.title: Belongings: Changing Hands and Shifting Meanings in African Arts
shows.description:
Most museum displays of African art present objects at the moment of their making, explaining how a mask or figure was meant to be used within its originating community. This show does something different: it tracks what happened to these objects afterward — the string of hands, markets, and meanings they passed through on the way from Africa to a Los Angeles museum vitrine.

Organized around four stages of an object's journey — from original owners, to colonial-era acquisition, to the European secondary market, to arrival at the Fowler — the exhibition uses carved masks, figures, and other historical African works as case studies in the politics of collecting. A featured Bamileke Tsesah mask from Cameroon, gifted via the Wellcome Trust, stands as a good example of the kind of object under scrutiny here: beautifully carved, but carrying a provenance far more tangled than a simple label usually admits.

The show is explicitly an argument about museum authority — it wants visitors to understand that no wall text is the final word, and that objects "contain multitudes" as they move between owners and contexts. That makes it a useful, slightly uncomfortable companion piece to more celebratory African-art displays, and a good entry point for anyone curious about restitution debates playing out at museums across the US and Europe right now.

shows.title: (Be)Spoken: Poems from Our Asian American Voices
shows.description:
Spoken word gets a gallery treatment in this show co-curated by rapper and poet Jason Chu, who assembled seven voices from LA's Asian American poetry and performance scene — Tanzila "Taz" Ahmed, arianna lady basco, Emdash, Sun Luu, Michelle Myers, STEADY, and Catzie Vilayphonh. Rather than simply mount text on the wall, the museum translates their poems into installation, photography, and staged imagery, treating performance as a visual medium as much as a verbal one.

The result is less a literary archive than an immersive listening room: visitors move through pieces that foreground identity, resilience, and community across generations of Chinese American and broader AAPI experience. It's a fitting complement to CAM's historical galleries next door, pulling the museum's mission — preserving Chinese American history — into the present tense of contemporary voice and protest poetry.

Closing September 6, this is a last chance to catch a show that treats poetry as a communal, embodied act rather than a page-bound one.

shows.title: We Belong Here
shows.description:
We Belong Here turns the exterior walls of LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes into a rotating outdoor gallery of projections and neon signage, made in coordination with four other Los Angeles institutions — the California Community Foundation, JANM, MOLAA, and SPARC — each showing its own selection on its own building. The work leans hard into protest graphics: Lalo Alcaraz, Ernesto Yerena Montejano, Man One, and others contribute images that speak directly to immigration enforcement, detention, and the experience of being undocumented in this political moment.

It's public art in the most literal sense — visible from the street after dark, free to encounter without a ticket — and it functions as a companion piece to CCF's "Am I Next" campaign against silence in the face of ICE activity in Los Angeles. Content shifts by site, so LA Plaza's Main Street-facing selection is only part of a citywide project, but the images shown here (including Alcaraz's recurring "ICE Out of LA" motif) are pointed, current, and unambiguous about whose side the institution is on.

Given the museum's mission as a keeper of Latino LA history, the piece reads as an extension of its core work rather than a departure — using its own walls to make a case for who the city belongs to.

venue.name: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes

shows.title: ReVOlt 1680/2180: Sirens & Sikas
shows.description:
Cochiti Pueblo artist Virgil Ortiz turns the history of the 1680 Pueblo Revolt into speculative fiction, imagining a future in which the rebels who drove Spanish colonizers from Puebloan land have interstellar allies. The exhibition presents Ortiz's sculptural figures — armored "Sirens," alien "artificers," and other characters rendered in the artist's distinctive blend of traditional Cochiti pottery techniques and sci-fi costuming — as part of an ongoing multi-chapter narrative he calls ReVOlt 1680/2180.

It's a sharp piece of world-building: Ortiz treats Po'pay's historic victory as the seed of an alternate timeline, using genre tropes (space travel, armor, insurgent technology) to keep a 340-year-old act of resistance alive as something forward-looking rather than archival. The figures are theatrical and highly detailed, closer to costume design and character concept art than to conventional ceramic sculpture.

The show is part of the Autry's larger Future Imaginaries: Indigenous Art, Fashion, Technology initiative and was produced under the PST ART: Art & Science Collide umbrella, so it sits at the intersection of contemporary Native art, fashion, and speculative design. Worth catching before it closes in early October — this run has been up since 2024 and is nearing the end of its extended stay at the museum.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: Jiroft: Seven Valleys in Bloom
shows.description:
Hiva Alizadeh takes her title from Jiroft, the southeastern Iranian archaeological site whose Bronze Age carved chlorite vessels rank among the oldest surviving examples of figurative art from the Iranian plateau. Working across painting and mixed media, Alizadeh translates that ancient visual vocabulary — spiraling florals, animal-headed motifs, dense surface patterning — into a contemporary register, treating the millennia-old carvings less as archaeology than as a living design language still available to draw from.

The paintings on view lean into saturated color and stylized botanical forms, suggesting gardens that are as much invented as remembered. There's a diaristic, almost devotional quality to the repetition of blooms and vines across the canvases, as if the artist is working through a personal iconography built from a shared cultural memory rather than direct observation.

The show is a fitting anchor: it treats a deep national history not as a fixed heritage to be illustrated but as material to be reactivated in paint. It's worth seeing alongside the two solo shows opening the same week at Gallery One, which round out a fuller picture of how different Iranian-American women artists are handling questions of memory, myth, and inheritance right now.

venue.name: Aabee Bleue Project
venue.about: Aabee Bleue Project is a contemporary art space in Downtown Los Angeles that builds connections among cultures, communities, and contemporary artistic practices. Through exhibitions, conversations, and public programs, the gallery introduces contemporary artists from Iran, the Middle East, and beyond to new audiences and contexts. It was founded by Sabrina Younesi and Narges Hamzianpour, and developed alongside Niloufar Binafard, who serves as Artist Liaison and Art Advisor. The program is driven by curiosity, collaboration, and a desire to create dialogue between artists, ideas, and communities, using art as a means to build cross-cultural dialogue, challenge perspectives, and create spaces for discovery.

shows.title: Storyless
shows.description:
Anali Taherian's Storyless is a brief, tightly wound solo presentation in the gallery's smaller Gallery One space — on view for just two weeks, which makes it feel more like a pointed statement than a survey. The title suggests a deliberate refusal of narrative, and the works lean into ambiguity: fragmented compositions and imagery that resist being read as illustration of any single event or memory.

There's a quietness to the installation that plays against the more maximalist, pattern-driven work showing concurrently in the Main Gallery. Taherian seems more interested in withholding than accumulating — leaving gaps in the picture plane, letting color and mark stand in for whatever story isn't being told.

Worth a visit if you're already coming for the Hiva Alizadeh show next door; the two exhibitions make an interesting pair, one insisting on inherited pattern and myth, the other stripping narrative away almost entirely.

Through exhibitions, conversations, and public programs, the gallery introduces contemporary artists from Iran, the Middle East, and beyond to new audiences and contexts. It was founded by Sabrina Younesi and Narges Hamzianpour, and developed alongside Niloufar Binafard, who serves as Artist Liaison and Art Advisor. The program is driven by curiosity, collaboration, and a desire to create dialogue between artists, ideas, and communities, using art as a means to build cross-cultural dialogue, challenge perspectives, and create spaces for discovery.

shows.title: Edmund Teske: On Olive Hill
shows.description:
Edmund Teske arrived at Olive Hill in 1943 as a young photographer who had studied under Frank Lloyd Wright at Taliesin, and this exhibition gathers his photographs of Hollyhock House during a formative, unstable moment in its history — the years before the site's major 1946 restoration, when the house was in visible disrepair. Aline Barnsdall invited Teske to live in a guest house on the property, giving him a darkroom and effectively making him an informal caretaker-in-residence.

The photographs on view document Wright's "California Romanza" in transition: sunlit courtyards and crumbling ornament, captured by an artist who described the place as sailing "with the clouds." Teske was known for double exposures and composite printing, techniques scholars have noted let him fold together different moments in time within a single frame — an approach especially suited to a building whose own history is one of decay, renewal, and reinvention.

All of the photographs were gifted to the City of Los Angeles by Michael and David Devine, and the show functions as a quiet historical counterpoint to the more polished, restored Hollyhock House visitors encounter today — a glimpse of the building's shabbier, more bohemian middle age, host to figures like Man Ray and John Lautner.

shows.title: Board Choice
shows.description:
For Avenue 50 Studio's 25th year, the gallery hands curatorial control to its own Board of Directors: each current or emeritus board member picked one or two artists whose work they personally admire, and the result is stitched together into a single group show. It's less a thematic exhibition than a group portrait of the people who've kept this Highland Park nonprofit running for a quarter-century — their taste, their relationships, their advocacy.

Artists span photography (Leopoldo Peña's black-and-white silver gelatin prints of Southern California vernacular structures), painting (Frank Romero, a name closely tied to LA's Chicano art history), and printmaking and mixed media from a roster of Eastside-connected artists including Armando Brito, Roberto Gutierrez, and Alex Donis. Because selections were made by personal admiration rather than a single curatorial thesis, expect real range in medium and generation.

Avenue 50 has been a fixture of the Highland Park/Northeast LA arts community since 2000, championing Latinx, Chicanx, and other under-recognized local artists, and this show doubles as an informal history lesson in who has shaped that mission from the inside.
