Founded in 2000 by Kathy Gallegos, who continues to serve as its Founding Executive and Artistic Director, the space describes its mission as bridging cultures through content-driven visual art grounded in Latina/o culture and the Northeast LA community. The program mixes exhibitions of emerging and established artists with literary programming, including a long-running poetry series, workshops, and community projects such as mural restoration. Governed by a volunteer board of directors alongside its staff, the studio positions itself as a destination gallery for socially engaged, culturally rooted contemporary art.

shows.title: Final Projects: Group LIX - spindrift LIX
shows.artist: Alexandra Kahl, Axel Koschier, and Sarah Silbernagel
shows.description:
Every six months, the MAK Center's Artists- and Architects-in-Residence program closes its cycle with a final-projects show at the Mackey Apartments, and this edition — Group LIX, titled spindrift LIX — presents new work by three residents: Sarah Silbernagel, an architect and filmmaker whose work engages social housing and participatory planning through film; Axel Koschier, an Austrian sculptor working across installation and mixed media; and Alexandra Kahl, whose practice spans posters, collage, flags, artist books, and video.

The show is necessarily a brief one — four days, capping a six-month residency — but it's a rare chance to see work made specifically in response to Rudolph Schindler's modernist Mackey Apartments, a building the residents have lived and worked in throughout their stay. Koschier arrives having recently shown at Art Sonje Center in Seoul; Silbernagel's films have been presented at the Venice Architecture Biennale and MUMOK Vienna.

Worth catching for anyone interested in the overlap between architecture and art practice, and in the MAK Center's role as one of the few L.A. institutions built around an international residency model rather than a permanent collection.

venue.name: MAK Center for Art and Architecture — Mackey Apartments
hours: By exhibition and event schedule; see makcenter.org

shows.title: Intervals of Presence: pentimento y esperanza
shows.description:
Yoab Vera builds his paintings out of oil, oil-stick, and concrete, layering and scraping back the surface so that older marks (pentimenti) show through the final image — a technique that gives the show its title and its central idea: hope and memory as things that get painted over but never fully erased. The large-format canvases on view balance warm, horizon-like bands of color with the rough, literal weight of concrete worked into the paint surface, pulling the work somewhere between landscape and material study.

Vera, who is Mexico City-born and LA-trained (MFA, UCLA), has been developing this vocabulary of sunrise and sunset imagery — some pieces explicitly dedicated "to Los Angeles" — across recent gallery and fair presentations in New York, Milan, and Mexico City. This body of work continues that trajectory with pieces that read as meditations on resilience and renewal, their titles mixing English and Spanish (esperanza, serenata) to match a practice that moves fluidly between places and languages.

It's a solid, mid-career survey of an artist whose surfaces reward close looking: what first appears as a simple warm gradient resolves, up close, into a history of the canvas's own making.

shows.title: Raina Lee
shows.description:
Raina Lee works mostly in ceramic, but much of her sculpture masquerades as something else: a painting, a postcard, a flat historical image reconstructed in fired clay. For this solo show she continues that sleight of hand with pieces like The Concert (after Vermeer, stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum) — a ceramic restaging of a famously unsolved art heist that turns an absence (the real painting has been missing since 1990) into a physical, handmade object again.

Lee, a Los Angeles-based artist who came to ceramics after a career shift and training at Glendale Community College, has built a practice around this kind of art-historical ventriloquism: remaking canonical images in an unglamorous, tactile medium that calls attention to the labor and translation involved in "returning" a lost or iconic picture to the world. It's a witty, conceptually sharp approach that treats ceramic sculpture as a vehicle for thinking about memory, loss, and reproduction.

Coming off a run of strong fair and gallery presentations, including Felix Art Fair and NADA New York, this is Lee's first solo outing at Make Room and a good opportunity to see a focused body of her postcard-and-painting-referencing sculpture together.

shows.title: Richard Avedon: Hollywood
shows.description:
This survey gathers more than 120 photographs Richard Avedon made of Hollywood across half a century, from the industry's golden age into the 2000s. It's less a greatest-hits package than an argument: that Hollywood itself, as Avedon photographed it, functions as a distinctly American myth-making machine, and that his portraits track how that myth was built, performed, and occasionally punctured.

The photographs span a huge range of subjects — actors, directors, writers, composers, producers — captured in Avedon's characteristic stark studio style, stripped of backdrop and ornament so that gesture, expression and costume carry all the information. Expect icons of old Hollywood (Charlie Chaplin, Humphrey Bogart, Katharine Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe) hung alongside later subjects like Nastassja Kinski, Tilda Swinton and Philip Seymour Hoffman, tracing a long arc of how fame gets pictured.

Avedon had his own complicated flirtation with the industry — he consulted on the 1957 musical "Funny Face," a film loosely inspired by his own early career, and reportedly considered leaving photography for directing — which gives this particular body of work a personal edge beyond simple assignment photography. Curated by the Richard Avedon Foundation, the show opens November 4 with a reception that evening.

shows.title: Night Carries Color
shows.description:
Lacey Stoffer's new body of work treats a painting's surface as a site of accumulated decisions rather than a single finished gesture. Working across linen, oil paint, hand-dyed yarn and thread, collage, and small hand-sculpted paper-clay pins, she builds up color fields and organic forms, then interrupts them — sewing yarn directly through the canvas, pinning and repositioning cut linen shapes before committing them with paint. The darker tones that give the show its title aren't meant as erasure; they're a kind of container that holds earlier layers in place even as they recede from view.

What makes this work compelling is the visible evidence of revision: pentimenti, holes left by yarn that was later removed, pin punctures that direct the eye like punctuation across the composition. Stoffer treats the linen almost as an instrument worked from both sides, and the physical back-and-forth of that process is legible in the final surface — nothing here is a clean first take.

This is Stoffer's solo debut at Good Mother Gallery's West Adams space, bringing a Los Angeles-based practice that's as much about tactile, durational process as it is about color and composition. For viewers who like to get close to a painting's surface, this is a rewarding show to spend time with.

shows.title: NextGEN: A New Generation of Artists
shows.description:
This group exhibition is a joint presentation between Thinkspace Projects and the Chicago-based All Star Press, pairing up artists from each gallery's roster rather than running two separate shows. The pitch is generational: a roster of emerging East and West Coast artists working across illustration-rooted painting, pop-surrealism, and street-art-adjacent styles, shown together to take the temperature of where contemporary low-brow and new-contemporary painting is headed next.

From the Thinkspace side the lineup includes Alex Achaval, Raymond Argumedo, Crisselle, and Brandon Hurley among others — artists whose work has moved through Thinkspace's program over the past few years — paired with All Star Press names like Adam Lister and Arrington Porter. The result functions less like a tightly curated thesis show and more like a snapshot survey, useful for seeing how a dozen-plus younger artists are each developing a distinct visual voice within a shared sensibility.

It's a good entry point if you're new to the gallery's program: rather than committing to one artist's full body of work, you get a sampler of the artists Thinkspace and its peer gallery are betting on right now.

shows.title: Ava McDonough
shows.description:
Ava McDonough paints in a meditative, almost obsessive register: small repeating strokes of oil, laid down one at a time until a canvas is completely covered, building images of butterfly wings, fish scales, and close-cropped lawns that read as much as fields of pure pattern as they do botanical studies. The Los Angeles-based, self-taught painter has described her process as a way of returning to an imagined rather than observed landscape, and the resulting works sit somewhere between hyperreal nature painting and abstraction.

This is House of Seiko's first show with McDonough, following her recent solo presentations in New York and a 2023 solo debut at Lowell Ryan Projects in Los Angeles. Given the gallery's program of pairing emerging West Coast voices with postwar historical material, her exacting, nature-driven paintings should make for a good counterpoint to the gallery's recent historical surveys.

shows.title: Keep This Between Us
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as the current show with no closing date published; opening reception was February 28th, 2026 but the show remains listed as current (not under "Past Exhibitions") as of this writing.
shows.description:
Brazilian artist Zé Tepedino's show spans Ysasi Gallery's West Adams space and the adjacent Espasso showroom, built around an immersive installation anchored by a 24-hour film shot during Carnival in Rio de Janeiro, layered with field-recorded sound from the city. It's less a conventional painting show than an environment: footage and audio running alongside studio works and pieces made on-site in Los Angeles, mixing film, installation, photography, and material experimentation.

The individual works on view — paintings and collages with titles like "Roxo," "Sol," and "Litoral" — read as fragments pulled from the same sensibility driving the film: color-saturated, loosely figurative, interested in beach culture, domestic objects, and the textures of everyday Brazilian life. Tepedino's own writing frames the show around the intimacy of shared secrets and chance encounters, and that conversational, unedited quality carries through the physical installation as well.

Given the collaboration with Espasso, a gallery devoted to Brazilian design, this is as much a cultural exchange project as a solo exhibition — a good opportunity to see contemporary Brazilian art and design in dialogue within a West Adams gallery not always associated with international programming.

shows.title: Men / Object Permanence
shows.dates_note: O-Town House's own site lists this under "Current" (home page nav: "Current --> Men / Object Permanence") with no opening or closing dates published; saved as on view now per the venue's own listing.
shows.description:
O-Town House's current presentation pairs two titles, Men and Object Permanence, announced together on a single gallery flyer and listed as the space's "Current" show. True to the apartment-gallery's longstanding format — exhibitions mounted inside founder Scott Cameron Weaver's own Granada Buildings residence — the hang unfolds across the home's domestic rooms rather than a conventional white cube, so works sit alongside furniture, windows, and the rhythms of a lived-in space.

The paired titles point toward two lines of inquiry rather than a single thesis: one keyed to questions of masculinity and the figure of "men" as subject, the other to object permanence, the idea that things (and perhaps feelings, or memories) persist even once they drop out of view. Read together, the pairing suggests a show interested in what endures and what is performed — bodies and objects both treated as evidence of something more lasting underneath.

As with many O-Town House presentations, detailed checklist and press information were not available ahead of a visit; the gallery's small, appointment-friendly scale rewards an in-person look more than a press release would. Visitors should expect an intimate, idiosyncratic hang typical of this project space's program rather than a conventional gallery install.
